edits.before:
Calibration is the work that makes measurements and commands refer to the same physical world. A camera pixel, depth value, joint encoder and motor command each has its own coordinate system, clock and error. A robot policy can learn around a stable bias; it cannot reliably absorb a transform that changes after every camera bump or a label stream shifted by a variable delay.

The useful unit is not one calibration file. It is a chain with a validation residual at every link: intrinsics, depth, camera-to-robot transform, robot kinematics, time alignment and actuator response.

Try the check below and choose the diagnostic that separates a fixed hand-eye error from random policy error.
edits.after: Robot calibration is the estimation of the parameters that make a robot's measurements and commands refer to the same physical world. Classical kinematic calibration has four steps: modeling, measurement, identification and correction <Cite id="roth-mooring-ravani-1987" />. A learning system adds cameras, depth, clocks and actuators to the chain.

A manipulation system carries <Term id="camera-intrinsics">camera intrinsics</Term>, depth alignment, camera extrinsics, joint zeroes and link parameters, tool and payload parameters, timestamps and latency, and actuator response. Each stage feeds the next. FoundationPose estimates and tracks novel-object poses with or without a model <Cite id="foundationpose-2024" />, yet a wrong hand-eye transform still sends the gripper to the wrong place. HALO first calibrates a humanoid's nominal model from real data, then identifies an unknown payload's mass distribution <Cite id="halo-payload-2026" />.

edits.before:
Intrinsics map pixels to rays. The core parameters are focal lengths, principal point and lens distortion. Zhang's planar-target method recovers them from several views of a flat pattern at unknown orientations, followed by nonlinear refinement <Cite id="zhang-2000-calibration" />. Its practical strength is that the target pose need not be measured.

Good calibration images cover the full field of view, vary distance and tilt, keep the target sharp, and avoid collecting many near-duplicate views. Report reprojection error and inspect its spatial pattern. A low mean can hide a bad corner of the image or a few dominant views.

Do not transfer intrinsics across a changed focus, resolution or crop without validation. Image resizing requires a corresponding scale of focal length and principal point. A model trained on undistorted images must receive the same transformation at deployment.
edits.after: Intrinsics map pixels to rays through focal lengths, principal point and lens distortion. Zhang's method recovers them from a planar pattern seen at a few unknown orientations, with a closed-form solution and nonlinear refinement <Cite id="zhang-2000-calibration" />. Kannala and Brandt's generic model covers conventional, wide-angle and fisheye lenses <Cite id="kannala-brandt-2006" />. AnyCalib estimates intrinsics from one in-the-wild image for pinhole, Brown-Conrady and Kannala-Brandt models <Cite id="anycalib-2025" />. Intrinsics need revalidation after any change of focus, resolution or crop.

edits.before:
Depth cameras do not produce uniformly accurate metric state. Stereo error grows with range, repetitive patterns create ambiguous matches, and low texture or specular surfaces can invalidate measurements. The RealSense tuning guide describes the distance-squared growth and the effects of scene texture and lighting <Cite id="realsense-tuning-2026" />. The D400 family datasheet documents false depth and saturation failure cases, so a single accuracy number would conceal these differences <Cite id="realsense-d400-datasheet-2026" />.

Calibrate depth scale against known distances across the operating range. Plot residual against range and image location. Measure invalid-pixel rate on the actual materials in the task. If color and depth sensors are separate, validate their registration after every resolution or firmware change.
edits.after: Stereo depth error scales with the square of distance, and repetitive structures make matches ambiguous <Cite id="realsense-tuning-2026" />. The D400 datasheet lists false depth from repetitive patterns and saturation from specular reflections <Cite id="realsense-d400-datasheet-2026" />. Kinect random error grows from a few millimeters to about 4 cm at maximum range <Cite id="khoshelham-kinect-2012" />, and a joint depth-color calibration with a depth-distortion model beat the manufacturer's calibration <Cite id="herrera-depth-color-2012" />. Learned camera depth models reach nearly simulation-level depth accuracy for manipulation <Cite id="camera-depth-models-2025" />.

edits.before: Hand-eye calibration solves the rigid relationship between camera motion and robot motion. For a wrist camera, the unknown is usually the transform from gripper to camera; for a fixed camera, it is base to camera. Shiu and Ahmad framed wrist-mounted sensor calibration as solving homogeneous transform equations of the form $AX = XB$ <Cite id="shiu-ahmad-1989" />; Tsai and Lenz gave the classic efficient solution <Cite id="tsai-lenz-1989" />.
edits.after: Hand-eye calibration finds the gripper-to-camera transform for a wrist camera, or base-to-camera for a fixed one. Shiu and Ahmad cast it as $AX = XB$ <Cite id="shiu-ahmad-1989" />. Tsai and Lenz's solution takes about ${}100 + 64N$ arithmetic operations for $N$ robot stations, and a few milliseconds <Cite id="tsai-lenz-1989" />. Park and Martin derived closed-form exact and least-squares solutions on the Euclidean group <Cite id="park-martin-1994" />, and Daniilidis solved rotation and translation together with dual quaternions <Cite id="daniilidis-1999" />. AprilTag targets give a full 6-DoF pose from one image <Cite id="apriltag-2011" />.

edits.before: The dataset needs rotational diversity. Motions around nearly one axis leave parts of the transform weakly constrained. Use many poses across the workspace, reject target detections with poor geometry, and hold out some poses to validate the solution.
edits.after: OpenCV needs at least two motions with non-parallel rotation axes, so three poses, and strongly recommends many more <Cite id="opencv-hand-eye-docs-2026" />. MoveIt's tutorial reports that accuracy plateaus after about 12 or 15 samples in most cases <Cite id="moveit-hand-eye-tutorial-2026" />. Validation belongs in robot coordinates, because reprojection error alone does not close that loop.

edits.before: Validate in the units the task cares about. Place the calibration target at several distances and orientations, transform its detected pose into the robot frame, and measure translation and rotation residuals. Then execute slow reaches to independent landmarks. Reprojection error alone does not close the robot-coordinate loop.
edits.after: Markerless methods now rival targets. DREAM's single-image accuracy is comparable to multi-frame offline calibration <Cite id="dream-2019" />. EasyHeC uses differentiable rendering and automatic joint-space exploration <Cite id="easyhec-2023" />, and Kalib needs only the kinematic chain and a tracked reference point <Cite id="kalib-2024" />. Hydra reaches 5 mm task-space accuracy against 7 mm for classical methods <Cite id="hydra-hand-eye-2025" />. DRHeC's authors report 88.9% grasp success on a UR5e, 46.3 points above EasyHeC <Cite id="drhec-2026" />.

edits.before:
Nominal link lengths and joint zeroes describe the design. Encoder offsets, compliance and tool mounting error can shift the assembled machine's end effector. The forward-kinematics model in [kinematics](/classical/kinematics) shows how each parameter contributes to the final pose <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />.

At minimum, define and verify the tool center point. Touch a fixed physical point from several tool orientations. If the estimated point moves, the tool transform is wrong. For higher accuracy, fit joint offsets and selected link parameters from external pose measurements, then validate on a held-out workspace grid.

Do not fit every possible parameter without an observability analysis. Flexible models can trade one incorrect link length against another and reproduce the calibration poses while extrapolating poorly.
edits.after: Manufacturing errors and joint compliance shift an assembled arm from its nominal [kinematics](/classical/kinematics) <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. A tool center point is checked by touching one fixed point from several orientations. Fitting every parameter without an observability check lets errors trade off. Nguyen and colleagues calibrated a humanoid from 31 chosen postures and cut RMS error 2.3-fold against the manufacturer's model <Cite id="humanoid-geometric-calibration-2025" />. OmniCalib found CAD wrist-camera extrinsics off by up to 10.56 mm and 1.74 degrees, and writes back only corrections its observability checks support <Cite id="omnicalib-2026" />.

edits.before:
Spatial calibration assumes simultaneous measurements. A camera frame at time $t$ paired with joint state at $t + \Delta t$ creates a pose error proportional to motion speed. At slow motion the system looks calibrated; at production speed it misses.

Use hardware timestamps where available. Record camera exposure time, robot-state time, command time and arrival time separately. Estimate offset by correlating a motion visible in both streams, such as a tracked tool moving through a known trajectory. Repeat under load because buffering and network transport can add variable latency.

For learned policies, perform alignment before forming observation-action pairs. A fixed temporal shift changes the apparent control law and can make a policy look temporally unstable.
edits.after: A camera frame at time $t$ paired with joint state at $t + \Delta t$ creates a pose error proportional to speed. Kalibr estimates time offsets jointly with spatial transforms, to a fraction of the smallest measurement period <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />. IEEE 1588 clock synchronization reaches sub-microsecond accuracy across networked devices <Cite id="ieee-1588-2019" />. On a RealSense D435 and Airbot Play rig, Realtime-VLA V2 measured camera, proprioception and motion delays of 55, 50 and 150 ms <Cite id="realtime-vla-v2-2026" />.

edits.before: Sim-to-real work often calls this system identification. Measure how commanded position, velocity or torque becomes realized motion. Fit latency, gains, friction and actuator response at the operating amplitudes and rates.
edits.after: Sim-to-real work calls this system identification. Atkeson, An and Hollerbach identified load and link inertial parameters by least squares, beating CAD-derived predictions <Cite id="atkeson-an-hollerbach-1986" />. Swevers and colleagues optimize finite-Fourier-series excitation for parameter uncertainty <Cite id="swevers-excitation-1997" />. Gaz and colleagues first identified the Franka Panda's dynamics, joint friction and feasible parameters <Cite id="gaz-panda-dynamics-2019" />.

edits.before:
Hwangbo and colleagues identified actuator-model error as a central transfer obstacle on ANYmal and learned an actuator network from real measurements to replace the inadequate analytic component <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />. This is calibration by residual learning: known rigid-body structure remains, while the hard actuator mapping is estimated from data.

Record both commands and measured response. A dataset that stores only the command cannot distinguish policy error from controller tracking error.
edits.after: Hwangbo and colleagues found actuator dynamics central to ANYmal's transfer gap and learned an actuator network from real measurements <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />. SPI-Active chooses identification data actively and beats baselines by 42 to 63% in locomotion transfer <Cite id="spi-active-2025" />. Bjelonic and colleagues transferred policies to 13 legged robots without randomizing dynamics <Cite id="bjelonic-sim2real-2025" />. A dataset that stores commands without measured response cannot separate policy error from tracking error.

edits.before:
Visual servoing closes the loop on image error and can reduce sensitivity to an imperfect global pose estimate. The task-function formulation uses the relationship between feature motion and camera motion to drive features toward a target <Cite id="espiau-1992" />.

It does not make calibration irrelevant. The interaction model, velocity command and safety geometry still need consistent conventions. It changes which errors become steady-state bias and which bend the path.
edits.after: Visual servoing puts the vision sensor inside the control loop and drives image features toward a target through a task function <Cite id="espiau-1992" />. Its interaction model, velocity commands and safety geometry still need consistent conventions.

edits.before:
Calibration is an operational asset. Store it with hardware serial numbers, camera settings, tool identity, software version, date, temperature where relevant, procedure and validation results. Define triggers for revalidation: camera remount, collision, tool change, firmware update, focus change or a residual crossing its threshold.

Build a short automated check that can run before data collection and evaluation. Fixed landmarks should transform into the robot frame within tolerance; timestamps should stay within a bound; commanded and measured motion should agree under a standard sequence.

Record the measured residuals, operating range and owner as the calibration output. That record helps distinguish a learner's failure from a disagreement between coordinates.
edits.after: Calibrations drift. DROID's per-session checkerboard calibrations were not always accurate, and the dataset provides camera-to-base calibrations for about 36,000 scenes <Cite id="droid-2024" />. Most public datasets lack extrinsics, and CalibAll recovered them for about 97,000 episodes across 16 datasets <Cite id="calib-all-2025" />. Each calibration should be stored with hardware serials, camera settings, tool, software version, date, procedure and residuals, and redone after a remount, collision, tool or firmware change.

edits.before:
Control is what makes a robot actually go where [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning) decides it should, in a world where the model is slightly wrong, the payload shifted, and the floor is never quite flat. The tool is feedback: measure where the robot is, compare it to where it should be, and correct. That loop runs at every level of the stack, from the motor current loops deep inside an actuator to the whole-body torque controller of a humanoid, and it keeps running underneath whatever learned policy sits on top.

Start with the simplest feedback law: correct the measured error, accumulate a persistent offset, and respond to how quickly the error changes. Those are the three actions in PID control. State feedback and constrained optimization ask what to do when that single-error loop is not enough.

The loop is below, on the smallest problem that still shows everything: an inverted pendulum with a payload bolted off-center. Guess first if you like, then press Run and drag the proportional gain to test it.
edits.after: Control is the use of feedback to make a robot follow a reference, such as a [motion plan](/classical/motion-planning), despite model error and disturbances: measure the state, compare it with the reference, and correct <Cite id="fbs-2020" />. Loops run at every level, from motor drivers to whole-body torque control, beneath any learned policy.

edits.before: Ziegler and Nichols described proportional response as valve movement proportional to the measured displacement; automatic reset moves the valve to eliminate a sustained offset; and pre-act adds movement proportional to the rate of pen movement <Cite id="ziegler-nichols-1942" />. In the equation above, these are the proportional, integral and derivative actions. For a constant disturbance in this lab, proportional action alone leaves an offset; integral action accumulates that residual error to remove it, while derivative action responds to the rate of change.
edits.after: Ziegler and Nichols described proportional response as valve movement proportional to the measured displacement, automatic reset as movement that eliminates a sustained offset, and pre-act as movement proportional to the rate of pen movement. These are the proportional, integral and derivative actions. Their 1942 tuning rules drive the loop into oscillation with proportional gain alone, then back off from the critical gain and period by fixed fractions <Cite id="ziegler-nichols-1942" />.

edits.before: Tuning those three gains is its own craft. The Ziegler-Nichols rules of 1942, drive the loop into oscillation with proportional gain alone, then back off from the critical gain and period by fixed fractions, are still printed in every textbook <Cite id="ziegler-nichols-1942" />. The failure modes are just as canonical: integral windup, where a saturated actuator lets the integrator accumulate error it can never repay, and derivative kick, where a setpoint step spikes the derivative term.
edits.after: Integral action gives zero steady-state error, so it removes the offset a constant disturbance leaves under proportional control. Under actuator saturation it needs anti-windup compensation to avoid integrator windup. Åström and Murray quote a survey in which 97% of over eleven thousand regulatory controllers in refining, chemicals and pulp and paper used PID <Cite id="fbs-2020" />.

Write a linear plant in state-space form, $\dot{x} = Ax + Bu$, and close the loop with $u = -Kx$: each state contributes to the control input. edits.after: The optimal gain is $K = R^{-1} B^{\top} P$, where $P$ solves the algebraic Riccati equation <Cite id="tedrake-underactuated" />:

edits.before:
That is the linear quadratic regulator. Two design knobs, $Q$ and $R$, replace per-gain intuition with a statement of what you care about: penalize angle deviation heavily and the controller gets stiff; penalize torque and it gets gentle. And the connection back is direct. Linearize the pendulum above, choose a diagonal $Q$ weighting angle and rate, and the LQR gain is a PD controller. The sliders you just moved were a hand-tuned version of what Riccati solves in one shot <Cite id="tedrake-underactuated" />.

The catch is in the word "linearized". LQR's guarantee is local to the operating point; swinging the pole up from hanging takes a different controller entirely (energy shaping), with LQR catching it at the top <Cite id="tedrake-underactuated" />. Real systems run a gain schedule: different $K$ for different regions of the state space.
edits.after: The weights $Q$ and $R$ state what matters: a heavy angle penalty stiffens the controller, and a torque penalty softens it. For the linearized pendulum with a diagonal $Q$ on angle and rate, the LQR gain is a PD controller. The guarantee is local: swinging the pole up from hanging takes an energy-shaping controller, with LQR catching it at the top <Cite id="tedrake-underactuated" />.

edits.after: <Term id="mpc">Model-predictive control</Term> solves a short-horizon optimal control problem at every control step, from the measured state and subject to the binding constraints <Cite id="mayne-2000" />:

edits.before: Then apply only the first input, measure the new state, and solve again. Each new solve corrects model error against the measured state. Torque limits, joint limits, and friction cones enter the optimization directly, where the solver can account for them before the control is applied. Making that rigorous took decades; the modern stability theory, terminal costs and constraint sets that guarantee the receding-horizon loop inherits the infinite-horizon optimum, was consolidated by Mayne and collaborators in 2000 <Cite id="mayne-2000" />.
edits.after:
Only the first input is applied before the next solve, so feedback absorbs part of the model error, and torque limits, joint limits and friction cones enter the optimization directly. Mayne and collaborators consolidated the stability theory in 2000: the online finite-horizon problem equals an infinite-horizon problem, exactly or in modified form, so infinite-horizon advantages carry over <Cite id="mayne-2000" />.

MPC grew out of 1970s and 1980s power-plant and refinery practice, where slow, constrained, multivariable plants defeated PID <Cite id="garcia-1989" /><Cite id="qin-badgwell-2003" />. A mid-1999 vendor survey counted more than 4,600 applications, concentrated in refining and petrochemicals <Cite id="qin-badgwell-2003" />. Di Carlo and colleagues ran convex MPC on the MIT Cheetah 3 as a single rigid body with contact forces as decision variables. Horizons reached half a second, each QP took under a millisecond at 20 to 30 Hz, and one gain set served every gait from standing to gallop <Cite id="di-carlo-2018" />.

edits.before: The industrial lineage is older than the theory. MPC grew out of power-plant and petroleum-refinery practice in the 1970s and 1980s, where slow, constrained, multivariable plants were exactly what PID could not handle <Cite id="qin-badgwell-2003" />; by 2003 a vendor survey counted thousands of installed applications, still concentrated in refining and petrochemicals <Cite id="qin-badgwell-2003" />. What changed since is compute. Di Carlo and colleagues put convex MPC on the MIT Cheetah 3 by simplifying the robot to a single rigid body with contact forces as decision variables: prediction horizons up to half a second, each QP solved in under a millisecond, replanned 20-30 times per second, one set of gains for every gait from standing to gallop <Cite id="di-carlo-2018" />. And in 2026, Zhang and collaborators showed the simplification is no longer forced: plain iLQR with MuJoCo dynamics and finite-difference derivatives runs whole-body MPC in real time on quadrupeds and a full-size humanoid, transferring to hardware with few sim-to-real accommodations <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />. The standing assumption that full-order MPC is too slow for legged robots no longer holds, and the debate between MPC and learned policies has its own module in [reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc).
edits.after: Full-order MPC has run on legged hardware for a decade. Koenemann and colleagues applied whole-body MPC in real time on the HRP-2 humanoid in 2015, the first such controller on a complex dynamic robot by their account <Cite id="koenemann-2015" />. Neunert and colleagues ran whole-body nonlinear MPC through contacts on a quadruped at up to 190 Hz with a half-second horizon <Cite id="neunert-2018" />. DIAL-MPC optimizes full-order quadruped dynamics in real time without training and beats RL policies by 50% on climbing tasks <Cite id="dial-mpc-2024" />. Zhang and colleagues offer an easy-to-reproduce baseline: iLQR with MuJoCo dynamics and finite-difference derivatives, running whole-body MPC on quadrupeds and a full-sized humanoid with few sim-to-real considerations <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />. [Reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) compares it with learned policies.

edits.before: Below the planner and the MPC layer sits the fastest loop in a legged or humanoid robot: the whole-body controller, which turns desired accelerations and contact forces into joint torques hundreds to thousands of times per second. Khatib's operational-space formulation from 1987 writes the dynamics at the end-effector, in task space <Cite id="khatib-1987" />:

The modern implementation collapses that hierarchy into one quadratic program per control tick:

Sentis and Khatib extended it to a task hierarchy, so a humanoid guarantees contact and joint-limit constraints first, then balance and reaching tasks, while posture fills the remaining <Term id="degrees-of-freedom">degrees of freedom</Term> <Cite id="sentis-khatib-2005" />. A position-controlled, non-backdrivable geared arm cannot regulate contact force at all: it has no force channel, so the contact force is set by the position error, the gear ratio, and whatever the surface does, which is to say by nothing the controller commanded. seeAlso: - "data-hardware/datasets" - "manipulation/cross-embodiment" - "world-models/generative-sim" --- import { GraspWrenchLab } from '@/components/interactive/grasp-wrench-lab'; Grasp planning is the discipline that answers from geometry whether a grasp will hold: where to put the contacts, how hard to squeeze, and how to know before lifting that the grasp will survive the task. Every act of manipulation ends the same way: some part of the robot touches some part of the world, and the physics of that interface decides what happens next. [Kinematics](/classical/kinematics) can place the fingers and [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning) can route the arm, and [perception](/classical/perception) is what hands this module the known object pose in the robot's frame that every wrench computation below starts from. But once the fingers close, the question is mechanical. Will this hold, or will the object slip? The answer turns out to be a convex polytope. Map everything the contacts can do into a space of forces and moments, take a convex hull, and ask whether the origin sits inside it. That one geometric fact, force closure, organizes most of classical grasp theory, and the distance from the origin to the hull's boundary became the field's standard quality metric. ## The wrench space, live The lab below is that polytope. A square object, contacts sliding along its perimeter, and the hull of everything they can do plotted beside it with the origin marked. Drag the friction coefficient slider from 0.7 down toward zero and watch the hull shrink until the origin falls outside it: that is the grasp failing. The rest of this module derives what you are looking at. ## Contact models
A contact model says which forces a fingertip can transmit. The simplest is the frictionless point contact: it pushes along the surface normal and nothing else. Real fingers have friction, and the standard point contact with friction obeys Coulomb's law: the tangential component of the contact force can grow to at most a fixed fraction $\mu$ of the normal component before the contact starts to slide . $$ \lVert f^t \rVert \le \mu \, f^n $$ Geometrically, the admissible forces form a cone around the inward normal, the friction cone, with half-angle $\alpha = \arctan \mu$ . In the plane the cone is a wedge bounded by two edge rays; in three dimensions it is a quadratic cone, usually approximated by a polyhedral one so the analysis stays linear. A soft-finger contact adds one more channel: a torsional moment about the contact normal, bounded by a torsional coefficient times the normal load, which models the small contact patch of a real fingertip . One choice comes before any of this analysis: what kind of grasp you want at all. Cutkosky's taxonomy separates power grasps, which wrap the object and trade dexterity for stability, from precision grasps, which hold the object with the fingertips and trade stability for the ability to reorient it . The mechanics below applies to both, but the wrench budget a task demands depends heavily on which style you picked. ## The grasp wrench space A force applied at a contact point does two things to the object: it pushes the center of mass, and it twists. Package both into one vector, the wrench. For a contact at position $r_i$ applying force $f_i$ about the object's reference frame, the wrench is the force stacked over its moment: $$ w_i = \begin{bmatrix} f_i \\ r_i \times f_i \end{bmatrix} $$ In the plane this is a three-vector $(f_x, f_y, \tau)$ with $\tau = r_x f_y - r_y f_x$. Every admissible contact force maps to a point in wrench space, and since a grasp's contacts act simultaneously, the net wrench the grasp can produce is the Minkowski sum of what each contact can produce. Friction cones are convex, so the sum is a convex hull: the grasp wrench space is the convex hull of the primitive wrenches, the wrenches along the cone edges at unit normal force . $$ \mathcal{W} = \operatorname{conv}\left\{ w_{ij} \right\}, \qquad w_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix} n_i \pm \mu \, t_i \\ r_i \times (n_i \pm \mu \, t_i) \end{bmatrix} $$ This construction is the whole trick. Questions about contact forces, which live on separate fingertips and interact through friction inequalities, become questions about one polytope. ## Force closure A grasp has force closure when it can resist any externally applied wrench: push the object in any direction, twist it either way, and some feasible combination of contact forces inside the friction cones cancels the disturbance. In wrench space, resisting any direction means the hull must surround the zero wrench from every side. Force closure holds exactly when the origin lies strictly inside the grasp wrench hull : $$ \exists \, \varepsilon > 0 : \quad B_\varepsilon(0) \subset \mathcal{W} $$ The strictness is load-bearing. An origin resting exactly on the hull's boundary means there is a wrench the grasp cannot quite resist, and since the task gets to choose the disturbance, "almost everywhere" is a failure mode, not a pass. This is why friction does so much work in practice. Without friction, the cone collapses to the normal ray, and the hull has no volume to spare: form closure, closure by geometry alone, demands at least four contacts in the plane and seven in space. That lower bound is older than robotics: Reuleaux stated it in 1875 and Somoff in 1897, as Markenscoff, Ni, and Papadimitriou recount on their way to the matching sufficiency results. Four contacts achieve form closure for any planar object with a piecewise smooth boundary, a circle being the one exception, and in space twelve contacts suffice for any object without rotational symmetry, with seven enough under very general conditions . Mishra, Schwartz, and Sharir supplied the algorithmic side: tight finger-count bounds for each equilibrium case of a frictionless grip, and linear-time synthesis of such grips on polyhedral objects . Friction relaxes all of this: with point contacts with friction, three contacts are necessary and sufficient in the plane and four in space . The cleanest sufficient condition in the whole theory is Nguyen's antipodal grasp theorem: a planar two-fingered grasp with frictional contacts is force closure if and only if the line connecting the two contact points lies inside both friction cones . The proof sketch is worth keeping: either contact can lay off any force in the wedge where the two cones overlap, the partner squeezes harder along the shared line to absorb the excess, and because the line is interior the cone edges supply torques of both signs about the center. This is the theorem a parallel-jaw gripper runs every time it pinches opposite sides of a box, and its strictness is visible in hardware: grasp the box too close to an edge of the cone and a light sideways nudge slides it out. ## Grasp quality: the epsilon metric Force closure is binary, while the disturbance a closed grasp can absorb before contact saturation varies. Ferrari and Canny turned the hull geometry into a number: the quality $\varepsilon$ is the radius of the largest ball centered at the origin that still fits inside the grasp wrench space . $$ \varepsilon = \min_{F_k \in \partial \mathcal{W}} \; \operatorname{dist}\!\left( 0, F_k \right) $$ Because the hull is a polytope, the largest inscribed ball touches a facet, so $\varepsilon$ is just the distance from the origin to the nearest hull facet. The unit-normal-force convention makes it concrete: $\varepsilon$ is the worst-case disturbance wrench, per unit of normal force at the contacts, that the grasp guarantees it can absorb. Roa and Suárez review quality measures based on contact locations and hand configuration, illustrating their behavior with simple examples without recommending a universally best measure. For the largest-minimum resisted wrench criterion, they identify two choices that affect its value: the origin used to compute torques, and the metric that scales torques relative to forces. They also distinguish a shared total-force limit from independent per-finger limits; a grasp optimal under one constraint need not be optimal under the other. Most of their analysis is quasi-static. Those choices and the task assumptions need to accompany interpretation of the reported value . ## Reading the hull Read the lab above as mechanics. On the left is the object with each contact's friction cone. On the right is the grasp wrench space projected from $(f_x, f_y, \tau)$: the hull of the primitive cone-edge wrenches. The origin ring is green exactly when the grasp is force closure, and the readout reports $\varepsilon$. The default tripod of top, right, and bottom contacts is force closure at $\mu = 0.7$. Remove the third contact and the remaining pair, one on the top edge and one on the right, fails Nguyen's test: the line between them sits at 45 degrees to each normal while the cones open only $\arctan 0.7 \approx 35$ degrees, and the hull collapses onto the origin. Now slide contact 2 down onto the bottom edge, opposite contact 1. The pair becomes antipodal, the connecting line is the shared normal, and the hull re-inflates around the origin for any positive friction at all. Finally, drag $\mu$ down and watch $\varepsilon$ fall: the metric is pricing the friction you just removed. ## Where this meets the learned stack Dex-Net 2.0 uses analytic grasp metrics to label synthetic training data. The paper reports 6.7 million training datapoints drawn from 1,500 3D object models; it also describes over 6.7 million aligned grasp images. These are synthetic training examples, with no count of physical trials or necessarily distinct scene views. A positive training label requires expected epsilon quality above 0.002 and no modeled collision with the object or table. The expected quality accounts for uncertainty in object pose, gripper pose, and friction. The GQ-CNN consumes a grasp-aligned depth crop and the gripper depth relative to the camera, and predicts robustness under this binary success model. It does not regress the raw epsilon score. The paper’s label threshold does not apply to the lab above . The basic planner samples antipodal parallel-jaw candidates from depth-image gradients, ranks them with the GQ-CNN, and executes the highest-ranked candidate that is reachable and does not collide with the table. Its stated assumptions are isolated rigid objects on a planar worksurface and a single-view depth image; synthetic dataset generation additionally assumes known gripper geometry and camera intrinsics. The physical benchmark used an ABB YuMi with custom silicone fingertips and a Primesense Carmine 1.08 camera. A grasp counted as successful only if it held the object after lifting, transporting, and shaking . For the eight known, 3D-printed adversarial objects, Dex-Net 2.0 reports 93% success for GQ-L-Adv over 80 trials, ten per object. GQ-L-Adv was initialized from the model trained on the large synthetic dataset and then fine-tuned on synthetic examples of those adversarial objects. A separate, CEM-augmented experiment ran 100 trials on 40 novel household objects, including articulated and deformable objects: it reported 94% success overall and 99% precision, with 68 successes among 69 grasps classified as robust. Here precision is success among grasps whose estimated robustness exceeds 50%; overall success and synthetic classification accuracy are different measures. These results come from separate physical evaluations, so they cannot be pooled into one success rate . Missing depth on thin parts and object collisions remained observed failure modes . That pattern generalizes. Modern learned manipulation, including the [diffusion policies](/manipulation/diffusion-policy) covered in the manipulation modules, rarely re-derives contact mechanics; it learns from data what the classical theory says a good contact looks like, and it inherits the theory's failure modes when it strays from the data. And the reason grasping resists the [sim-to-real recipe that conquered locomotion](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion) is precisely the physics of this module: millimeter-accurate contact geometry and friction coefficients are what simulators approximate worst. The classical stack, [kinematics](/classical/kinematics) through [control](/classical/control), ends here, at the interface where the robot finally touches the world.

A differentiable estimator later made force closure an optimization objective that tests closure within milliseconds for arbitrary hands . ## Grasp quality: the epsilon metric Ferrari and Canny turned the binary test into a number: the quality $\varepsilon$ is the radius of the largest origin-centered ball inside the grasp wrench space . $$ \varepsilon = \min_{F_k \in \partial \mathcal{W}} \; \operatorname{dist}\!\left( 0, F_k \right) $$ Because the hull is a polytope, $\varepsilon$ is the distance from the origin to its nearest facet . Kirkpatrick, Mishra and Yap formalized this inscribed-ball notion of grasp efficiency with a quantitative Steinitz theorem . With an $l$-edge polyhedral cone, $\varepsilon$ is an approximation, and Pokorny and Kragic proved it Lipschitz-continuous in the grasp parameters . Under unit normal force, $\varepsilon$ is the worst-case disturbance the grasp absorbs per unit of contact force, under the nominal friction model. In FIRMGrasp's tests, 53% of nominally force-closed grasps lost closure in the adverse friction tail . In a shake test, the nominal margin ranked a successful grasp above a failed one with probability only 0.53 . In most cases the grasp most robust to pose error is not the one with the highest $\varepsilon$ . Predicting grasp stability well required a combination of metrics . Li and Sastry's task-oriented measure models tasks as ellipsoids in wrench space . Borst, Fischer and Hirzinger trace most metrics' drawbacks to mixing force and torque dimensions . Roa and Suárez review measures based on contact locations and hand configuration and show that the largest-minimum resisted wrench depends on the torque origin and on the force-torque metric. A grasp optimal under a shared total-force limit need not be optimal under per-finger limits, and most of their analysis is quasi-static . FRoGGeR's min-weight metric approximates $\varepsilon$ differentiably and synthesizes grasps in a median 0.834 s . ## Reading the hull The lab draws the object with each contact's friction cone beside the grasp wrench space projected from $(f_x, f_y, \tau)$. The origin ring turns green under force closure, and the readout reports $\varepsilon$. The default tripod of top, right and bottom contacts is force closure at $\mu = 0.7$. Without the bottom contact, the top-right pair's connecting line sits 45 degrees from each normal, outside cones of half-angle $\arctan 0.7 \approx 35$ degrees, so it fails Nguyen's test . Sliding contact 2 onto the bottom edge makes the pair antipodal and restores closure for any positive friction. Lowering $\mu$ lowers $\varepsilon$. ## Where this meets the learned stack Dex-Net 2.0 labels synthetic data with analytic metrics: 6.7 million datapoints from 1,500 object models, positive when expected $\varepsilon$ under object-pose, gripper-pose and friction uncertainty exceeds 0.002 and no collision is modeled. Its GQ-CNN takes a grasp-aligned depth crop and the gripper depth, and predicts robustness without regressing $\varepsilon$ . The planner samples antipodal parallel-jaw candidates from depth gradients and executes the most robust [reachable](/classical/kinematics), [collision-free](/classical/motion-planning) one. It assumes isolated rigid objects on a planar worksurface and one depth camera with known intrinsics. On an ABB YuMi with silicone fingertips and a Primesense Carmine 1.08, a success meant the object stayed held through lifting, transport and shaking . On eight 3D-printed adversarial objects, GQ-L-Adv, fine-tuned on synthetic examples of them, succeeded in 93% of 80 trials. A separate CEM-augmented run of 100 trials on 40 novel household objects, including articulated and deformable ones, reported 94% success and 99% precision: 68 of 69 grasps rated above 50% robustness succeeded. The two evaluations cannot be pooled, and missing depth on thin parts and object collisions remained failure modes . Dex-Net 4.0 cleared bins of up to 25 novel objects with over 95% reliability at more than 300 mean picks per hour . GraspNet-1Billion scores over one billion grasp poses on 97,280 RGB-D images by analytic computation , and DexGraspNet 2.0 holds 427 million grasps . NVIDIA's GraspGen labels over 53 million grasps by simulating a shaking motion in Isaac . GraspGen-X conditions a diffusion grasp generator on a swept-volume encoding of the gripper; trained on procedural grippers and 2 billion grasps, it generalized zero-shot to novel real grippers . Learned [diffusion policies](/manipulation/diffusion-policy) take contacts from data, yet dexterous data pipelines still solve contact mechanics. BODex approximates friction cones with 8-vertex pyramids and synthesizes over 49 grasps per second on one RTX 3090 GPU . DexEvolve's authors note that analytic synthesis needs simplifying assumptions that yield infeasible grasps, which must be filtered in high-fidelity simulation . A 2026 [controller](/classical/control) enforces the quality margin during execution, keeping a median 94% of it at 0.09 ms per solve . [Sim-to-real transfer](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion) remained hard for dexterous grasping: Get a Grip found most multi-finger methods degrading on hardware . DexGraspNet 2.0 transferred zero-shot to real clutter at 90.7% success , and RobustDexGrasp, trained in simulation, reached 94.6% on 512 real objects . GraspVLA pretrains on SynGrasp-1B, a billion-frame synthetic dataset , and DexGraspVLA reports over 90% success in thousands of unseen cluttered scenes . Adding wrench and tactile feedback to vision raised one policy from 14 to 24 successes in 25 real trials . GENESIS-Handover, from Marco Hutter (ETH Zurich) and colleagues (October 2026), chooses how a robot presents an object by matching generated task-specific grips to the person's live hand . On a legged manipulator, handovers needing no adjustment rose from 6 to 16 of 60 against AFT-Handover .

seeAlso: - "manipulation/cross-embodiment" - "data-hardware/teleop-rigs" --- import { PlanarFkArm } from '@/components/interactive/planar-fk-arm'; import { DhParameterTable } from '@/components/mdx/dh-parameter-table'; Kinematics is the geometry of a robot's motion, studied without modelling its forces or torques. Joint angles and link lengths determine where the end of an arm lands. Simulators integrate dynamics on top of a kinematic chain, teleoperation rigs map an operator's hand through one, and learned manipulation policies eventually emit commands in the robot's coordinates. Two directions dominate. Forward kinematics takes joint angles and computes the end-effector pose. Inverse kinematics asks the reverse question: which joint angles place the end effector here? The first direction is a plain composition of transforms, cheap and unique. The second is a nonlinear inverse problem that can have no solution, one solution, or many. Most of the classical machinery, and most of this module, concerns that asymmetry. In the arm lab below, move the base joint slider and watch every downstream link move with it. Then try to put the fingertip at a chosen point using the sliders alone. That is the inverse problem.
## Forward kinematics A serial arm is a chain: a fixed base, then alternating rigid links and joints. Attach a coordinate frame to each link at its joint. Each joint contributes one rigid transform from the frame below it to the frame above it, parameterized by the joint variable, and multiplying the transforms in order carries the base frame to the tool frame. A rigid transform packages a rotation $R$ and a translation $p$ into one matrix: $$ T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ The forward-kinematics map is the ordered product, one factor per joint: $$ T_0^{n}(q) = T_0^1(q_1)\,T_1^2(q_2)\,\cdots\,T_{n-1}^{n}(q_n) $$ Evaluating it costs $n$ matrix multiplications. The map is deterministic and smooth in the joint angles, and one evaluation is cheap enough to run inside every control cycle. That is the entire forward problem . In the plane the product collapses into something you can watch. Each link is a vector of length $l_i$ pointing along the cumulative angle $q_1 + \cdots + q_i$, and the end-effector position is the running sum of those vectors: $$ x = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l_i \cos\left(q_1 + \cdots + q_i\right) \qquad y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l_i \sin\left(q_1 + \cdots + q_i\right) $$ The arm at the top of this module evaluates exactly that expression: three revolute joints, each angle measured relative to its parent link. Keep the downstream dependence in mind; it is the seed of the Jacobian. ## Denavit-Hartenberg parameters The transform product answers the question once the frames are fixed, but the frames still need assigning. LaValle describes the Denavit-Hartenberg convention for a chain connected by revolute joints using four parameters: an offset along a rotation axis, an angle about that axis, the distance between successive rotation axes, and the angle between those axes . His notation is $d_i$, $\theta_i$, $a_{i-1}$ and $\alpha_{i-1}$; the page's distance-definition sentence instead writes $a_i$. Frame assignment and transform order matter: the matrix below defines the convention used for this example, rather than reproducing LaValle's matrix. The per-joint transform is a fixed sequence of four elementary motions, rotation about $z$, translation along $z$, translation along $x$, rotation about $x$: $$ A_i = \mathrm{Rot}_z(\theta_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_z(d_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_x(a_i)\,\mathrm{Rot}_x(\alpha_i) $$ $$ \def\arraystretch{0.9} A_i = \begin{bmatrix} R_i & t_i \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad t_i = \begin{bmatrix} a_i\cos\theta_i \\ a_i\sin\theta_i \\ d_i \end{bmatrix} $$ $$ \def\arraystretch{0.9} R_i = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i & -\sin\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & \sin\theta_i\sin\alpha_i \\ \sin\theta_i & \cos\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & -\cos\theta_i\sin\alpha_i \\ 0 & \sin\alpha_i & \cos\alpha_i \end{bmatrix} $$ For the planar arm above the table is short. All motion stays in one plane, so every twist and offset is zero, and the whole chain reduces to three link lengths and three angles. This represents the inter-link geometry with four parameters. It has costs. Frame assignment is fiddly, and the parameters become ill-conditioned: as two consecutive joint axes drift toward parallel, the common normal they define can vary wildly with small changes in the axes' orientation, so a small mechanical change can jump a table entry. The product-of-exponentials formulation avoids that ill-conditioning by describing each joint as a screw about a fixed axis, and it is the treatment Modern Robotics uses throughout . The output of either notation is the same transform product; the convention is a choice of bookkeeping. The 3D playground reads the SO-101 chain directly from its URDF, a tree of links and joints where each joint carries an origin transform and a rotation axis . ## The Jacobian Forward kinematics maps angles to pose. The Jacobian is the derivative of that map: the linear relation between joint velocities and end-effector velocity, $$ \dot{x} = J(q)\,\dot{q} $$ with one column per joint. For revolute joint $i$ with axis $z_i$ located at $p_i$, the column is the cross product of the axis with the vector from the joint to the end effector, stacked above the axis itself; a prismatic joint contributes its axis directly: $$ J_i = \begin{bmatrix} z_i \times (p_\mathrm{ee} - p_i) \\ z_i \end{bmatrix} $$ The same matrix does double duty in statics: the transpose maps a wrench at the end effector to the joint torques that balance it, $\tau = J^{T}(q)\,F$. Velocities map one way through $J$, forces the other way through $J^{T}$ . The Jacobian depends on configuration, and it can lose rank. When the arm is fully extended, or when joint axes line up, columns become dependent and the velocity map stops covering every task-space direction. Those configurations are singularities. Near one, a modest end-effector speed can demand arbitrarily large joint speeds, because the inverse of a nearly rank-deficient matrix blows up. Any velocity-level controller has to say what happens there. Whitney's resolved motion rate control gave the classical answer in 1969: the operator commands desired hand motion along axes relevant to the task ; the classical rate-control relations then invert the Jacobian to obtain joint rates, $$ \dot{q} = J^{-1}(q)\,\dot{x} $$ or, when the arm is redundant and $J$ is not square, use the pseudoinverse $J^{+} = J^{T}(JJ^{T})^{-1}$, whose extra degrees of freedom can absorb secondary objectives such as staying away from joint limits. The idea turned the Jacobian from a descriptive quantity into a control law, and it is still the skeleton of most task-space controllers. ## Inverse kinematics Inverse kinematics asks for the preimage: given a target $x_d$, find $q$ with $k(q) = x_d$. Three facts make it hard. The map $k$ is nonlinear in $q$, so no single matrix inversion applies. It is many-to-one where it is onto: a point inside the workspace is usually reachable with several distinct configurations, elbow left or elbow right, and a redundant arm reaches the same pose through a continuum of postures. And it is not onto everywhere: targets outside the workspace have no solution at all, and a solver should say so rather than pretend otherwise. Closed-form solutions exist for special geometries, most famously six-revolute arms whose last three axes intersect at the wrist, but the general tool is iterative: linearize around the current configuration, take a step, repeat, $$ \Delta x = J(q)\,\Delta q \qquad \Delta q = J^{+}(q)\,\Delta x $$ Explore the SO-101 arm in the [3D kinematics playground](/playground): joint sliders for forward kinematics, click-to-reach targets for inverse kinematics, and a live residual and iteration count in the HUD. The arm model comes from TheRobotStudio's SO-ARM100 project . ## The same geometry, inside learned policies It is fair to ask how much of this matters once policies learn end to end. The learned part still lives inside the kinematic structure, in practice. [Action chunking](/manipulation/action-chunking) with ACT predicts continuous joint-space targets, fourteen dimensions across two 6-DoF arms and their grippers . GR00T's recent releases shifted to a shared relative end-effector action space so that human hand data and robot grippers live in one frame, a coordinate choice with direct consequences for what pretraining data is usable . Simulators integrate a kinematic chain under their dynamics either way, teleoperation rigs still retarget human motion into joint space, and a residual policy trained on top of a classical controller inherits its coordinate system. The policies changed who picks the numbers. They did not change what the numbers mean. Forward kinematics multiplies transforms in order. Inverse kinematics searches for joint angles that reach a target. Planning, control, and learning use both operations. ## Treat coordinate frames as an API The learned and classical stacks meet at a coordinate contract. A Cartesian policy output is incomplete until it names the reference frame, translation units, rotation representation, composition order and whether the command is absolute or relative. A joint-space output needs the joint ordering, sign convention, limits and controller interpretation. Shape agreement is not semantic agreement: the dataset, policy, controller and robot must interpret a command as the same physical motion. Make that contract executable. Round-trip known poses through forward and inverse kinematics, verify frame transforms against measured calibration targets, and test commands at workspace and singularity boundaries. Record the URDF and calibration versions beside every dataset and checkpoint. The [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) covers how those transforms are estimated; the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces) covers how a policy should expose them. When a learned policy fails after a robot or camera change, this boundary is the first place to test.

Forward kinematics maps joint angles to the end-effector pose, a unique composition of transforms. Inverse kinematics maps a pose back to joint angles and can have no solution, one, or many .
## Forward kinematics A serial arm is a chain of rigid links and joints, with a coordinate frame on each link. A rigid transform packs a rotation $R$ and a translation $p$ into one matrix : $$ T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ The ordered product of one transform per joint carries the base frame to the tool frame : $$ T_0^{n}(q) = T_0^1(q_1)\,T_1^2(q_2)\,\cdots\,T_{n-1}^{n}(q_n) $$ The map is a product of $n$ joint transforms, smooth in the joint angles and cheap to evaluate . In the plane, each link is a vector of length $l_i$ along the cumulative angle, and the end effector sits at their sum : $$ x = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l_i \cos\left(q_1 + \cdots + q_i\right) \qquad y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l_i \sin\left(q_1 + \cdots + q_i\right) $$ Moving one joint moves every later link, the dependence the Jacobian captures . ## Denavit-Hartenberg parameters Denavit and Hartenberg's 1955 matrix notation describes the kinematics of all lower-pair mechanisms . LaValle gives the Denavit-Hartenberg convention four parameters per revolute joint: an offset along a rotation axis, an angle about it, the distance between successive axes, and the angle between them . LaValle writes them $d_i$, $\theta_i$, $a_{i-1}$ and $\alpha_{i-1}$; the example here uses $a_i$ and $\alpha_i$. Standard and modified variants coexist, and Corke factors a string of elementary motions into either . The standard form is : $$ A_i = \mathrm{Rot}_z(\theta_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_z(d_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_x(a_i)\,\mathrm{Rot}_x(\alpha_i) $$ $$ \def\arraystretch{0.9} A_i = \begin{bmatrix} R_i & t_i \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad t_i = \begin{bmatrix} a_i\cos\theta_i \\ a_i\sin\theta_i \\ d_i \end{bmatrix} $$ $$ \def\arraystretch{0.9} R_i = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i & -\sin\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & \sin\theta_i\sin\alpha_i \\ \sin\theta_i & \cos\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & -\cos\theta_i\sin\alpha_i \\ 0 & \sin\alpha_i & \cos\alpha_i \end{bmatrix} $$ A planar arm has zero twists and offsets, leaving link lengths and angles . DH parameters are ill-conditioned when consecutive axes are nearly parallel . Product-of-exponentials (POE) parameters vary smoothly as the axes change, removing DH's ad hoc singularity fixes . POE, which Brockett applied to manipulators in 1984, treats each joint as a screw about a fixed axis, the form Modern Robotics uses . The 3D playground reads the SO-101 chain from its URDF, where each joint carries an origin transform and a rotation axis . URDF is the most common description format, yet a dataset of 322 URDF files held only 195 unique robots . ## The Jacobian The Jacobian relates joint velocities to end-effector velocity, one column per joint : $$ \dot{x} = J(q)\,\dot{q} $$ In Modern Robotics' space Jacobian, column $i$ is joint $i$'s screw axis at the current pose, in base-frame coordinates . A revolute joint with unit axis $\omega_i$ through point $p_i$ gives the first form; a prismatic joint sliding along unit direction $v_i$ gives the second : $$ J_i = \begin{bmatrix} \omega_i \\ -\omega_i \times p_i \end{bmatrix} \qquad J_i = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ v_i \end{bmatrix} $$ The transpose maps an end-effector wrench to balancing joint torques, $\tau = J^{T}(q)\,F$ . At singularities, such as a fully extended arm, the Jacobian loses rank, and nearby a modest end-effector speed demands unbounded joint speeds . Yoshikawa's 1985 manipulability measure scores how well an arm can position and orient its end effector . Whitney's resolved motion rate control (1969) let an operator command hand motion along task axes , with the inverse Jacobian giving joint rates: $$ \dot{q} = J^{-1}(q)\,\dot{x} $$ A redundant arm uses the pseudoinverse $J^{+} = J^{T}(JJ^{T})^{-1}$, whose spare freedom can serve goals such as avoiding joint limits . Siciliano and Slotine's 1991 task-priority framework manages such goals alongside the end-effector task . Near singular points, Nakamura and Hanafusa's singularity-robust inverse returns a motion close to the desired path . ## Inverse kinematics Inverse kinematics seeks $q$ with $k(q) = x_d$ for a target $x_d$. The map is nonlinear: a reachable target can have several configurations, such as elbow left or right, a redundant arm has a continuum, and an unreachable target has none . Closed forms exist for special geometries, such as six-revolute arms with intersecting wrist axes . A general 6R arm reduces to one minimum-degree polynomial in a single joint variable , which Manocha and Canny's 1994 algorithm solved in 11 ms on average on an IBM RS/6000 workstation . Diankov's IKFast generates closed-form solvers that answer in about 6 microseconds, against about 10 milliseconds for most numerical solvers . The general tool is iterative: linearize, step, repeat : $$ \Delta x = J(q)\,\Delta q \qquad \Delta q = J^{+}(q)\,\Delta x $$ KDL's pseudoinverse solver repeatedly reports false failures on humanoids, and TRAC-IK finds solutions much more often . cuRobo solves over 7,000 collision-free IK queries per second , and PyRoki reports running 1.4 to 1.7 times faster than cuRobo's IK . For redundant arms, IKFlow samples 2,000 solutions in under 10 ms, within 10 mm and 2 degrees of exact . The [3D kinematics playground](/playground) solves IK on TheRobotStudio's SO-101 arm with a live residual and iteration count . ## The same geometry, inside learned policies [Action chunking](/manipulation/action-chunking) with ACT predicts 14 joint-space targets for two 6-DoF arms and their grippers . OpenVLA predicts 7-dimensional single-arm end-effector actions . Diffusion Policy did consistently better with position than velocity actions . Across 13,000+ real rollouts and 500+ models, delta actions consistently helped, joint space favored stability, and task space favored generalization . In vision-based reinforcement learning for picking and pushing, joint velocity beat three other action spaces for smoothness and final performance . GR00T N1 uses embodiment-specific action decoders. In its simulation benchmarks, a Panda arm acts in relative end-effector position and rotation, and the GR-1 humanoid in joint positions . N1.6 predicts state-relative chunks for most embodiments; NVIDIA reports smoother, more accurate motion than with absolute actions, but error accumulation on small datasets . NVIDIA says N1.7 shares one relative end-effector action space across robot and human data . Quaternions and Euler angles are discontinuous and hard for networks to learn, while 5D and 6D rotation representations are continuous . Teleoperation runs through the same chain: a GELLO leader copies its target arm's kinematic structure . Retargeting artifacts such as foot sliding significantly reduce the robustness of humanoid tracking policies . ## Treat coordinate frames as an API A Cartesian action must name its frame, units, rotation representation, composition order, and whether it is absolute or relative; a joint action needs joint order, signs, limits and controller semantics. ROS REP 103 makes frames right-handed, with x forward, y left and z up, and lists quaternions first, as compact and free of singularities . REP 105 separates the drifting `odom` frame from the `map` frame, which can jump . ROS built tf because developers often misapplied transforms . Round-trip kinematics tests and versioned URDF and calibration files keep the contract testable. LeRobot calibrates SO-101 leader and follower arms to read the same values in the same pose, so a network trained on one robot works on another . See the [calibration guide](/classical/calibration) and the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces).

Motion planning is finding a route from the robot's current configuration to a goal without collisions. [Kinematics](/classical/kinematics) gives the arm's pose for a set of joint angles; planning finds a sequence of configurations worth executing. A learned policy may propose a route or rely on a planner to check one.

Sampling-based planning and <Term id="trajectory-optimization">trajectory optimization</Term> start differently. A sampling planner explores configurations and connections; an optimizer starts with a complete candidate trajectory and improves an objective. Neither a smoothness objective nor an initial guess guarantees that local optimization will find a collision-free motion. CHOMP and TrajOpt both examine planning from infeasible guesses as well as refining existing trajectories <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />.

The lab below uses an authored 2D scene: a 100 by 64 world with five obstacles. Its seed 19981001, maximum step of 2 world units, cap of 900 accepted extensions, obstacle layout and 1.5% goal-sampling probability are teaching settings for this example. The lab's iteration control counts accepted extensions of this fixed-seed tree. Run, Step forward and the slider reveal that tree; Reset returns to its opening state. Sampling is otherwise uniform. This example establishes no planner-wide success rate, completeness or optimality guarantee. Drag the exploration-iteration slider to inspect the accepted extensions.
edits.after: Motion planning is the computation of a collision-free route from a robot's current configuration to a goal <Cite id="lavalle-2006" />. Sampling-based planners explore configurations and the connections between them; trajectory optimizers improve a complete candidate trajectory against an objective <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />. [Kinematics](/classical/kinematics) maps joint angles to poses, and planning sequences them.

edits.before: Planning in the physical workspace is awkward because the robot has extent: every link sweeps volume, and collision is a statement about whole bodies. The standard reformulation, due to Lozano-Pérez in 1983, moves the problem into <Term id="configuration-space">configuration space</Term> <Cite id="lozano-perez-1983" />. A configuration $q$ is one complete specification of the robot's posture, the vector of its joint values, and the configuration space $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of all of them. A point robot in the plane has a 2D configuration space; a 7-DoF arm has a 7-dimensional one, one axis per joint.

The set $\mathcal{C}$ of all of them is 2D for a point robot in the plane and 7-dimensional for a 7-DoF arm <Cite id="lozano-perez-1983" />.

edits.before: The classical construction shrinks the robot to a point and grows each obstacle by the robot's shape, so collision checking reduces to point membership <Cite id="lozano-perez-1983" />. Planning is then a clean statement: find a continuous curve in $\mathcal{C}_{free}$ from $q_{start}$ to $q_{goal}$. Constructing the collision-constrained space is difficult, but it does not become impossible beyond a fixed number of dimensions. LaValle describes explicit boundary or solid representations as difficult, but also gives constructive translational cases and explains that semi-algebraic models for chains and trees can be generated automatically. His PSPACE-hardness statement concerns the basic semi-algebraic mover problem when the number of <Term id="degrees-of-freedom">degrees of freedom</Term> is unbounded; it does not establish impossibility for every seven-joint arm <Cite id="lavalle-2006" />. Sampling-based methods avoid explicit obstacle construction by probing a collision module, while still needing to validate entire local paths. Closed-chain constraints can also make efficient sampling difficult <Cite id="lavalle-2006" />.

Hardness holds for a planar linkage with multiple links and for a multi-arm robot among 3D polyhedra; Canny's roadmap method is singly exponential <Cite id="solovey-complexity-2020" />.

Sampling-based methods skip building $\mathcal{C}_{obs}$ by querying a collision checker and validating whole local paths, though closed-chain constraints make sampling difficult <Cite id="lavalle-2006" />. On humanoids, manifold-constrained planners can take tens of seconds; a 2026 SIMD projection method reports speed-ups of up to 100 to 1000 times <Cite id="mcvamp-2026" />.

edits.before: Sampling-based planning can avoid an explicit configuration-space obstacle model by querying a collision-detection module for candidate configurations and validating local paths <Cite id="lavalle-2006" />. The probabilistic roadmap (PRM) of Kavraki, Svestka, Latombe, and Overmars samples configurations uniformly at random, keeps the collision-free ones as milestones, connects nearby milestones with a local planner, and answers queries by searching the resulting graph <Cite id="kavraki-1996" />. It is a multi-query method: build the roadmap once, plan many start-goal pairs against it.
edits.after: The probabilistic roadmap (PRM) of Kavraki, Svestka, Latombe, and Overmars samples configurations uniformly, keeps the collision-free ones as nodes and adds extra nodes where a heuristic marks the space as difficult. A local planner links nearby nodes, and queries become graph searches, so one roadmap serves many start-goal pairs <Cite id="kavraki-1996" />.

The book's step-size-free dense-tree construction assumes an infinite dense sample sequence; a random sequence, including a biased one, must be dense with probability one. Its obstacle-free construction reaches each sample, while collision checking limits extensions when obstacles are present. Probabilistic completeness describes a probability that tends to one as sampling continues; it gives no finite-budget assurance for an arbitrary existing path <Cite id="lavalle-2006" />. For a precise example, Karaman and Frazzoli state it for simplified PRM (sPRM) and their geometric RRT under the Euclidean model $X=(0,1)^d$, $d\geq2$, an open goal region, and robust feasibility: a solution path must have some positive clearance $\delta>0$. Their algorithms use independent uniform free-space samples, a fixed positive connection radius for sPRM, RRT steering capped by a positive distance parameter, and collision tests over entire straight-line connections. Under those assumptions the probability of finding a solution tends to one. The result does not automatically extend to implementation heuristics; their 1-nearest sPRM counterexample is not probabilistically complete <Cite id="karaman-frazzoli-2011" />.

The paper reports the underlying RRT\* completeness and optimality guarantees. Its linear expected-cost convergence calculation assumes no obstacles and a rewiring radius larger than the informed subset's diameter. Its simulation comparisons used common unoptimized code and 100 runs per variation on shared maps and seeds, with random-world refinement measured for 60 seconds after an initial solution. Those experiments found faster refinement than RRT\* in that setup. The paper's description of its Sample routine says every sampled state admits an improving path, a stronger claim than the admissible-superset construction in its algorithm supports. The Open Motion Planning Library's project documentation lists implementations of PRM and RRT, along with benchmarking tools for comparing planners. It solves difficult high-DoF problems in milliseconds where other almost-surely asymptotically optimal planners failed to find solutions consistently within seconds <Cite id="aorrtc-2025" />.

edits.before: Trajectory optimization makes the trajectory the decision variable. Smoothness, obstacle clearance, and task requirements enter an objective or constraints. A local solution can still miss a feasible global route.
edits.after: <Term id="trajectory-optimization">Trajectory optimization</Term> makes the trajectory the decision variable, with smoothness, clearance and task terms in the objective or constraints. Neither the objective nor an initial guess guarantees a collision-free result. CHOMP and TrajOpt both plan from infeasible guesses as well as refine existing trajectories <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />. Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) poses planning as a mixed-integer program with a very tight convex relaxation, so in most cases a cheap rounding suffices for globally optimal trajectories <Cite id="gcs-2022" />.

edits.before: The retained CHOMP body is an eight-page preprint, distinct from the landing page's six-page ICRA publication. The first derivative term penalizes squared velocity; higher-order terms can penalize other dynamics. This discrete expression uses the source's explicit half-weighted formula. The continuous prior has its own normalization <Cite id="ratliff-2009" />.
edits.after: The first-derivative term penalizes squared velocity; higher-order terms penalize other dynamics. The obstacle cost integrates a signed-distance penalty over the robot's body, weighted by arc length so that moving faster through a costly region cannot lower it. Covariant descent uses the inverse smoothness metric to spread each gradient step smoothly along the trajectory <Cite id="ratliff-2009" />.

edits.before: The obstacle cost integrates over the robot's body elements and their arc length through the workspace. A workspace signed-distance field is negative inside an obstacle and positive outside; its penalty discourages low clearance. Arc-length weighting prevents merely moving faster through a costly region from reducing that obstacle cost. Covariant descent uses the inverse of a smoothness metric to distribute a gradient update along the trajectory while retaining smoothness. It is not a rule that selects large steps at cheap locations and small steps at expensive ones <Cite id="ratliff-2009" />.
edits.after: On the first six joints of a seven-DoF Barrett WAM, CHOMP solved 99 of 105 problems from 15 endpoint configurations. With a $50\times50\times50$ voxel grid and a Matlab distance field, 400 iterations took about 12 seconds; the core optimization finished within the first 100, about 3 seconds, in most runs. On LittleDog it ran inside a footstep controller with a separate footstep planner and a ZMP preview controller seeding the trunk. Trajectories were computed before execution because worst-case optimization took about 1.5 times as long as execution <Cite id="ratliff-2009" />.

CHOMP can turn an infeasible initial guess into a useful trajectory without a separate motion planner on many queries. edits.before: Checking only waypoints can miss a collision in the motion between them. TrajOpt therefore considers a modeled swept volume. cuRobo runs many parallel optimizer seeds on GPUs and solves difficult motion generation problems within 50 ms on average, 60x faster than state-of-the-art trajectory optimization <Cite id="curobo-2023" />. In a 2025 industrial integration with a 7th-axis gantry, cuRobo planned in 45 ± 8 ms against 1,200 ± 400 ms for MoveIt with OMPL's RRTConnect <Cite id="industrial-curobo-2025" />.

edits.before: Both methods need an initial trajectory and can remain trapped in a bad local minimum. That does not make a sampling-based preplanner mandatory. CHOMP compared straight-line and RRT initializations; among queries where collision removal succeeded, straight-line initialization often produced the better objective. TrajOpt likewise evaluated planning from infeasible seeds and found that multiple initializations changed success rates <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />.
edits.after:
CHOMP and TrajOpt both need an initial trajectory and can stall in bad local minima. In CHOMP's tests, straight-line seeds often beat RRT seeds on the objective where collision removal succeeded; in TrajOpt's, multiple initializations changed success rates <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />. The GPU multi-robot planner MR. POP supplies diverse seeds that raise downstream optimizer success, for example from 4% to 72% <Cite id="mr-pop-2026" />.

Ratliff and colleagues describe PRM and RRT as commonly deployed in two phases: find a feasible path, then remove redundant or jerky motion. Schulman and colleagues give trajectory optimization two roles, refining another method's output or planning from scratch <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />. Shortcutting, a cheap second stage, repeatedly picks two trajectory points and tries to replace the segment between them with a shorter collision-free one <Cite id="hauser-shortcut-2010" />.

edits.before: Ratliff and colleagues describe PRM and RRT as typically used in a two-phase process: first find a feasible path, then remove redundant or jerky motion. Schulman and colleagues distinguish two roles for trajectory optimization: refining a trajectory generated by another method, or planning from scratch. These papers describe research methods; they do not establish a standard industrial pipeline today <Cite id="ratliff-2009" /><Cite id="schulman-2013" />.
edits.after: As of January 2023, MoveIt 2 recommends Time-Optimal Trajectory Generation (TOTG) for time parameterization <Cite id="moveit-trajectory-processing-2026" />. Because TOTG sets no jerk limits, Ruckig jerk-limited smoothing can follow it as a further post-processing step <Cite id="moveit-time-parameterization-2026" />. PickNik's MoveIt Pro 10.1.0, released September 18, 2026, includes a ProRRT shortcut stage <Cite id="moveit-pro-10-1-2026" />.

edits.before: Sampling planners still label demonstration data, verify that a proposed motion is feasible, and generate the diverse training scenes that [generative simulation](/world-models/generative-sim) pipelines rely on. Optimization survives inside model-predictive control, which replans a short horizon at every control cycle, a design whose tradeoffs against learned policies have their own module in [reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc). Hierarchical robot learning, from SayCan onward, lets a learned system emit goals for a classical planner to execute; end-to-end policies learn to plan within the policy.
edits.after:
Motion Policy Networks trained on over 3 million motion planning problems in over 500,000 [environments](/world-models/generative-sim) <Cite id="mpinets-2022" />. Neural MP distills motion-planner data into a reactive generalist policy and adds lightweight optimization for safety. Its authors report success gains of 23%, 17% and 79% over sampling, optimization and learning-based planners <Cite id="neural-mp-2024" />. A 2026 survey of neural motion planners finds that they often struggle to generalize to unseen, out-of-distribution planning settings <Cite id="neural-motion-planner-survey-2026" />.

Deep Reactive Policy replaced AIT\* with cuRobo as its expert planner because GPU acceleration let it scale to 10 million expert trajectories. Its authors report that AIT\* achieved 0% success on all dynamic tasks, and cuRobo fell to 3.00% when the goal was temporarily obstructed <Cite id="deep-reactive-policy-2025" />.

edits.before: What end-to-end policies do not escape is the geometry. A diffusion policy's action chunk is a trajectory in configuration space; an RRT's path is a trajectory in configuration space. The difference is who computed it, a planner with an explicit collision model or a network with an implicit one. The modules that follow, [control](/classical/control) and state estimation, assume some such trajectory exists and ask how to track it and where the robot actually is while doing so.
edits.after: Receding-horizon model-predictive control keeps optimization inside the feedback loop <Cite id="mayne-2000" />; [reward design and the MPC debate](/rl-sim2real/reward-design-mpc) weighs it against learned policies. Diffusion Policy represents a visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process run with receding-horizon control <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. [Control](/classical/control) and state estimation track the resulting trajectories and locate the robot.

edits.before: A deployable planner consumes more than a start and goal. It needs the robot model, current state, collision geometry, allowed contacts, attached objects, joint limits, timing limits and a controller capable of executing the returned trajectory. Give each input a freshness rule. A collision-free path against a stale scene is not a safe path, and a valid geometric path can still violate velocity or torque limits after time parameterization.
edits.after: A deployable planner needs the robot model, current state, collision geometry, allowed contacts, attached objects, joint and timing limits and a controller that can execute the result. A path checked against a stale scene is unsafe. TOTG time-parameterizes a path, computing the time-optimal trajectory that exactly follows a differentiable joint-space path within velocity and acceleration bounds <Cite id="totg-2012" />. Ruckig adds real-time jerk-limited generation; its authors tested it on over 1,000,000,000 random trajectories <Cite id="ruckig-2021" />. The cuRoboV2 authors note that fast planners output physically unexecutable trajectories, and report 99.7% success under a 3 kg payload against 72 to 77% for baselines <Cite id="curobo-v2-2026" />.
