import { ComparisonMatrix } from '@/components/interactive/comparison-matrix';

The comparison matrix is a table of the major robot policies compared on eight architectural axes, from action representation to openness. RT-2’s reported rates depend on the model and serving setup. Its 55B PaLI-X variant runs at 1 to 3 Hz, while the 5B variant runs at around 5 Hz, using a multi-TPU cloud service queried over the network. <Cite id="rt2-2023" />

OpenVLA reports approximately 6 Hz inference on one NVIDIA RTX 4090 in bfloat16, without compilation, speculative decoding, or other inference speed-up tricks. <Cite id="openvla-2024" /> Set the weights filter to Downloadable and the table keeps only the methods with published weights.

<ComparisonMatrix className="my-6 wide-measure" />

## The eight axes

**Action representation** describes the output mechanism: continuous regression, discrete action tokens, or a generative head such as diffusion or <Term id="flow-matching">flow matching</Term>. Training supervision and runtime action generation need not use the same representation.

**Horizon** separates the planned chunk length $H$ from the steps executed $\hat{H}$ before re-planning: the <Term id="predicted-horizon">predicted horizon</Term> and the <Term id="committed-horizon">committed horizon</Term>. <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" /> The Diffusion Policy CNN Push-T configuration predicts 16 steps and executes 8; these are not universal settings for every architecture or task. <Cite id="pi07-2026" /> π0.7 predicts 50 and executes 15 or 25; the paper reports no other executed length and maps neither choice to particular robots.

**Control frequency** needs a named measurement setting. <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" /> ACT's ALOHA setup runs at 50 Hz; with <Term id="temporal-ensembling">temporal ensembling</Term>, the policy is queried at every timestep. <Cite id="rt1-2022" /> RT-1 commands the Everyday Robots platform at 3 Hz. Neither statement is a standalone transformer-throughput benchmark.

**Backbone**, **conditioning**, and **cross-embodiment** describe the model components, their inputs, and the scope of robot-body transfer. Distinguish mixed-embodiment training, direct use of a checkpoint on multiple bodies, and finetuning on a new body; the three count as different kinds of transfer evidence.

**Hierarchy** distinguishes an internal high-level stage from a separately paired system. <Cite id="pi05-2025" /> π0.5 predicts a semantic subtask before generating low-level actions. <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" /> In the N1.7 SONIC workflow, a separate whole-body controller decodes the VLA's latent action tokens into joint commands. Here, external names the pairing itself; the controller decodes the VLA's tokens and carries no reasoning role of its own. **Weights** records download availability; license openness is a separate question, and the notes identify the checked source scope.

<Cite id="rt1-2022" /> RT-1’s “limited” cross-embodiment label refers to mixing Kuka IIWA data with Everyday Robots data, then evaluating on Everyday Robots. No single checkpoint was demonstrated controlling both robot bodies in that paper.

<Cite id="act-aloha-2023" /> ACT’s 100-step entry names the paper’s k=100 chunk-ablation reference; temporal ensembling queries the policy every timestep. The paper trains a roughly 80M-parameter model from scratch for each task and announces software and hardware. That does not establish pretrained-checkpoint downloads or one checkpoint transferring across embodiments; those cells are source-scoped as not disclosed.

<Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" /> Diffusion Policy’s CNN Push-T reference uses observation/prediction/execution horizons of 2/16/8. Its real-world UR5 Push-T experiment predicts commands at 10 Hz and interpolates them to 125 Hz. Each is a named setting; other tasks and backbones carry their own. The checked paper announces code, data and training details and lists no pretrained-checkpoint catalogue; no shared-checkpoint cross-embodiment result is established here.

<Cite id="rt2-2023" /> RT-2’s multi-TPU cloud service runs PaLI-X-55B at 1 to 3 Hz and the 5B version at around 5 Hz. The paper also studies PaLM-E-12B and a separate Language-Table model. “Limited” denotes these separate setup-specific models; one checkpoint controlling both bodies is outside what it demonstrates. The action-only table entry excludes the separately evaluated chain-of-thought prompting variant. The inspected paper does not establish model-specific weight-release terms.

<Cite id="openvla-2024" /> OpenVLA reports approximately 6 Hz inference on one RTX 4090 in bfloat16, without compilation, speculative decoding or other speed-up tricks. Its Franka-Tabletop and Franka-DROID fine-tuning setups separately use 5 Hz and 15 Hz non-blocking controllers. The paper describes single-step action prediction, multi-robot pretrained use and fine-tuning for new setups, and explicitly releases downloadable checkpoints. Its 7B label names the language-model scale; the visual encoder is separately reported as 600M parameters.

<Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" /> The OFT row uses the paper's ALOHA OFT+ setting: 25 predicted and executed actions at a 25 Hz controller. LIBERO instead predicts and executes eight. Its limited cross-embodiment label means adaptation from the pretrained model to separate tasks and robot setups; one unchanged checkpoint controlling every body is outside what it demonstrates.

<Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" /> Gemini Robotics 1.5's model card does disclose continuous numerical action outputs. It does not identify the action-head family, action-chunk length, robot-command rate, or parameter count. Internal refers to thinking within the VLA; the report also pairs it with a separate GR-ER 1.5 orchestrator. The generalization and cross-embodiment experiments use one checkpoint across ALOHA, bi-arm Franka, and Apollo; the separate long-horizon agent experiment adds post-training on bi-arm Franka. An unset field here is source-scoped, a distinct case from inapplicable.

<Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" /> The Gemini Robotics 2 row describes the VLA in DeepMind's July 30, 2026 announcement. External hierarchy means the separate ER 2 model coordinates with that VLA, whose action head stays internal. The same-checkpoint result covers Apollo 2 with SharpaWave hands, Apollo 2 with Inspire hands, and Franka Duo with Robotiq; the On-Device adaptations sit outside that result. The announcement does not specify the VLA backbone, output parameterization, chunk lengths, control frequency, or parameter count. AI Studio, private preview, and early-access partnerships are access channels and carry no weight-license classification.

<Cite id="skild-series-c-2026" /> Skild's 2026 row is scoped to its January 14 Series C announcement; the model-release date itself is unverified. The company describes its data sources and makes an omni-bodied capability claim, but does not specify a reproducible cross-embodiment evaluation or the runtime architecture, inputs, hierarchy, chunk lengths, control frequency, and weight-release terms used by these cells. The empty conditioning list means undisclosed in this source, a distinct case from no inputs or n/a.

## Helix 02 and GO-2 disclosure limits

<Cite id="helix-02-2026" /> Figure’s Helix 02 announcement describes S1 joint targets at 200 Hz and S0 actuator commands at 1 kHz, but does not specify the output-head training loss. The representation cell is therefore not classified as continuous regression here. Its statement about generalization across Figure’s fleet is not evidence of one checkpoint transferring between different robot bodies; that field remains not disclosed for this source.

<Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" /> AgiBot describes lower-frequency System 2 semantic planning and higher-frequency System 1 action following; the announcement gives qualitative frequency roles and no numerical control rate for either. The inspected announcement text does not establish the backbone, output encoding, action-chunk lengths, cross-body checkpoint transfer, or trained-policy weight-release terms. Those fields remain undisclosed for this source, a distinct case from n/a or closed. The 2026 year is supported by an HTML publication timestamp in a commented span; it is not an independently established release date.

## What the matrix can establish

<Cite id="act-aloha-2023" /> ACT fixes its CVAE latent to the prior mean, zero, to decode deterministically at test time. <Cite id="pi0-2024" /> π0 instead uses an action expert trained with flow matching to generate continuous action chunks. These are concrete differences between output mechanisms; whether every later policy abandoned regression is a separate question.

<Cite id="pi05-2025" /> The π0.5 paper distinguishes FAST-token training from continuous-action generation with flow matching. It describes autoregressive action decoding as expensive at inference time. That qualitative comparison is not a measured factor-of-two task-completion or inference-latency result for π0-FAST.

<Cite id="pi07-2026" /> π0.7 uses five denoising steps to generate 50 actions, then executes either 15 or 25. Its UR5e robots run at 20 Hz; the other tested robots run at 50 Hz. <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" /> Real-time chunking addresses inference delay by guiding generation of the next chunk while the current one is executing. These execution details matter more than ranking methods by predicted horizon alone.

<Cite id="pi06-model-card-2025" /> The π0.6 card reports 63 ms to produce an action chunk with five denoising steps, three camera inputs, and one H100. It does not disclose a robot-control rate or a predicted/executed chunk length. <Cite id="helix-02-2026" /> Figure reports Helix 02 S1 joint targets at 200 Hz and S0 actuator commands at 1 kHz. The latter are different stages of a single control stack, so one model call never sits behind both numbers.

<Cite id="rt1-2022" /> The RT-1 paper announces code, which does not establish pretrained-weight availability. <Cite id="helix-02-2026" /> Figure's Helix 02 announcement does not state a chunk horizon or weight-release terms. Their availability cells therefore read "not disclosed" for these checked sources. <Cite id="openpi-repo-2024" /> The pinned openpi README lists π0, π0-FAST, and π0.5 checkpoints. <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" /> The N1.7 README lists downloadable weights, while its License section distinguishes Apache 2.0 code from the NVIDIA Open Model License for weights. These release statements do not establish a global generation ranking or closed licensing for an unlisted model.

The Control Hz column is not an inference-throughput comparison. <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" /> ACT's 50 Hz ALOHA loop, <Cite id="helix-02-2026" /> Helix's 200 Hz S1/1 kHz S0 stack, and <Cite id="pi07-2026" /> π0.7's 20 Hz UR5e/50 Hz other-robot settings describe different systems. π0.7 also trains with simulated inference delays; that does not turn these rates into a shared benchmark. Read the setting notes before comparing two cells.

## Use the matrix as a constraint solver

Start with elimination and leave ranking for the end. Remove models whose weights or training data cannot be used under the project's terms. Remove models whose action representation cannot map cleanly to the robot's controller, then those whose measured end-to-end latency misses the deadline. Next test observation compatibility and the amount of adaptation data the model requires. Only after those constraints should benchmark performance influence the shortlist.

For the surviving candidates, run one controlled comparison with the same cameras, action horizon, reset policy and physical trial protocol. Keep a simple behavior-cloning or action-chunking baseline in the evaluation. The [foundation-model guide](/manipulation/foundation-models) explains what prior each family contributes; the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces) explains whether its output is a fair fit. A matrix can expose missing evidence, but it cannot turn results from different robots and protocols into a universal leaderboard.

The comparison matrix is a table of major robot policies, from RT-1 (2022) to π0.7 (2026), compared on eight architectural axes <Cite id="rt1-2022" /> <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. The axes are action representation, horizon, control frequency, backbone, conditioning, cross-embodiment, hierarchy and weights. Each cell records what its named source discloses. Set the weights filter to Downloadable.

<ComparisonMatrix className="my-6 wide-measure" />

## Use the matrix as a constraint solver

Remove models whose weights or training data cannot be used under the project's terms; Gemini Robotics On-Device, for example, is reached through a trusted-tester SDK <Cite id="gemini-robotics-on-device-2025" />. Then remove models whose action representation, measured latency, observations or adaptation-data needs do not fit the robot. Benchmark performance comes last.

Compare the survivors under one trial protocol with the same cameras, action horizon and resets, and keep a behavior-cloning or action-chunking baseline. TRI's Large Behavior Model study used blind, randomized trials with statistical confidence <Cite id="tri-lbm-2025" />. RoboArena ranked seven generalist policies more accurately than centralized evaluation through over 600 double-blind pairwise real-robot episodes <Cite id="roboarena-2025" />. The [foundation-model guide](/manipulation/foundation-models/) explains what prior each family contributes, the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces/) whether its output fits, and the [evaluation crisis](/data-hardware/evaluation-crisis/) why protocols resist a shared leaderboard.

## The eight axes

Action representation is the output mechanism: continuous regression, discrete action tokens, or a generative head such as diffusion or <Term id="flow-matching">flow matching</Term>. Training supervision and runtime generation can differ. The π0.5 paper trains with FAST tokens and generates continuous actions with flow matching, and calls autoregressive decoding expensive at inference <Cite id="pi05-2025" />.

Horizon separates the planned chunk length $H$ from the steps executed $\hat{H}$ before re-planning: the <Term id="predicted-horizon">predicted horizon</Term> and the <Term id="committed-horizon">committed horizon</Term>. Diffusion Policy's simulated CNN Push-T reference uses observation, prediction and execution horizons of 2, 16 and 8 <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. π0.7 predicts 50 with five denoising steps and executes 15 or 25 <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. ACT's 100-step entry is its k=100 chunk-ablation reference <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. OFT's ALOHA OFT+ setting predicts and executes 25 actions at 25 Hz, and LIBERO eight <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />. [Real-time chunking](/manipulation/realtime-execution/) generates the next chunk while the current one executes <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" />.

Control frequency needs a named measurement setting. ACT's ALOHA setup runs at 50 Hz, with <Term id="temporal-ensembling">temporal ensembling</Term> querying the policy every timestep <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. RT-1 commands the Everyday Robots platform at 3 Hz <Cite id="rt1-2022" />. RT-2's multi-TPU cloud service runs PaLI-X-55B at 1 to 3 Hz and the 5B model at around 5 Hz <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. OpenVLA reaches about 6 Hz on one RTX 4090 in bfloat16 without speed-up tricks, and its Franka fine-tuning setups use 5 Hz and 15 Hz controllers <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. Diffusion Policy's real UR5 Push-T predicts at 10 Hz and interpolates to 125 Hz <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />.

Gemini Robotics splits a cloud backbone from an on-robot decoder, and multi-action chunks turn about 250 ms of end-to-end latency into a 50 Hz effective control frequency <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2025" />. GR00T N1 runs its VLM at 10 Hz on an L40 and samples a 16-action chunk in 63.9 ms <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />. The π0.6 card reports 63 ms per chunk with five denoising steps, three cameras and one H100 <Cite id="pi06-model-card-2025" />. π0.7 runs UR5e robots at 20 Hz and others at 50 Hz <Cite id="pi07-2026" />, and Generalist says GEN-1.5 produces 100 Hz action trajectories and keeps 30 seconds of video memory <Cite id="gen-1-5-2026" />.

Backbone, conditioning and cross-embodiment describe model components, inputs and the scope of robot-body transfer. Mixed-embodiment training, one checkpoint on several bodies and fine-tuning on a new body are different evidence. CrossFormer shows the strongest kind: the same weights control very different robots after training on 900K trajectories from 20 embodiments <Cite id="crossformer-2024" />. Skild says S1 executes a task shown in one video <Cite id="skild-s1-2026" />, which adds demonstration video as a conditioning input.

Hierarchy distinguishes an internal high-level stage from a separately paired system. π0.5 predicts a semantic subtask before low-level actions <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. In the N1.7 SONIC workflow, a separate whole-body controller decodes the VLA's latent action tokens into joint commands <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. RT-1 runs inside SayCan in its long-horizon kitchen experiments <Cite id="rt1-2022" />, and a separate high-level VLM gives π0 subtasks on several tasks <Cite id="pi0-2024" />.

Weights records download availability, separately from license. The pinned openpi README lists π0, π0-FAST and π0.5 checkpoints <Cite id="openpi-repo-2024" />. The N1.7 README lists downloadable weights, and its License section separates Apache 2.0 code from weights under the NVIDIA Open Model License <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. SmolVLA releases all code, pretrained models and training data <Cite id="smolvla-2025" />.

## Row notes

RT-1's "limited" cross-embodiment label means Kuka IIWA data mixed with Everyday Robots data and evaluated on Everyday Robots; the paper announces code <Cite id="rt1-2022" />. ACT trains a roughly 80M-parameter model from scratch for each task and announces software and hardware <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. Diffusion Policy announces code, data and training details <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. RT-2 also studies PaLM-E-12B; its robot data is RT-1's 13-robot kitchen set, and a separate PaLI 3B model covers Language-Table. The action-only entry excludes its chain-of-thought variant <Cite id="rt2-2023" />.

OpenVLA predicts single-step actions, supports multi-robot use and fine-tuning, and releases downloadable checkpoints; its 7B label names the language model, beside a 600M visual encoder <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. OFT's "limited" label means adapting the pretrained model to separate tasks and robot setups <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />. GR00T N1.6 predicts state-relative action chunks for most embodiments <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />. π*0.6 adds Recap post-training, which more than doubles throughput on some of the hardest tasks and roughly halves failure rates <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />.

Gemini Robotics 1.5's model card discloses continuous numerical action outputs but no action-head family, chunk length, command rate or parameter count. One checkpoint runs across ALOHA, bi-arm Franka and Apollo, its thinking is internal, and a separate GR-ER 1.5 orchestrator can pair with it; the long-horizon agent experiment adds post-training on bi-arm Franka <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />.

DeepMind's July 30, 2026 announcement pairs the Gemini Robotics 2 VLA with the separate ER 2 model. One checkpoint covers Apollo 2 with SharpaWave or Inspire hands and Franka Duo with Robotiq, while On-Device adaptations sit outside that result. The announcement gives no backbone, output parameterization, chunk length, control frequency or parameter count, and offers access through AI Studio, private preview and early-access partnerships <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />.

Skild's row rests on its January 14, 2026 Series C announcement, which describes data sources and an omni-bodied claim but no reproducible cross-embodiment evaluation or runtime details <Cite id="skild-series-c-2026" />.

## What the matrix can establish

ACT fixes its CVAE latent to the prior mean, zero, to decode deterministically <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />, while π0 generates continuous action chunks with a flow-matching action expert <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. Generalist says GEN-1's base model trains on wearable human data without robot data and reaches 99% average success where earlier models reached 64%, with 1 hour of robot data per task <Cite id="generalist-gen1-2026" />. On March 16, 2026, NVIDIA previewed GR00T N2, a robot foundation model based on DreamZero research <Cite id="nvidia-gtc-gr00t-n2-2026" />.

## Helix 02 and GO-2 disclosure limits

Figure's Helix 02 announcement gives S1 joint targets at 200 Hz and S0 actuator commands at 1 kHz, two stages of one stack. It names no output-head training loss, chunk horizon or weight-release terms <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />. Figure's February 2025 post on the first Helix disclosed a 7 to 9 Hz onboard VLM and an 80M-parameter S1 at 200 Hz over 35 degrees of freedom, trained end-to-end with a standard regression loss <Cite id="helix-2025" />. Figure reports that Index human-video pretraining, all else fixed, raised Helix 2.5's zero-shot success in 30 unseen homes from 9% to 56% <Cite id="helix-2-5-2026" />.

AgiBot describes lower-frequency System 2 semantic planning and higher-frequency System 1 action following, with no numerical rate, backbone, output encoding, chunk length, cross-body transfer or weight terms <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. The predecessor GO-1 uses latent action representations trained on AgiBot World's more than 1 million trajectories across 217 tasks <Cite id="agibot-world-2025" />.

## Counting robot and human data

π0's 10,000 hours are its own data from 7 robot configurations and 68 tasks, added to OXE, DROID and Bridge. By timesteps, open-source data is 9.1% of the mixture, against 903 million steps of π0's own <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. RT-X experiments used 9 of OXE's 22 embodiments <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" />. GR00T N1.7's rounded 20K pretraining hours are EgoScale human video <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />.

Moritz Reuss wrote in October 2025 that "OXE is mostly low-quality data" and that imitation learning lacks good ways to measure [data quality](/data-hardware/data-bottleneck/) <Cite id="oxe-quality-critique-2026" />. Re-Mix's learned mixture weights beat uniform weights by 38% on average and human-selected ones by 32% <Cite id="remix-2024" />. Toyota Research Institute's controlled study of 89 policies found that co-training with cross-embodiment robot data improves generalization to distribution shifts and unseen tasks <Cite id="lbm-cotraining-2026" />.

## Robot action interfaces

ACT's ALOHA action is a 14-dimensional absolute-joint vector for two 6-DoF ViperX arms with grippers, which the paper's observation description counts as "7+7=14 DoF" <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. π0 zero-pads every action vector to the largest robot's 18 dimensions <Cite id="pi0-2024" />.

Octo curates 25 <Term id="open-x-embodiment">OXE</Term> datasets with delta <Term id="end-effector">end-effector</Term> control, zero-pads missing camera channels and aligns grippers to +1 open, 0 closed; new spaces get lightweight encoders or heads on the kept transformer <Cite id="octo-2024" />. CrossFormer trains one transformer on 900K trajectories from 20 embodiments without manually aligning observation or action spaces <Cite id="crossformer-2024" />.

HPT maps each embodiment's proprioception and vision to a few tokens for a shared trunk, scaling to 52 datasets <Cite id="hpt-2024" />, and X-VLA learns one soft-prompt embedding set per data source as an embodiment prompt <Cite id="x-vla-2025" />. LAP writes low-level actions as natural language; LAP-3B reports over 50% average zero-shot success on unseen robots, about twice the strongest prior VLAs <Cite id="lap-2026" />.

edits.before: <Term id="diffusion-policy">Diffusion Policy</Term> is a visuomotor robot policy that generates its actions with a diffusion model. Human demonstrations are multimodal: faced with an obstacle, one operator goes left, another goes right, and both are correct. A policy trained with mean-squared error learns the average of the modes, and the average of "left" and "right" is "straight into the obstacle." Diffusion Policy, introduced by Chi et al. in 2023, sidesteps the averaging problem by generating a whole action sequence through conditional denoising instead of a single action <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. The extended journal version describes a 15-task evaluation. It reports a 46.9% average relative improvement for its simulation comparisons; the paper's baseline selection takes the strongest baseline and diffusion backbone per reported column and excludes multi-human results <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />.

## Multimodal demonstrations

Demonstrations are multimodal: one operator passes an obstacle on the left, another on the right, and mean-squared-error regression averages them into a collision. Energy-based implicit policies often beat such explicit policies <Cite id="implicit-bc-2021" />, and diffusion models learn an expressive distribution over the joint action space <Cite id="pearce-diffusion-bc-2023" />. Pan et al. (2025) contest this motivation: generative policies owe their gains to supervised iterative computation, and a two-step regression policy essentially matches flow policies <Cite id="much-ado-noising-2025" />. Fine-tuned OpenVLA-OFT, an L1-regression VLA, beat from-scratch Diffusion Policy and ACT by up to 15 points of average success <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />.

edits.before: Consistency Policy distills an EDM-based Diffusion Policy teacher into a consistency model with one- or three-step action-sequence generation, targeting compute-constrained robots. In its Robomimic Square ablation, teachers with success rates of 0.92, 0.88 and 0.84 produced students with success rates of 0.92, 0.92 and 0.88, respectively; the authors report robustness over this tested range <Cite id="consistency-policy-2024" />. edits.after: Iterative denoising is slow for mobile manipulators and quadrotors without high-end GPUs. Consistency models generate in one step by design <Cite id="consistency-models-2023" />, and Consistency Policy distills an EDM-based Diffusion Policy teacher into one- or three-step generation. On Robomimic Square, teachers at 0.92, 0.88 and 0.84 success yielded students at 0.92, 0.92 and 0.88, robust over that range <Cite id="consistency-policy-2024" />. One-Step Diffusion Policy lifts action prediction from 1.5 Hz to 62 Hz on real Franka tasks <Cite id="one-step-diffusion-2024" />, and MP1 averages 6.8 ms per one-step inference <Cite id="mp1-2026" />. The teacher-free One-Step Flow Policy outperforms 100-step diffusion and flow policies across 56 simulated tasks <Cite id="one-step-flow-policy-2026" />. Swapped into Diffusion Policy, one step matched or beat the 100-step original on 10 of 14 simulated task settings <Cite id="drifting-models-2026" />.

“Foundation model” is a claim about reuse, and a large neural network alone earns nothing by the label. In robotics, the useful test is whether one pretrained model supports materially different downstream tasks, environments or embodiments after bounded adaptation. Parameter count alone does not establish that property, and a model trained across many tasks can still be a closed, fixed policy with no foundation role for new ones.

Three families currently carry the label: <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action models</Term> that emit controls, predictive world models used for planning or representation learning, and multimodal backbones adapted into either. They share pretraining scale and diverge at the output interface.

## Predictive foundations: represent or simulate the future

World-model families pretrain a different capability. V-JEPA 2 uses over 1M hours of internet video for representation learning; its action-conditioned stage uses fewer than 62 hours of unlabeled DROID robot video <Cite id="vjepa2-2025" />. The transferable asset is a representation in which future states can be predicted and compared; no direct language-to-action map comes with it.

Cosmos 3 unifies understanding, generation, forward dynamics, inverse dynamics and policy-oriented outputs in an omnimodal model for physical AI <Cite id="cosmos-3-2026" />. Its scale supports several downstream roles, but each role still needs an evaluation suited to that output. A visually convincing future is not automatically a useful control model; inspect action sensitivity and policy-ranking evidence when evaluating one.

In February 2026, Seonghyeon Ye, Yuke Zhu and colleagues described DreamZero, a world action model that is built on a pretrained video diffusion backbone and predicts future video and actions together. In real-robot experiments it more than doubled generalization to new tasks and environments compared with state-of-the-art VLAs, and its 14-billion-parameter model ran closed-loop control at 7 Hz <Cite id="dreamzero-2026" />.

edits.before:
## How to evaluate a foundation claim

Look for a matrix instead of a highlight. Rows should vary tasks and environments; columns should vary embodiment, adaptation data and evaluation shift. Report the pretrained checkpoint, every tuned component and the amount of new robot interaction. Include a from-scratch baseline under the same data budget.

Then ask what failed. If transfer collapses when camera placement changes, the representation is less foundational than the task list suggests. If a new arm needs full retraining on a large dataset, the model may be a strong multi-task policy with a narrow embodiment boundary. If a small adapter works across genuinely new tasks, the foundation description has earned useful meaning.

The term is valuable when it predicts engineering leverage. Used precisely, it tells you which expensive capability has already been learned and which expensive capability you still have to supply.
edits.after: Look for a matrix: rows vary tasks and environments, columns vary embodiment, adaptation data and evaluation shift. Report the checkpoint, every tuned component, the new robot data and a same-budget from-scratch baseline. VLAs near 95% on LIBERO drop below 30% under modest camera or initial-state perturbations <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />, and models above 90% fall to 0.0% under LIBERO-PRO's generalized setting <Cite id="libero-pro-2025" />. A model that needs full retraining for each new arm has a narrow embodiment boundary.

The other generalist policies are the multi-task robot models outside two lineages, the VLA family from RT-1 to OpenVLA and [Physical Intelligence's pi line](/manipulation/pi-line). This module surveys the ones an ML engineer will actually meet in 2026: Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics, NVIDIA's GR00T, Figure's Helix, AgiBot's GO series, and Skild. The organizing axis here is access: which ones you can download, and how each one's claims are documented. Architecture takes second place. Keep two questions in mind throughout. Are the weights open? And is the evidence a paper, a repo, a lab blog, or a press release?

## Gemini Robotics: the strongest closed line, the thinnest disclosure

The March 2025 Gemini Robotics report introduces a Gemini 2.0-based model family. Gemini Robotics-ER extends spatial and temporal understanding for tasks including pointing, trajectory prediction, and grasp prediction; Gemini Robotics builds on ER to produce robot actions <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2025" />. The 1.5 technical report, first submitted to arXiv on October 2, 2025, describes three advances: natural-language thinking traces interleaved with VLA actions when thinking is enabled; Motion Transfer, a training recipe for learning across robot embodiments; and the separate GR-ER 1.5 embodied-reasoning model used as an orchestrator. The report varies ER's thinking-token budget and finds that the useful amount of thinking depends on the task. The submission date is a report date; the product-release date is unestablished. <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" /> Both releases have technical reports on arXiv, which puts them a tier above most of this module in provenance.

Google DeepMind announced Gemini Robotics 2 on July 30, 2026 as three models: the Gemini Robotics 2 VLA converts vision and language into motor control; Gemini Robotics ER 2 is a separate embodied-reasoning VLM; and Gemini Robotics On-Device 2 is a VLA optimized for local operation. <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />

The announcement describes Apollo 2 whole-body control, including walking, crouching, and stretching to manipulate objects. DeepMind contrasts this with its earlier humanoid models' upper-body tabletop tasks. These are reported capabilities and examples; the announcement claims no universal whole-body generalization. The five-fingered SharpaWave hand has 22 <Term id="degrees-of-freedom">DoF</Term>; the Franka Duo uses two-fingered parallel grippers. The results caption identifies one model checkpoint across three configurations: Apollo 2 with SharpaWave hands, Apollo 2 with Inspire hands, and Franka Duo with the Robotiq gripper. That checkpoint statement does not extend to every new body adapted by On-Device 2. <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />

ER 2 plans multi-step tasks lasting several minutes, tracks progress, and coordinates with the VLA; the announcement also introduces collaboration between robots. On-Device 2 is reported to adapt to new bi-arm embodiments in a few hours of adaptation time, typically with fewer than 200 examples. The examples are Dexmate, SO101, and Trossen. The source does not provide separate example counts or evaluation protocols for each platform, and its introductory “few hours of data” wording should not be read as a measured compute-only training time. <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />

DeepMind's whole-body chart labels report 76.3% for picking from a shelf, 68.4% from a table, and 45.7% from the floor on Apollo with Inspire hands. The separate Apollo-with-Sharpa-hands chart reports individual-task results of 92% for unscrewing a bulb, 44% for tying a trash bag, 40% for Ziplock, and 32% for Dustpan. These values are explicitly written in the announcement's image alt text; none is estimated from bar heights. The caption describes the whole-body bars as average success rates over multiple tasks within each skill category, while the multi-finger bars are individual-task performance. Trial counts and the meaning of the error bars are not disclosed in the captured announcement. DeepMind's conclusion is that “the multi-finger dexterous manipulation remains challenging.” <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />

Disclosure is partial. The Gemini Robotics 1.5 report describes the orchestrator/VLA split and Motion Transfer at a high level, and its model card explicitly specifies continuous numerical robot actions plus text when thinking is enabled. It does not identify an action-head family, predicted/executed action-chunk lengths, a robot-command frequency, or a parameter count. <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />

The Gemini Robotics 2 announcement describes three model roles and says On-Device 2 inherits Motion Transfer from 1.5. It does not provide an internal Motion Transfer implementation, an action-output parameterization or head family, chunk lengths, a robot-command rate, or a parameter count. At that announcement, ER 2 was available on Google AI Studio and in private preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform; the VLA and On-Device models were available to early-access partners. Those access channels do not establish downloadable weights or a model-specific closed license. ## GR00T: the open humanoid line

The GR00T N1 report, first submitted in March 2025, describes a <Term id="vision-language-model">VLM</Term> backbone coupled to a <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> diffusion-transformer action head. Vision-language tokens condition the action head through cross-attention. The inspected revision links the public GR00T-N1-2B checkpoint; it does not establish that this is the closest architectural analogue to π0 <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />.

The captured Isaac-GR00T repository lists the N1.7 release on April 18, 2026. Its README describes a Cosmos-Reason2-2B backbone using the Qwen3-VL architecture and a 3B-parameter base checkpoint. The flow-matching DiT changes from 32 to 16 layers; the state/action interface expands to 132 dimensions and the prediction horizon to 40. NVIDIA describes a relative end-effector action space shared across robot and human embodiments, and reports 20K hours of EgoScale human video in N1.7 pretraining <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. That README population should not be conflated with the EgoScale paper's separately reported dataset of over 20,854 hours <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />. The README lists one GPU with 16 GB or more VRAM for inference; it is a hardware requirement, a separate quantity from any measured latency or throughput. Prediction horizon does not specify how many actions execute per policy call <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />.

The README's License section assigns Apache 2.0 to code and NVIDIA Open Model License to model weights. Its introductory paragraph also says N1.7 is "fully commercially licensable under Apache 2.0". Those statements differ in scope; this survey records both and certifies no Apache license for a particular checkpoint's weights <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />.

NVIDIA describes N1.7 as comparable to N1.6, with improved generalization and language following. That wording does not establish that the backbone change was merely a platform decision or that there was no capability improvement. The sources used here are the N1 technical paper and the captured N1.7 README, which links earlier N1.5 and N1.6 releases. ## Figure Helix: the most detailed vendor blog

Figure’s February 20, 2025 Helix announcement describes S2, an internet-pretrained VLM, producing a continuous latent task representation, and S1, a latent-conditioned visuomotor transformer, consuming that representation together with image and robot-state inputs. Figure reports S2 at 7 to 9 Hz and S1 at 200 Hz. S1 outputs desired wrist poses, finger flexion and abduction, torso and head orientation targets, and a synthetic task-completion output; the output goes beyond a vector of upper-body joint targets. The post describes the S2 backbone as open-source and open-weight; that is not a statement that the full Helix policy was released <Cite id="helix-2025" />.

Figure’s January 27, 2026 Helix 02 announcement describes a three-layer hierarchy, and only two of its layers carry numerical rates. S2 interprets scenes and language and sequences latent goals. S1 maps head and palm cameras, fingertip tactile sensing, and full-body proprioception to full-body joint targets at a reported 200 Hz. S0 is a 10M-parameter whole-body controller that outputs joint-level actuator commands at a reported 1 kHz. Figure says S0 uses over 1,000 hours of joint-level retargeted human motion and is trained entirely in simulation across more than 200,000 parallel environments with domain randomization; the announcement also describes sim-to-real reinforcement learning. Figure says this learned controller replaces 109,504 lines of hand-engineered C++. S2 does not plan low-level footsteps: S1 interprets its semantic latents into motor commands and S0 executes them. The post describes its dishwasher demonstration as a continuous four-minute autonomous task with 61 loco-manipulation actions, implicit error recovery, no resets, and no human intervention. Those are Figure’s descriptions of the demonstration; no independently timed trial or aggregate success-rate estimate sits behind them <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />.

These are Figure’s own architecture descriptions and demonstrations; no independent replication exists behind them. The two linked announcement texts do not provide repeated-trial success-rate tables or release terms for the trained Helix policies. The 2025 post identifies an open-weight VLM backbone; that is not a release of the complete trained Helix policy. Read the videos as demonstrations; treat them as no substitute for success-rate estimates <Cite id="helix-2025" /> <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />.

## AgiBot: GO-1 and GO-2

The AgiBot World report, first submitted in March 2025, introduces GO-1. Its inspected methods describe a hierarchical vision-language-latent-action (ViLLA) framework: a latent action model learns from consecutive video frames, a VLM-conditioned latent planner predicts latent action tokens, and an action expert generates low-level actions conditioned on the preceding modules. The paper explicitly includes human video without action labels and cross-embodiment robot data in training. It describes Colosseo as an open-sourced platform of data, models, benchmarks, and an ecosystem; that description does not establish that GO-1 checkpoints and the dataset were released together <Cite id="agibot-world-2025" />. AgiBot's later GO-2 announcement also names ViLLA when describing GO-1 <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />.

AgiBot presents GO-2 as a response to what it calls the “Semantic-Actuation Gap” between reasoning signals and motor commands. Its Action Chain-of-Thought generates a high-level sequence of action intents as a macro-plan. In the asynchronous dual system, the lower-frequency Semantic Planning Module (System 2), called the “General Commander,” generates structured action sequences through Progressive Refinement. The higher-frequency Action Following Module (System 1), called the “Agile Executor,” combines those intents with real-time observations and uses Residual Refinement to compensate for noise. Teacher forcing is described as a training mechanism for following approximately correct but imperfect reasoning; it adds no inference-time controller. The announcement gives relative frequencies for the two modules; no numerical planner, follower, or robot-control rate appears in it <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />.

AgiBot’s announcement reports an average success rate of 98.5% across LIBERO Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long; 86.6% zero-shot success in LIBERO-Plus environments with disturbances; and, under its Genie Sim 3.0 sim-to-real heading, 82.9% real-world success for a model trained solely on simulation data. It claims superiority over π0.5 and NVIDIA GR00T, but the announcement text does not give the trial denominators, uncertainty estimates, disturbance protocol, or comparator versions needed to reconstruct a matched comparison. These are vendor-reported summaries, and they do not interchange as measures of frontier capability <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. AgiBot also says the action-reasoning contribution was accepted at CVPR 2026 and the asynchronous architecture at ACL 2026. That is the vendor’s acceptance claim; the conference record itself was not checked. This announcement does not establish trained GO-2 weight availability; no universal “no paper” or “closed weights” conclusion follows <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />.

## Skild: what the Series C announcement discloses

Skild AI's January 14, 2026 Series C announcement reports a \$1.4 billion raise at a valuation of over \$14 billion. The valuation is stated as over \$14 billion, a lower bound with no exact figure given. Skild calls its model “omni-bodied” and claims it can control robots without prior knowledge of their body form; this is the company's assertion, and universal capability remains undemonstrated. <Cite id="skild-series-c-2026" />

The announcement does contain technical descriptions: it names simulation and Internet video for pretraining, and teleoperation and deployments for post-training. Its teleoperation description maps images and proprioception to sequences of joint torques; it is a description of data, and the runtime action-head architecture stays undisclosed. The captured announcement does not specify model architecture, parameter count, control frequency, action-chunk horizon, a reproducible benchmark protocol, or weight-download and licensing terms. That bounded disclosure gap is more precise than saying that nothing technical is publicly verifiable. <Cite id="skild-series-c-2026" />

## The field at a glance

Return to the timeline with all thirteen entries described. Selecting any node gives its capability annotation and primary source, and the π entries are cross-references to [The Pi Line](/manipulation/pi-line), included so the open and closed sides can be compared on one axis.

<Callout variant="warn" title="Vendor-reported is not verified">
  The timeline is a selected reading list; its records are issuer-reported, and no entry here stands as an independent replication. Attribute an announcement’s numerical claims to its issuer; an announcement is not independent verification.
</Callout>

The split that matters for your own work is the open column. Everything downloadable as of August 2026, GR00T N1.x, GO-1, π0.5 and its predecessors, Octo, OpenVLA, sits at least one generation behind the closed frontier, and the gap is largest exactly where the vendors aim their marketing: zero-shot, open-world behavior that saturated simulation benchmarks cannot measure. The human-video transfer question is not scale alone versus a universally required alignment interface. Simar Kareer and colleagues at Physical Intelligence report transfer when π0.5 is co-fine-tuned on human data represented by 3D hand positions and relevant robot data, without a special transfer-learning mechanism; their experiments tie improved transfer to the quantity and diversity of robot pretraining <Cite id="pi-human-to-robot-2025" />. Ruijie Zheng and colleagues’ EgoScale combines relative wrist motion and retargeted hand actions with aligned human-robot mid-training, and reports that scale and this alignment are complementary in its dexterous-manipulation setting <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />. These are different recipes and evaluations; neither conclusion is shown to be universal. [Cross-embodiment transfer](/manipulation/cross-embodiment) examines their qualifications.

A generalist robot policy is one learned model trained to perform many tasks, often on several robot bodies <Cite id="tri-lbm-2025" />.

Outside the [VLA line](/manipulation/vla-models/) and [Physical Intelligence's π models](/manipulation/pi-line/), the main 2026 lines are Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />, NVIDIA's GR00T, Figure's Helix, AgiBot's GO series, Skild AI and Generalist AI. Filter the timeline's 13 selected records, an authored selection, with Downloadable only.

<GeneralistReleaseTimeline className="my-6" />

## Gemini Robotics

DeepMind's March 2025 report introduces a Gemini 2.0-based family. Gemini Robotics-ER extends spatial and temporal understanding for pointing, trajectory prediction and grasp prediction, and Gemini Robotics builds on ER to produce robot actions <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2025" />. The March 12, 2025 launch post says Gemini Robotics more than doubles performance on a comprehensive generalization benchmark against other state-of-the-art VLAs, announces an Apptronik humanoid partnership and gives ER to trusted testers <Cite id="gemini-robotics-blog-2025" />.

The 1.5 report, first submitted to arXiv on October 2, 2025, interleaves natural-language thinking with VLA actions, introduces Motion Transfer across embodiments and uses the separate GR-ER 1.5 model as an orchestrator. Varying ER's thinking budget shows that the useful amount of thinking depends on the task <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. The launch post, dated September 25, 2025, made ER 1.5 available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Gemini Robotics 1.5 to select partners <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-blog-2025" />.

Gemini Robotics On-Device (June 2025) was the first DeepMind VLA offered for fine-tuning, through an SDK for trusted testers <Cite id="gemini-robotics-on-device-2025" />. ER 1.6, released on April 14, 2026 through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, added reading of gauges and sight glasses, a use case found with Boston Dynamics <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-1-6-2026" />.

On July 30, 2026, DeepMind announced Gemini Robotics 2 as three models: a VLA that converts vision and language into motor control, the embodied-reasoning VLM ER 2, and On-Device 2 for local operation. Apollo 2 walks, crouches and stretches to manipulate objects, where earlier humanoid models did upper-body tabletop tasks. The SharpaWave hand has 22 <Term id="degrees-of-freedom">DoF</Term>, and the Franka Duo uses two-fingered parallel grippers. One checkpoint runs Apollo 2 with SharpaWave hands, Apollo 2 with Inspire hands and Franka Duo with the Robotiq gripper <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />.

ER 2 plans multi-step tasks lasting several minutes, tracks progress, coordinates with the VLA and supports collaboration between robots. DeepMind says On-Device 2 adapts to new bi-arm embodiments in a few hours, typically with fewer than 200 examples, shown on Dexmate, SO101 and Trossen <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />. The ER 2 post adds success detection on raw video feeds and instrument reading tested on 10 instrument types <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-2-2026" />.

DeepMind's image alt text reports whole-body averages on Apollo with Inspire hands of 76.3% for picking from a shelf, 68.4% from a table and 45.7% from the floor. Single-task results on Apollo with Sharpa hands are 92% for unscrewing a bulb, 36% for screwing one in, 44% for tying a trash bag, 40% for Ziplock and 32% for Dustpan. Trial counts and error bars are unexplained, and DeepMind concludes that "the multi-finger dexterous manipulation remains challenging" <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />.

The 1.5 model card specifies continuous numerical actions, plus text when thinking is enabled, but no action-head family, chunk lengths, command rate or parameter count <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. The Gemini Robotics 2 announcement also omits them and Motion Transfer internals. ER 2 launched on Google AI Studio and in private preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the VLA and On-Device 2 went to early-access partners, and weight and licence terms are undisclosed <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />. DeepMind validates its Veo-based [world-model](/world-models/) policy simulator against more than 1,600 real trials of eight Gemini Robotics checkpoints <Cite id="veo-world-simulator-2025" />.

## GR00T: the open humanoid line

GR00T N1, first submitted in March 2025, couples a <Term id="vision-language-model">VLM</Term> backbone to a <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> diffusion-transformer action head that reads vision-language tokens through cross-attention, and links the public GR00T-N1-2B checkpoint <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />. N1.5, dated June 11, 2025, freezes the VLM in pretraining and fine-tuning and was trained for 250K steps on 1K H100 GPUs <Cite id="gr00t-n1-5-2025" />. N1.6, dated December 15, 2025, doubles the DiT to 32 layers, and NVIDIA reports it outperforms N1.5 in simulation and on real YAM, AgiBot Genie-1 and Unitree G1 robots <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />.

The Isaac-GR00T repository lists N1.7 on April 18, 2026, with a Cosmos-Reason2-2B backbone on the Qwen3-VL architecture and a 3B-parameter base checkpoint. The DiT returns from 32 to 16 layers, the state and action interface grows to 132 dimensions, and the prediction horizon to 40. Actions are relative end-effector deltas shared by robot and human embodiments, and pretraining adds 20K hours of EgoScale human video. Inference needs one GPU with 16 GB or more of VRAM <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. The EgoScale paper itself reports over 20,854 hours <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />.

The README's licence section assigns Apache 2.0 to code and the NVIDIA Open Model License to weights, while its introduction calls N1.7 "fully commercially licensable under Apache 2.0". NVIDIA describes N1.7 as comparable to N1.6, with better generalization and language following <Cite id="isaac-gr00t-repo-2026" />. On March 16, 2026, NVIDIA put N1.7 into early access with commercial licensing and previewed GR00T N2, a DreamZero-based model slated for year-end that it says succeeds at new tasks more than twice as often as leading VLAs <Cite id="nvidia-gtc-gr00t-n2-2026" />.

## Figure Helix

Figure's February 20, 2025 Helix post pairs two systems. S2, an internet-pretrained VLM, produces a continuous latent task representation at 7 to 9 Hz, and S1, a latent-conditioned visuomotor transformer, reads it with images and robot state at 200 Hz. S1 outputs wrist poses, finger flexion and abduction, torso and head orientation targets, and a synthetic task-completion signal. The post calls the S2 backbone open-source and open-weight <Cite id="helix-2025" />.

Figure's January 27, 2026 Helix 02 post adds a third layer. S2 interprets scenes and language and sequences latent goals. S1 maps head and palm cameras, fingertip touch and full-body proprioception to full-body joint targets at 200 Hz. S0, a 10M-parameter whole-body controller, outputs joint-level actuator commands at 1 kHz. Figure says S0 trains entirely in simulation on over 1,000 hours of joint-level retargeted human motion, using sim-to-real reinforcement learning across more than 200,000 domain-randomized parallel environments. It replaces 109,504 lines of hand-written C++. Its dishwasher demonstration is described as one continuous four-minute task with 61 loco-manipulation actions, implicit error recovery, no resets and no human intervention <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />. Neither Helix post gives repeated-trial success tables or release terms for the trained policies <Cite id="helix-2025" /> <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />.

In September 2025 Figure reported that robots trained only on egocentric human video navigate from commands like "go to the fridge" <Cite id="figure-go-big-2025" />. Its August 25, 2026 Index announcement counts over 16M uploaded videos and commits over \$1B over 12 months to data and compute <Cite id="figure-index-2026" />. Figure reports that Index pretraining, all else fixed, lifted Helix 2.5's zero-shot success in 30 unseen homes from 9% to 56% <Cite id="helix-2-5-2026" />.

## AgiBot: GO-1 and GO-2

The AgiBot World report, first submitted in March 2025, introduces GO-1 and its vision-language-latent-action (ViLLA) framework. A latent action model learns from consecutive video frames, a VLM-conditioned planner predicts latent action tokens, and an action expert generates low-level actions. Training includes unlabeled human video and cross-embodiment robot data, and the report presents Colosseo as an open platform <Cite id="agibot-world-2025" />. The repository dates AgiBot World Beta, with 1,003,672 trajectories, to March 1, 2025 and the open-sourcing of GO-1 to September 19, 2025 <Cite id="agibot-world-repo" />.

AgiBot presents GO-2 as closing a "Semantic-Actuation Gap" between reasoning and motor commands. Its Action Chain-of-Thought first generates a macro-plan of action intents. A lower-frequency System 2, the "General Commander", generates structured action sequences through Progressive Refinement, and a higher-frequency System 1, the "Agile Executor", combines them with live observations and corrects noise with Residual Refinement. Teacher forcing trains the executor to follow imperfect reasoning. The announcement gives only relative rates for the two modules <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. AgiBot says its action-reasoning work was accepted at CVPR 2026 and its asynchronous architecture at ACL 2026 <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. The ACoT-VLA paper's arXiv record confirms the CVPR acceptance <Cite id="acot-vla-2026" />.

AgiBot reports 98.5% average success across LIBERO Spatial, Object, Goal and Long; 86.6% zero-shot in LIBERO-Plus environments with disturbances; and 82.9% real-world success for a model trained only on simulation, under a Genie Sim 3.0 heading. It claims superiority over π0.5 and GR00T without trial counts, uncertainty, disturbance protocol or comparator versions <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. On LIBERO-Plus, typical VLAs drop from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />.

## Skild AI

Skild AI's January 14, 2026 [Series C](/market-map/) raised \$1.4 billion at a valuation of over \$14 billion. Skild calls its model "omni-bodied" and says it can control robots without prior knowledge of their body form. It names simulation and Internet video for pretraining and teleoperation and deployments for post-training, with teleoperation mapping images and proprioception to joint-torque sequences. Architecture, parameter count, control rate, chunk horizon, benchmark protocol and weight terms are not given <Cite id="skild-series-c-2026" />.

A July 2025 Skild post describes a low-frequency manipulation and navigation policy that feeds a high-frequency low-level policy <Cite id="skild-brain-2025" />, and a September 2025 post describes training on 100,000 simulated robots <Cite id="skild-omni-bodied-2025" />. Skild presents S1 (August 18, 2026) as an in-context learner: shown a video of a task, it executes it. On unseen long-horizon tasks of 4 to 8 minutes, Skild reports 66% cumulative per-step success at 100k hours of pretraining, against 9% for language prompting <Cite id="skild-s1-2026" />. Skild says S1 then learned soccer through 140 years of simulated self-play before transfer to a robot <Cite id="skild-self-play-2026" />. The company also reports passing \$100M in annual recurring revenue with 60+ paying customers <Cite id="skild-arr-2026" />.

## Generalist AI

Generalist AI says GEN-0 (November 2025) is pretrained on over 270,000 hours of [real-world manipulation data](/data-hardware/data-bottleneck/), growing by 10,000 hours a week, and tested on 6-DoF, 7-DoF and 16+-DoF semi-humanoid robots <Cite id="generalist-gen0-2025" />. It reports that GEN-1 (April 2026), trained from scratch on half a million hours, reaches 99% average success on tasks where earlier models achieve 64%. It also reports GEN-1 works about 3 times faster than the state of the art, with 1 hour of robot data per task <Cite id="generalist-gen1-2026" />. Generalist says GEN-1.5 (August 2026) outputs 100 Hz actions and learns a task from 3 to 12 seconds of one demonstration in context, with 59% average one-shot success across 10 tasks <Cite id="gen-1-5-2026" />.

## Independent evaluation

RoboArena ranks generalist policies through double-blind pairwise trials at seven institutions, with more than 600 real-robot episodes across seven policies <Cite id="roboarena-2025" />, and TRI evaluates its Large Behavior Models in blind, randomized trials with statistical confidence <Cite id="tri-lbm-2025" />.

## Human-video transfer

Simar Kareer and colleagues at Physical Intelligence and Georgia Tech co-fine-tune π0.5 on human data, with 3D hand positions as actions, and relevant robot data, with no special transfer mechanism. Transfer improves with the quantity and diversity of robot pretraining <Cite id="pi-human-to-robot-2025" />. Ruijie Zheng and colleagues' EgoScale adds aligned human-robot mid-training to relative wrist motion and retargeted hand actions, and finds scale and alignment complementary <Cite id="egoscale-2026" />. [Cross-embodiment transfer](/manipulation/cross-embodiment/) compares them.

edits.after: ## Learned and orchestrated hierarchies, 2025 to 2026

edits.before: Read the current frontier systems side by side and the same pattern appears in each one.
edits.after: Figure's Helix pairs a 7B VLM at 7 to 9 Hz with an 80M-parameter visuomotor policy at 200 Hz, trained end-to-end <Cite id="helix-2025" />. GR00T N1 runs its VLM at 10 Hz on an L40 GPU and its action module at 120 Hz <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />, and Fast-in-Slow partially shares parameters between the two, reaching 117.7 Hz with eight-action chunks <Cite id="fast-in-slow-2025" />.

edits.before:
- **π0.5** co-trains on robot data, semantic subtask labels, and multimodal web tasks. Pretraining uses discrete tokens; post-training adds the continuous action expert. At inference, the same model predicts a high-level language subtask and then conditions low-level actions on it. High-level inference runs less frequently than low-level action inference; this does not establish a numerical inference rate <Cite id="pi05-2025" />.
- **Hi Robot** uses two separately trained policies initialized from PaliGemma: a high-level VLM and a low-level π0 VLA. The high level reads camera images and open-ended instructions, then sends simpler language commands to the low level, which also receives images and robot state. High-level inference is rerun when one second has elapsed or new human feedback arrives; users can intervene with text or transcribed speech and can signal a return to the prior task <Cite id="hi-robot-2025" />. The training combines human-labelled demonstrations with synthetic interactions, with a separate high-level policy for each task domain in the reported experiments. Evaluations cover table bussing, sandwich making and grocery shopping. This hierarchy does not guarantee successful execution: the authors report missing high-level memory, low-level instruction violations and difficulty recovering from dropped objects <Cite id="hi-robot-2025" />.
- **Gemini Robotics 1.5** combines both patterns: with thinking enabled, the VLA appends natural-language reasoning to its context before emitting actions; the agentic system pairs it with a separate GR-ER 1.5 orchestrator. Internal VLA thinking and the external orchestrator therefore coexist <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />.

Its Semantic Planning Module (System 2) generates action intents through Progressive Refinement at a lower frequency; its Action Following Module (System 1) combines intents and real-time observations through Residual Refinement at a higher frequency. edits.before: ## The verdict
edits.after: π0.7 can condition actions on subgoal images from a BAGEL-initialized world model; subtask and image generation run in separate threads, and the VLA uses the latest outputs <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. In π0.6-MEM, a high-level policy predicts the next language subtask and an updated memory summary, and the low-level policy acts on the subtask and a shorter observation history <Cite id="mem-2026" />. VISTA's high-level world-model planner raises the same VLA from 14% to 69% in novel scenarios <Cite id="vista-2026" />. SeeQ, from Saksham Singh, Aviral Kumar and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon (September 2026), puts the subtask inside the value function: it names the active subtask in language before estimating that subtask's value <Cite id="seeq-2026" />.

edits.before: Two claims are worth stating plainly, and both need framing.
edits.after: AgiBot describes GO-2 as a unified system with an asynchronous two-module hierarchy: a lower-frequency System 2 generates action intents through Progressive Refinement, and a higher-frequency System 1 combines them with observations through Residual Refinement. It gives no numerical rates or shared-weights claim; GO-2 trains with teacher forcing <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. Figure's Helix 02 adds S0 beneath S2's behavior sequencing and S1's 200 Hz full-body joint targets from vision, touch and proprioception. S0 is a 10M-parameter network that outputs actuator commands at 1 kHz; Helix 02 does not restate the S2 rate <Cite id="helix-02-2026" />.

edits.before: First: **the five cited examples place high-level guidance at different interfaces.** π0.5 uses the same model to infer a language subtask and actions conditioned on it <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. The π0.6-MEM report describes a high-level policy that predicts the next subtask and updated language memory, with a low-level policy conditioned on that subtask and recent observations <Cite id="mem-2026" />. π0.7 can use subgoal images from a BAGEL-initialized world model; when those images are used, subtask and image generation run asynchronously in separate threads <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. With thinking enabled, Gemini Robotics 1.5 appends natural-language reasoning to the VLA context before actions, while its agentic system retains a separate GR-ER 1.5 orchestrator <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. AgiBot describes GO-2 as a lower-frequency semantic planning module paired with a higher-frequency action-following module <Cite id="agibot-go2-2026" />. This is a comparison of reported mechanisms; it supplies no evidence that separate planners have been superseded across the field.
edits.after: With thinking on, Gemini Robotics 1.5 appends natural-language reasoning before acting, and its agentic system adds a separate GR-ER 1.5 orchestrator whose useful thinking budget depends on the task. ER 1.5 also produces point sequences that trace trajectories <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. Google made ER 1.5 broadly available as a high-level model that can call a VLA or user-defined functions <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-15-dev-2025" />. In [Gemini Robotics 2](/manipulation/generalist-policies/), DeepMind calls ER 2 the robot's high-level brain; it coordinates with the VLA and tracks multi-minute tasks <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />. Google says ER 2 hands off motor execution to any lower-level VLA and reports 57.4% accuracy on progress classification <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er-2-2026" />.

edits.before: Second: **geometric supervision in training does not establish the disappearance of geometric reasoning at runtime.** π0.5’s paper describes training the model to predict relevant bounding boxes before subtask labels, and adding indoor-scene and household-object data with bounding-box annotations to its web-data mixture <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 also reports complex pointing, including point sequences that can represent motion trajectories and paths <Cite id="gemini-robotics-15-2025" />. That is evidence of a geometric reasoning capability; it proves nothing about a specific deployed controller using a keypoint loop. The scope here is those reported mechanisms, short of an exhaustive inventory of 2026 frontier systems; no field-wide absence of runtime keypoint interfaces is claimed.

edits.before:
<Term id="knowledge-insulation">Knowledge insulation</Term> is a training recipe that keeps action learning from damaging a vision-language-action model's pretrained backbone. RT-2 represents robot actions as tokens, using the discretization introduced for RT-1: each continuous action dimension is divided into 256 uniform bins. Its robot inputs pair a camera image with a task instruction <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. π0 instead adds a continuous <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> action expert to a pretrained <Term id="vision-language-model">VLM</Term> <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. Knowledge Insulation, studied by Physical Intelligence in 2025, combines the two: discrete actions train the backbone’s representations while a continuous-action expert trains alongside it without sending gradients back into the backbone.

<Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> The paper distinguishes the earlier two-stage π0.5 recipe from simultaneous single-stage training.

<Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" /> The research note calls this single-stage model π0.5 + KI.

The barrier is below, on the backward pass. Turn off "Protect language skills", which removes the stop-gradient: the damage the recipe exists to prevent runs straight back into the pretrained backbone.
edits.after: <Term id="knowledge-insulation">Knowledge insulation</Term> (KI) is a training recipe that keeps action learning from damaging a vision-language-action model's pretrained backbone. Discrete FAST action tokens train the backbone, while a stop-gradient keeps a <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> action expert's gradients out of it <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />. Turn off "Protect language skills" to remove the stop-gradient.

edits.before: The 7.5x figure compares training steps to similar table-bussing performance; inference latency and equal wall-clock training budgets are different axes. The paper reports about 20% extra training cost from the combined objectives. The paper's architecture details describe a 2B language-model backbone within the complete VLM and a 300M action expert; the research note labels the complete VLM as 3B <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
edits.after: ## Origins

edits.before: ## What naive joint training breaks
edits.after: RT-2 tokenizes each continuous action dimension into 256 uniform bins, as RT-1 did <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. Physical Intelligence's 2025 KI note judges such fixed-bin tokens unsuitable for high-frequency, precise or fluent motions <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />, and the 7B token-based OpenVLA decodes at about 6 Hz on an RTX 4090 <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. π0 adds a continuous action expert to a pretrained <Term id="vision-language-model">VLM</Term> <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. π0.5 trained 280k steps on discrete tokens, then post-trained a randomly initialized flow-matching expert <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. KI makes this a single stage <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />, called π0.5 + KI <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.

edits.before: The paper studies a pretrained VLM with a newly initialized continuous-action expert. It finds that expert gradients can interfere with the image encoder and language backbone during adaptation, slowing learning and weakening language following. The proposed explanation is interference with pretrained representations; the paper measures no claim that every early gradient is large or that the model can never recover <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after: ## Naive joint training

edits.before: One qualitative example illustrates the problem with π0: instructed to bus a spoon into the bin, it grasps trash instead. The research note describes the target as the dish container and explicitly calls its explanation a hypothesis: disrupted language processing may lead the model to learn other correlations first <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />. The note’s phrase "not suitable for high-frequency, precise, or fluent motions" refers to the earlier simple fixed-bin action representation and to no other tokenized-action method <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
edits.after: Fine-tuning a pretrained network through a random head distorts its features and raises out-of-distribution error <Cite id="kumar-finetuning-distorts-2022" />. The KI paper finds the same in VLAs: gradients from a new action expert degrade the backbone, slowing training and weakening language following. Told to bus a spoon into the bin, π0 grasps trash <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />. The note hypothesizes that disrupted language processing lets the model learn other correlations first <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.

edits.before: ## The recipe, in three parts
edits.after: ChatVLA calls this spurious forgetting, robot training overwriting visual-text alignments <Cite id="chatvla-2025" />, and InstructVLA reports catastrophic forgetting of vision-language skills in existing VLAs <Cite id="instructvla-2025" />. Between robot tasks, pretrained VLAs resist forgetting; simple experience replay sometimes removes it <Cite id="vla-continual-forgetting-2026" />.

edits.before: Knowledge Insulation separates the learning signals <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />:
edits.after: ## Recipe

edits.before:
1. **The action expert trains with flow matching** to generate continuous action chunks at inference.
2. **The backbone learns from discrete FAST <Term id="action-tokenization">action tokens</Term>**, alongside general vision-language and robot-planning data. FAST normalizes actions, applies a DCT separately along time for each action dimension, scales and rounds the coefficients, then uses byte-pair encoding to compress the flattened sequence. Coefficient quantization is lossy; BPE losslessly compresses the resulting integer sequence <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.
3. **Stop-gradient blocks the expert’s updates to the backbone.** The expert can attend to the image/language/state prefix and its own continuous-action tokens. It does not attend to FAST action tokens, and the backbone does not attend to the expert. The attention equations apply stop-gradient to the backbone keys and values read by the expert, leaving forward information available while blocking that backward path <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after:
1. The action expert trains with flow matching, regressing vector fields of fixed conditional probability paths <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />, and generates continuous action chunks at inference <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
2. The backbone learns from discrete FAST <Term id="action-tokenization">action tokens</Term> plus vision-language and robot-planning data. FAST normalizes actions, applies a DCT to each action dimension over time, and scales and rounds the coefficients, the lossy step. Byte-pair encoding then compresses the flattened sequence losslessly <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.
3. Stop-gradient blocks the expert's updates to the backbone. The expert attends to the image, language and state prefix and to itself, never to FAST tokens; the backbone never attends to it. Stop-gradient on the backbone keys and values the expert reads keeps the forward path and cuts the backward one <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

edits.before: The figure at the top of this module walks both passes through the two stacks, including the failure mode with the barrier removed.
edits.after: Training both outputs costs about 20% more compute. The paper's backbone is a 2B language model with a 300M expert <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />; the note labels the complete VLM 3B <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />, the size of PaliGemma, which pairs a SigLIP-So400m encoder with Gemma-2B <Cite id="paligemma-2024" />.

edits.before: ## Why the barrier alone is not enough
edits.after: FAST tokens are π0.5 + KI's training representation and continuous flow actions its runtime output <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />, so a [comparison matrix](/manipulation/comparison-matrix/) needs both columns.

edits.before: Stopping expert gradients is not the same as adapting the backbone for robot control. Without another robot-learning signal, the pretrained backbone’s representations remain unadapted to the task. In the paper’s frozen-backbone ablation, shirt-folding performance is reported as 0%; that is an outcome for this tested configuration and proves nothing about all frozen-backbone policies <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after: ## Limits and alternatives

edits.before: FAST-token supervision supplies the missing action-learning signal while the gradient barrier blocks updates from the newly initialized expert. The paper also finds that vision-language co-training can give the joint-training baseline good language following even without stop-gradient. The evidence supports the combined recipe; it makes no claim that continuous gradients always destroy knowledge or that cross-entropy guarantees perfect preservation <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after: Stopping expert gradients does not adapt the backbone: with the backbone frozen, the paper's shirt-folding policy scores 0%. FAST supervision supplies that signal, and vision-language co-training can give plain joint training good language following without stop-gradient <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

edits.before: ## What it buys
edits.after: GR00T N1 freezes the language part of its VLM <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />. NVIDIA reports that N1.5, which froze the whole VLM among other changes, raised real GR-1 language following from 46.6% to 93.3% <Cite id="gr00t-n1-5-2025" />; N1.6 unfreezes the top 4 layers <Cite id="gr00t-n1-6-2025" />. BLIP-2 bridges frozen image encoders and language models <Cite id="blip2-2023" />. VLM2VLA writes actions as language and trains only LoRA adapters <Cite id="vlm2vla-2025" />. UAM keeps over 95% of its VLM's multimodal capability with no freezing, gradient stopping or co-training <Cite id="uam-forgetting-2026" />.

edits.before: The paper separates two table-bussing comparisons. For a generalist trained on many embodiments, π0 needs 7.5 times as many training steps as π0.5 + KI to reach similar performance. For specialist models trained on one embodiment, the authors report that π0-FAST needs twice the wall-clock time to solve the task. That second result is task-completion time; a generic twofold inference-latency multiplier or a comparison across all robot tasks is a different claim <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
edits.after: Figure's Helix instead backpropagates from its fast policy into the VLM through their shared latent vector <Cite id="helix-2025" />. HybridVLA trains discrete and diffusion action prediction together, using a collaborative recipe against interference <Cite id="hybridvla-2025" />.

edits.before: The table-bussing task starts with 12 objects and scores correct placement into the dish and trash receptacles. The paper reports ten episodes per real-world task and policy. In a separate mobile-manipulation object-generalization experiment, the robot moves unseen objects from a counter into an already-open drawer; the research note says web-data co-training boosted generalization most in that comparison. These are different evaluation populations and form no single combined benchmark <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
edits.after: ## Results

edits.before: Language following also improves in the items-in-drawer comparison, but remains imperfect. The paper notes that VLM co-training can help the joint-training baseline follow language even without stop-gradient <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
edits.after: A many-embodiment π0 generalist needs 7.5 times the training steps of π0.5 + KI to reach similar table-bussing performance. Single-embodiment π0-FAST specialists need twice the wall-clock time from slow inference <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />. Table bussing starts with 12 objects for dish and trash receptacles, at ten episodes per task and policy. When a mobile robot moves unseen objects into an open drawer, web-data co-training boosts generalization most, and language following improves but stays imperfect <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.
