edits.before: The pi line is Physical Intelligence's series of vision-language-action models. The [VLA module](/manipulation/vla-models) ended on a bottleneck: <Term id="action-tokenization">discrete action tokens</Term> let a web-pretrained model emit actions with the machinery it already has, but autoregressive decoding caps the control rate an order of magnitude below what dexterous manipulation needs. Physical Intelligence's pi line answers it with a different split of labor. Keep the pretrained backbone, replace the token head with a <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> action expert, and then keep fixing what that first design got wrong. This module walks the line from π0 (October 2024) to π0.7 (April 2026), including what the pinned checkpoint catalogue actually lists.
edits.after: The pi line is Physical Intelligence's series of [vision-language-action models](/manipulation/vla-models/), from π0 (October 2024) to π0.7 (April 2026) <Cite id="pi0-blog-2024" /> <Cite id="pi07-2026" />.

edits.before: π0 grafts a second transformer onto a pretrained <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term> <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. The first set of weights handles image and text tokens and is initialized from PaliGemma. The second set, the action expert, handles robotics-specific tokens and has approximately 300M parameters in the paper’s implementation. The structural point matters for anyone implementing one: the action expert is a second set of transformer weights inside a single model, in the paper's words "a single transformer with two sets of weights (also known as experts)." It is a full transformer whose 50 action tokens attend into the backbone's activations at every layer through shared self-attention, with a bidirectional mask among themselves. Observations are 2 or 3 RGB images, tokenized language, and proprioceptive state; the model predicts H = 50 actions. The paper’s UR5e and Franka setups run at 20 Hz and execute 16 actions before another inference; other tested robots run at 50 Hz and execute 25 <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. Whether the system then runs all fifty of those actions is a separate question: this is the predicted horizon, and how much of it a π release actually commits before the next inference is what the later sections of this module track.

edits.before: Where [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy) denoises with a DDPM, π0 trains the expert with conditional flow matching on a straight transport path. Sample noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, form the interpolant $A_t^\tau = \tau A_t + (1 - \tau)\varepsilon$, and regress the network $v_\theta$ onto the target vector field $u = A_t - \varepsilon$, with the training timestep $\tau$ drawn from a beta distribution weighted toward the noisy end. At inference, integrate from $\tau = 0$ to $\tau = 1$ with forward Euler in 10 steps; the image-text-state prefix is KV-cached once, so each step recomputes only the action-token suffix, which is what makes 10 steps affordable <Cite id="pi0-2024" />.
edits.after: Where [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy/) denoises with a DDPM, π0 trains the expert with conditional flow matching on a straight path. Sample noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, form $A_t^\tau = \tau A_t + (1 - \tau)\varepsilon$, and regress $v_\theta$ onto $u = A_t - \varepsilon$, drawing $\tau$ from a beta distribution weighted toward the noisy end. Inference integrates from $\tau = 0$ to $\tau = 1$ in 10 forward-Euler steps; the image-text-state prefix is KV-cached once, so each step recomputes only the action suffix <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. Lipman et al. found optimal-transport paths more efficient than diffusion paths for training and sampling <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />.

edits.before: <Term id="cross-embodiment">Cross-embodiment</Term> training combines data from robot types with different configuration spaces and action representations, including single-arm, dual-arm and mobile manipulators <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. The paper separates broad pre-training from task-specific post-training: the base model performs tasks at what the authors call “rudimentary proficiency,” while complex tasks such as laundry folding use curated post-training data <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. Its execution description commits 16 of the 50 predicted actions on UR5e/Franka and 25 on the other tested robots; no universal 50-step commitment is made. The RTC paper later evaluates asynchronous execution against stopping between chunks using π0.5; that experiment is not evidence that every original π0 deployment executed all 50 predictions <Cite id="real-time-chunking-2025" />.

edits.before: Flow matching's selling point over diffusion is path geometry. A DDPM trajectory curves through noise space; the rectified flow path from noise to action is nearly a straight line, so a coarse Euler integration tracks it well. That is what the figure at the top of this module measures: samples start as Gaussian noise in a 2D action space and are transported toward two action modes under a fixed integration budget.
edits.after: A DDPM path curves through noise space, while rectified flow straightens paths so that coarse time steps simulate them accurately <Cite id="rectified-flow-2022" />. Each Euler step costs a forward pass through the expert: π0 uses 10 steps <Cite id="pi0-2024" />, π0.6 uses five and reports 63 ms per chunk on one H100 with three cameras <Cite id="pi06-model-card-2025" />, and π0.7 also uses five <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. NVIDIA's Jetson AI Lab measured π0.5 (LIBERO checkpoint, action horizon 10) on Jetson AGX Thor at about 132 ms in PyTorch BF16 and about 49 ms with TensorRT FP8 and NVFP4 <Cite id="jetson-ai-lab-openpi-thor" />. Consistency and one-step distillation, covered in [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy/), pursue the same saving.

edits.before: Each Euler step samples the field once and cuts the corner on everything the field does between samples, which is why one or two steps miss. The shape of that curve is the whole deployment argument. Every step costs a forward pass through the expert, and at 50 Hz the budget is fixed by physics; GPU spend cannot move it: π0 uses 10 integration steps <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. π0.6 reports five steps and 63 ms per chunk on one H100 with three cameras <Cite id="pi06-model-card-2025" />. π0.7 also uses five denoising steps in its experiments <Cite id="pi07-2026" />. Those step counts and π0.6’s hardware-specific chunk latency do not measure a common robot-control frequency. The consistency and one-step distillation line covered in [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy) exists for the same reason.

edits.after: ## π0-FAST: compressed action tokens

edits.before: <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" /> FAST diagnoses a weakness of simple per-dimension, per-timestep binning: highly correlated action tokens can make next-token prediction too easy, for example by copying a previous token. In the paper’s evaluations, policies trained with this naïve tokenization make no progress on table bussing at 20 Hz or T-shirt folding at 50 Hz. This is a result for those training setups and claims nothing about every discretization.
edits.after: FAST traces the failure of per-dimension, per-timestep binning to highly correlated tokens, which make next-token prediction trivial, for example by copying the previous token. Policies with this naive tokenization make no progress on table bussing at 20 Hz or T-shirt folding at 50 Hz <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.

edits.before: FAST normalizes each action dimension, applies a discrete cosine transform along time, scales and rounds the coefficients, and byte-pair-encodes their flattened sequence. Rounding trades reconstruction fidelity for compression; the BPE stage losslessly compresses the quantized integers. The universal FAST+ tokenizer is trained on approximately one million one-second action chunks, spanning different embodiments, action spaces and control frequencies. The abstract calls these trajectories, while the paper’s method description states the more precise chunk unit <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.
edits.after: FAST normalizes each action dimension, applies a discrete cosine transform along time, scales and rounds the coefficients, and byte-pair-encodes the flattened sequence. Rounding trades fidelity for compression, and BPE compresses the integers losslessly. The universal FAST+ tokenizer is trained on about one million one-second action chunks across embodiments, action spaces and control frequencies <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />, or "1M real robot action sequences" in PI's post <Cite id="pi-fast-blog-2025" />.

edits.before: The paper trains π0-FAST on a 10k-hour cross-embodied robot-data mixture. In its generalist comparison, π0-FAST matches the compared π0 task performance with five times fewer GPU hours of training. The abstract summarizes the benefit as "up to 5x"; it is a training-compute result, so read it as neither an inference speedup nor a universal training-step ratio <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. Inference is a separate trade-off. The FAST paper reports approximately 750 ms per one-second action chunk on an NVIDIA 4090 for π0-FAST, versus within 100 ms for its diffusion π0 comparison; decoding typically requires 30 to 60 action tokens instead of ten diffusion steps. Separately, the Knowledge Insulation note reports that π0-FAST took twice as long to solve the single-embodiment table-bussing task in its comparison. That is task wall-clock time and carries no generic twofold inference ratio <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" /> <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />. The later KI recipe uses FAST tokens for backbone training while retaining continuous-action inference.
edits.after: Trained on a 10k-hour cross-embodied mixture, π0-FAST matches π0's generalist performance with up to five times fewer GPU hours <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. Inference costs more: about 750 ms per one-second chunk on an NVIDIA 4090, against within 100 ms for diffusion π0, since decoding needs 30 to 60 tokens instead of ten steps <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />. The Knowledge Insulation note reports that π0-FAST took twice as long to finish single-embodiment table bussing <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-2025" />.

edits.before: π0.5 targeted generalization, with speed a secondary concern <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. The architecture keeps the π0 skeleton, but the training mixture adds hybrid multimodal examples that interleave image observations, language commands, object detections, semantic subtask predictions, and low-level actions in a single sequence. The subtask prediction makes the model internally hierarchical: at inference it first predicts a high-level language subtask at low frequency ("pick up the plate"), then conditions the action expert on that subtask at high frequency. There is no separate planner. The paper evaluates long-horizon mobile manipulation in new home environments, and the paper's ablations show the heterogeneous mixture carries the result: removing either cross-embodiment data source significantly degrades the home-task scores, while web data, whose removal was not statistically significant there, has a large effect on language following and high-level subtask inference <Cite id="pi05-2025" />.
edits.after: π0.5 targets open-world generalization <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. It keeps the π0 skeleton and adds hybrid examples that interleave images, language commands, object detections, semantic subtask predictions and low-level actions. At inference it first predicts a language subtask ("pick up the plate") at low frequency, then conditions the action expert on it at high frequency, with no separate planner. In long-horizon mobile manipulation in new homes, removing either cross-embodiment data source significantly hurts home-task scores; removing web data changes them insignificantly and strongly hurts language following and subtask inference <Cite id="pi05-2025" />. Hi Robot had already placed π0 as "System 1" under a high-level VLM with the same backbone <Cite id="hi-robot-blog-2025" />.

Its qualitative example shows π0 being instructed to bus a spoon into the bin but grasping trash instead. The authors extend the earlier two-stage π0.5 approach into a single-stage recipe that trains discrete and continuous actions together:
edits.after: The Knowledge Insulation paper studies how a newly initialized continuous expert interferes with pretrained VLM representations; in one example π0, told to bus a spoon, grasps trash instead. It turns the two-stage π0.5 approach into one stage. The expert trains with flow matching for continuous inference, and the backbone trains on discrete FAST tokens, vision-language data and planning data. Expert gradients stop at the backbone keys and values, the expert attends only to the image, language and state prefix, and the backbone does not attend to the expert <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

edits.before:
1. Train the action expert with flow matching for continuous-action inference.
2. Train the backbone with discrete FAST action tokens, vision-language data and robot-planning data.
3. Stop expert gradients at the backbone keys and values. The expert attends to the image/language/state prefix; the FAST action tokens stay outside its attention. The backbone does not attend to the expert.

In the paper’s frozen-backbone ablation, shirt-folding performance is 0%. FAST supplies a robot-learning signal to adapt the backbone without updates from the action-expert loss. For the generalist table-bussing comparison, π0 needs 7.5 times as many training steps to reach similar performance. These results describe π0.5 + KI and the tested configurations; every other model carrying the π0.5 name stays outside them <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

The language-following evidence also has a qualification: vision-language co-training can give the joint-training baseline good language following without stop-gradient. The authors report improved but still imperfect language following; complete immunity to interference is a stronger claim than they make <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.

<Aside title="Separate training tokens from runtime actions">
  In this recipe, FAST tokens supervise the backbone during training and the flow-matching expert generates continuous actions at inference. A comparison should record both roles for this model and resist inferring the same architecture for every frontier VLA <Cite id="knowledge-insulation-paper-2025" />.
</Aside>

edits.after: ## RL tokens

edits.before:
The MEM report evaluates π0.6-MEM with two complementary memory scales. Its video encoder interleaves bidirectional spatial attention with causal-temporal attention across observations, while a high-level policy predicts updated natural-language summaries of earlier semantic events. Those summary predictions are trained using labels generated by an off-the-shelf language model; they are not an external agent writing the runtime notes <Cite id="mem-2026" />.

The authors report tasks requiring up to fifteen minutes of memory, including recipe setup and kitchen cleanup; the fifteen minutes names the memory span, and no fifteen-minute dense-video input sits behind it. Their separate adaptation experiments train on targeted corrections: adjusting chopstick grasp height after misses and changing which way a refrigerator door is opened. Both memory and memoryless policies receive correction data. Chopstick evaluation uses the lowest table-height setting after collecting data in the upper half of the height range; refrigerator success requires opening within four grasps. The reported in-context adaptation is therefore conditioned on this training and evaluation setup; untrained, indefinite continual learning is a different claim <Cite id="mem-2026" />.

seeAlso: - "data-hardware/hardware-taxonomy" - "manipulation/rl-finetuning" - "classical/control" --- import { ControlLoopBudget } from '@/components/interactive/control-loop-budget'; import { ExecutionModes } from '@/components/interactive/execution-modes'; Real-time execution is the problem of delivering a policy's actions on its controller's clock while the next inference is still running. A policy that needs 60 ms per inference cannot finish a new inference within every 20 ms tick of a 50 Hz controller. Chunked execution can still provide commands at 50 Hz. The control period at 50 Hz is 20 ms, and every component in the loop, cameras, network, preprocessing, model, spends from that budget. The earlier modules treated action chunking as an algorithmic choice; this module is about what happens when the algorithm meets the clock. Real-time execution turns out to be a first-class architectural problem. The way a policy hands off from one chunk to the next while inference is still running changes what the robot physically does, and the naive ways to do it fail in documented, measurable ways . The teaching model below compares one synchronous inference with a 20 ms tick. Its slider uses illustrative scaling and a deliberately chosen 3.0B reference coordinate; it is not a hardware profiler or a proof that a chunked 50 Hz robot controller cannot run. Slide the model-size control and the missed-deadline count follows the new inference time.
## Where the milliseconds go The Real-Time Chunking paper reports a π0.5 latency breakdown with inference on an RTX 4090 in bfloat16, five denoising steps and a wired LAN. Across 50 inference calls during a real episode, mobile total latency is 138.98 ± 6.71 ms: model 96.89 ± 0.16, network 21.20 ± 3.12, image resizing 11.22 ± 5.00 and other work 9.67 ± 3.20 ms. The non-mobile total is 108.76 ± 2.34 ms; the ± values are one standard deviation. Image resizing uses an Intel i7-1260P NUC in the mobile case and an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X workstation in the non-mobile case . At 50 Hz, the mean totals span about 6.95 and 5.44 control periods. Their reciprocals, about 7.20 and 9.19 inferences per second, do not establish the actual replanning or robot-control rate; the RTC experiment uses chunked execution. Jiang, Clemons, Sankaralingam and Kozyrakis study the scaling picture with VLA-Perf, a roofline-based analytical model with no hardware-wide profiling campaign behind it . Its predictions assume optimistic software and attainable peak compute and memory bandwidth. The paper compares them with an optimized π0 Triton implementation on an RTX 4090: the implementation reaches 73.3 to 82.6% of predicted throughput under the tested one-, two- and three-camera settings, with 10 flow-matching steps, chunk size 63 and an empty language prompt. In its separate B100 π0 model sweep, increasing denoising steps from 10 to 50 at chunk size 50 multiplies action-expert latency by 5, but total VLA latency by 2.15. Increasing chunk size from 50 to 250 at 10 steps raises expert latency by 40% and total latency by 11% . Chunk size matters less in this experiment, though it still carries cost; expert latency is one part of the pipeline. ## The hardware wall VLA-Perf predicts π0 inference at 162.5 Hz on H100 and 19.0 Hz (52.57 ms) on Jetson Thor, excluding network latency . The baseline is 2.7B parameters: a 0.4B vision encoder, 2B VLM and 0.3B action expert. It models three 224×224 cameras, 32 language tokens (800 input tokens total), 14 action dimensions, chunk size 50, 10 denoising steps and batch size one, using BF16 or FP16 where BF16 is unsupported. These are inferences per second; robot and controller Hz are different quantities, and sensing and robot execution latency sit outside the analysis. The 9.1B π0-L result, 3.9 Hz on Thor, is for a hypothetical variant built from a 1.1B SigLIP-Giant encoder, 6.5B Llama2 backbone and 1.5B action expert; no measured deployed policy sits behind it . The control-loop interactive above uses a separate teaching curve; its 3.0B coordinate is not the paper’s 2.7B baseline. VLA-Perf defines 10 Hz inference as “acceptable” and 100 Hz as “high-performance” relative to common camera rates; these are the authors’ analysis targets and bind no universal robot-control requirement . For their on-device π0 setup, the predicted 19 Hz exceeds the first target. They propose smaller models, fewer denoising steps or lower-precision quantization to approach 100 Hz. This does not show that future hardware cannot help. The baseline π0 vision encoder, VLM and action expert are all memory-bound on the modeled Thor configuration. On the other evaluated GPUs, vision and VLM work are compute-bound while the action expert remains memory-bound. The component-scaling experiment finds approximately linear latency growth with parameter count . These results do not characterize every possible workload on Thor. The study assumes adequate model accuracy and evaluates BF16/FP16 inference; its quantization recommendation is not an FP4/FP8 2 to 4× speedup result or an accuracy-loss validation. Server placement also depends on the modeled network . For synchronous π0 inference, RTX 4090 over WiFi 6 is 38.7 ms versus Thor’s 52.6 ms, but RTX 4090 over 5G is slower at 55.7 ms. B100 over the same 5G model is 27.8 ms. The paper's network model assumes WiFi 6 upload/download bandwidth of 560/800 Mbps and 3.5 ms base latency, versus 80/500 Mbps and 10 ms for 5G. In the cloud examples, B100 with Ethernet 10G plus the fast-cloud link is 23.4 ms, while 4G plus the slow-cloud link is 273.4 ms. The fast/slow cloud links use 10/1 Gbps and 10/100 ms base latency; the 4G hop uses 19/75 Mbps and 25 ms. These are specified link assumptions and measure no arbitrary deployed network. ## Three ways to hand off a chunk Suppose inference takes d milliseconds. The policy has emitted a chunk, the robot is executing it, and a new chunk is on the way. What happens at the boundary is a design decision, and there are three options on the table. **Synchronous execution** waits: execute a chosen part of the current chunk, pause while the next one is computed, then resume. Do not equate that executed part with the whole predicted chunk: π0 predicts 50 but executes 16 actions on the 20 Hz UR5e/Franka setups or 25 on the other 50 Hz robots . The RTC paper evaluates stopping between chunks as a π0.5 baseline. Its discussion links altered motion dynamics to distribution shift, and its real-world comparison reports faster progress with RTC even after inference pauses are removed from elapsed time . **Naive switching** never waits: the instant the new chunk arrives, execution jumps to it. There is no dead time, but there is a discontinuity. The new chunk was inferred from an observation d milliseconds old, the world has moved since, and the two chunks disagree about what to do right now. The command steps by the full disagreement in a single control tick: a jerk event the hardware feels. **Temporal ensembling**, ACT’s 2023 method, queries the policy at every timestep and combines predictions for that same timestep with weights $w_i=\exp(-mi)$. The paper assigns $i=0$ to the oldest retained prediction, so for positive $m$ older predictions receive greater weight; it does not say newer observations dominate . Averaging predictions from different action modes need not produce a valid action. In the RTC paper’s π0.5 real-robot comparison, both temporal-ensembling variants trigger the robot’s protective stop at +100 and +200 ms of injected latency . **Real-Time Chunking** guides generation of a new action chunk while the current one executes. Its inpainting guidance assigns weight 1 to the first $d$ actions, which will execute during inference; weight 0 to the non-overlapping tail; and decaying intermediate weights to the remaining overlap. These are soft-mask guidance weights; the paper makes no claim that transformer attention itself is partially disabled . The original method is an inference-time procedure for diffusion/flow policies without retraining. In the paper’s six-task π0.5 real-robot evaluation with five denoising steps, RTC’s aggregate throughput shows no degradation over the tested +0, +100 and +200 ms injected delays. The paper also illustrates precise match-lighting at total inference delay above 300 ms; that is not a claim that every dynamic task succeeds under every such delay . The comparison below is an illustrative hand-off model; it implements and measures nothing of RTC. One delay slider drives three constructed velocity traces. The values use arbitrary velocity units; the 0.30 per-tick threshold is a discontinuity proxy standing in for physical jerk. Its five-tick linear blend is a teaching assumption and models neither transformer attention nor the paper’s inpainting solver. ## Training the tolerance in π0.7 uses a training-time version of Real-Time Chunking. Its paper states that training simulates delays of 0 to 12 timesteps, corresponding to a maximum inference latency of 240 ms on a 50 Hz robot . Treat that as a stated training setting; it carries no measured worst-case latency guarantee and proves no production deployment. The experiments predict 50 actions and execute either 15 or 25; UR5e robots run at 20 Hz and the other tested robots at 50 Hz. The paper does not assign the execution choices to specific robots . In September 2026, Fanding Huang, Cheng Chi, Zhi Wang and colleagues reported ChunkTrust, which infers how many actions to execute before replanning from the policy's own outputs while it runs. Its training-free horizon selector combines the stability of each generated chunk with its continuity with the actions already executed. Over all 50 RoboTwin2.0 tasks it raised π0.5's task-averaged success by 6.80 percentage points, and on four real household tasks it raised the mean normalized process score from 50.4% to 57.5% . ## Spending the step budget VLA-Perf’s π0 sweep shows that step count affects expert and total latency by different factors . The following papers report their own step settings. pi0 integrated its flow with 10 Euler steps per chunk . pi0.6 cut that to 5, landing at 63 ms per chunk on a single H100 with three cameras . pi0.7 stays at 5 . These three source-specific choices do not establish field-wide nonadoption of one-step distillation or show that it matters chiefly on edge hardware. π0.7’s paper documents its own five-step policy with training-time RTC and surveys no other laboratories . VLA-Perf’s values are analytical roofline predictions; no five-GPU robot measurement stands behind them. Its π0-L is hypothetical, and it assumes adequate accuracy and validates no quantization accuracy. The control-loop curve is a separate teaching model: it places the 52.57 ms reference at a deliberately chosen 3.0B coordinate instead of the paper’s 2.7B, uses linear and power-law scaling, and reports reciprocal inference rate, a different quantity from robot rate. The hand-off traces use arbitrary velocity units and an illustrative 0.30 per-tick discontinuity proxy; the five-tick blend is not RTC’s inpainting algorithm. The retained measured references have different meanings: RTC reports 108.76 ms non-mobile and 138.98 ms mobile mean total latency in its RTX 4090/wired-LAN setup; the π0.6 model card reports 63 ms per chunk on one H100 with five steps and three cameras. π0.7’s 240 ms is its stated maximum simulated training delay at 50 Hz and carries no measured tolerance guarantee. None of these is a shared controller-frequency benchmark.

edits.before: RL fine-tuning is the use of reinforcement learning to improve a pretrained robot policy from its own successes and failures. <Term id="imitation-learning">Imitation learning</Term> gets a policy that is good on the demonstration distribution and brittle off it, because small per-step errors compound into states the demonstrator never visited <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. Physical Intelligence states the operational version of the same problem: it is relatively easy to get a VLA to succeed at a task some of the time, and quite hard to make it succeed reliably <Cite id="pistar06-blog-2025" />. Reinforcement learning is the only mechanism in the toolbox that learns from failure as well as from success. The obstacle is cost: naive online RL on a multi-billion-parameter VLA, on real hardware, at control rates, is infeasible. Everything in this module is a way around that constraint, and by 2026 the field has converged on a small set of recipes that demonstrably work.

edits.before: Modern policies emit actions through diffusion or <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> heads, and that choice breaks the standard policy-gradient machinery. <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term>-style updates need the log-likelihood of the action the policy actually took; for a flow-matching head the "action" is the endpoint of an ODE integration, and its likelihood under the model is intractable. For two years this was the standard argument for why RL could not touch the frontier VLAs directly. Three methods dissolve it in different ways <Cite id="dppo-2024" /> <Cite id="conrft-2025" /> <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />.
edits.after: <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term> runs several epochs of minibatch updates on a clipped surrogate objective <Cite id="ppo-2017" />, which needs the likelihood of each action taken. <Term id="flow-matching">Flow matching</Term> trains by regressing vector fields along fixed conditional probability paths <Cite id="lipman-flow-matching-2022" />, so the executed action's log-likelihood is intractable <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" />. Applying online RL directly to large VLAs also brings training instability and compute beyond most local machines <Cite id="ire-vla-2025" />.

edits.before: **DPPO** (Ren et al., 2024) embeds the diffusion denoising process inside the environment MDP. Each policy action in this combined MDP is a denoising transition with an analytically evaluable Gaussian likelihood; the environment advances and supplies reward only after the final denoising step. PPO updates the denoising policy while the environment dynamics stay fixed. Environment-discounted advantages are multiplied by a separate denoising discount that downweights earlier, noisier steps. The value function depends on the environment state. The paper also fine-tunes only the last selected denoising steps, using a frozen original network for earlier steps and a trainable copy for the selected steps <Cite id="dppo-2024" />.
edits.after: DPPO (Ren et al., 2024) follows DDPO, which posed diffusion denoising as a multi-step decision problem <Cite id="ddpo-2023" />. DPPO embeds denoising inside the environment MDP: each denoising transition has an analytic Gaussian likelihood, and the environment advances and pays reward only after the final step. Environment-discounted advantages are multiplied by a denoising discount that downweights earlier, noisier steps, and the value function depends on the environment state. Only the last selected denoising steps are fine-tuned, with a frozen copy of the network for earlier ones <Cite id="dppo-2024" />.

edits.before: Perry Dong, Kuo-Han Hung, Tian Gao, Dorsa Sadigh and Chelsea Finn (Stanford) attack the problem from the value side. Their EXPO algorithm trains a large flow or diffusion base policy with a stable imitation objective, plus a lightweight Gaussian edit policy that nudges sampled actions toward higher value; an on-the-fly policy then executes and backs up the value-maximizing candidate among the base and edited actions, sidestepping gradient propagation through the denoising chain. The paper reports up to 2-3x sample-efficiency improvements on average over prior methods, both when fine-tuning a pretrained policy from offline data and when training online from it <Cite id="expo-2025" />.
edits.after: EXPO (Perry Dong, Qiyang Li, Dorsa Sadigh and Chelsea Finn; ICLR 2026) trains a large flow or diffusion base policy with a stable imitation objective plus a lightweight Gaussian edit policy that nudges sampled actions toward higher value. An on-the-fly policy executes and backs up the best of the base and edited actions, avoiding gradients through the denoising chain. EXPO reports up to 2 to 3× better sample efficiency on average, both when fine-tuning a pretrained policy from offline data and when using offline data to train online <Cite id="expo-2025" />.

edits.before:
EXPO-FT turns that algorithm into a full fine-tuning system for a frontier VLA <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" />. It extends EXPO to the action chunks VLAs emit natively, adds human teleoperation corrections during online training, and runs on π0.5 initialized from a task-specific supervised-finetuning checkpoint. Tasks the base policy cannot already do zero-shot receive imitation fine-tuning to around 40% success before online RL starts. Rewards are sparse and binary, from rule-based success detectors the paper reports at over 95% accuracy, and the robot takes end-effector velocity commands at 10 Hz.

The headline result: 30/30 successes on every evaluated task, within an average of 19.1 minutes of online robot data across the eight task variants <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" />. The chart shows the paper's own four-task comparison against supervised finetuning, HG-DAgger, DSRL and HIL-SERL.

With extra samples, HIL-SERL reaches 27/30 and 13/30 on those two tasks. A 5.5/30 average under this protocol is evidence about initial-state breadth, and the original HIL-SERL results above stand on their own protocol <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" /> <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" />.

edits.before: DSRL represents a third position in the same comparison: keep the base policy frozen entirely and run RL over its latent-noise space, with black-box access and no weight updates <Cite id="dsrl-2025" />. Its authors demonstrate real-world autonomous improvement of diffusion policies and pretrained generalists this way. Dong and Finn argue the approach has a ceiling: “If the skill a robot needs isn't already somewhere in what the base model learned during pretraining, no amount of noise-searching will produce the action.” In their four-task comparison, DSRL averages 19/30 <Cite id="perry-dong-post-training-2026" /> <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" />.

edits.before: Dong and Finn's September 2026 position, stated in a joint blog post, is that the field is at its GPT-2 moment: capable demos from pretrained VLAs, and no shared post-training recipe behind them. In their words, “RL shows incredible promise in training frontier robotics models, but it is not yet a recipe. It's a craft.” They argue robotics needs what language modeling has: a stable algorithm plus standard protocols for reward specification, resets, human input, hyperparameters and initialization. They attach their own limits to EXPO-FT: a human still defines success, resets the scene and intervenes; longer horizons strain the value function; and “Nineteen minutes of robot interaction is not nineteen minutes of post-training,” because gradient updates on a model this size dominate wall-clock time <Cite id="perry-dong-post-training-2026" />.

SeeQ, from Saksham Singh, Aviral Kumar and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon (September 2026), steers at test time with a value function. Picking the best of eight π0.5 action chunks raised shirt hanging from 10/24 to 22/24 and lid sealing from 10/24 to 15/24 <Cite id="seeq-2026" />.

## Real-world and fleet-scale results

edits.before: DPPO, ConRFT, EXPO-FT, HIL-SERL and pi_RL state that code is available. Those statements do not verify repository contents, particular downloadable weight checkpoints or license terms. The inspected PLD and DSRL sources do not establish a code or weight release. Recap's inspected report, blog and model card do not establish model-specific checkpoint availability or licensing; this is not a claim that the model is closed. The openness notes keep those source scopes with each row <Cite id="dppo-2024" /> <Cite id="conrft-2025" /> <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" /> <Cite id="pi-rl-2026" /> <Cite id="pistar06-2025" /> <Cite id="pistar06-blog-2025" /> <Cite id="pi06-model-card-2025" /> <Cite id="pld-2026" /> <Cite id="expo-ft-2026" /> <Cite id="dsrl-2025" />.
edits.after: RL-100, published in Science Robotics in July 2026, applies one clipped-PPO objective within the denoising process across offline and online stages. It reports 1000 of 1000 successful episodes on eight real tasks, including 250 consecutive successes on one <Cite id="rl-100-2025" />. LWD runs offline-to-online RL on a fleet of 16 dual-arm robots, where one generalist policy reaches 95% average success across eight real tasks <Cite id="lwd-2026" />. SOP's performance scales near-linearly with the number of robots in its fleet <Cite id="sop-2026" />. ENPIRE gives coding agents the whole real-robot improvement loop, from scene reset and verification to training-code changes. Its authors report 99% success on dexterous tasks such as fastening a zip tie, and eight agents cut the time to near-perfect pin insertion from over 1.5 hours to about 40 minutes <Cite id="enpire-2026" />.

edits.before: Liu et al.'s NeurIPS 2025 study reports that PPO beat the tested DPO/TPO and GRPO implementations in its OpenVLA pick-and-place setup, where preferences and returns came from sparse task rewards. The authors summarize the main OOD comparison with supervised fine-tuning as stronger semantic and execution generalization, with comparable visual robustness; arbitrary new-task generalization sits outside the test. The January 2026 revision adds a preliminary sim-to-real trial and an articulated-object task to a narrower main-text limitation statement. Its results are mixed: SFT wins on the articulated-task visual average and rephrased instructions, and on the action-chunking multi-receptacle test <Cite id="rl-vla-generalization-2025" />.
edits.after: Liu et al.'s NeurIPS 2025 study finds PPO beats the tested DPO/TPO and GRPO implementations for OpenVLA pick-and-place with sparse task rewards. Against supervised fine-tuning it reports stronger semantic and execution generalization and comparable visual robustness. A September 2025 revision adds appendix tests: a preliminary sim-to-real trial, an action-chunking comparison and an articulated-object task. SFT wins the articulated task's visual average and rephrased instructions, and the action-chunking multi-receptacle test. The main-text limitations still say all experiments are simulated pick-and-place <Cite id="rl-vla-generalization-2025" />.

edits.before: Peng et al.'s PAIR-VLA study addresses a related limitation in how RL treats visual changes. In simulated ManiSkill3 pick-and-place experiments with OpenVLA and π0.5, it adds paired-view invariance and sensitivity objectives to PPO: preserve action distributions for task-preserving changes and separate them for target-pose changes. The authors argue that task rewards alone give limited guidance about this distinction and report improved OOD success over standard PPO under the tested visual shifts. The sensitivity-only ablation loses to PPO on target-pose success; the separate camera-view experiment, using a different task-preserving view construction, also trails PPO slightly in-distribution despite its OOD gains. That comparison leaves reward design unisolated as the cause of a pre-to-post-RL loss of robustness; its task-preserving views also rely on simulator object masks, and real-world transfer remains untested <Cite id="pair-vla-2026" />.
edits.after: PAIR-VLA adds paired-view invariance and sensitivity objectives to PPO in simulated ManiSkill3 pick-and-place with OpenVLA and π0.5. It preserves action distributions under task-preserving changes and separates them under target-pose changes, arguing that task rewards alone give limited guidance here, and reports better OOD success than PPO under the tested shifts. The sensitivity-only ablation loses to PPO on target-pose success, the camera-view variant trails PPO slightly in-distribution, the task-preserving views rely on simulator object masks, and real-world transfer is untested <Cite id="pair-vla-2026" />.

edits.before:
The robot learning curriculum for ML engineers is a staged path through the robotics that policy experiments depend on, from coordinates to evaluation. Machine learning gives you optimization, representation learning, sequence models and experimental discipline. It does not give you coordinate frames, control loops, contact dynamics or a reliable definition of task success. A useful robot-learning roadmap therefore starts at the interfaces where a model meets a machine. The aim is not to learn all of robotics before training a policy. It is to learn each dependency just before an experiment needs it.

The shortest route has six layers: geometry, data, imitation, action representation, evaluation and deployment. Foundation models and reinforcement learning sit on top of those layers; they do not remove them.

Try the check below and choose the baseline you would run before a larger policy. The option names the first experiment that separates a data problem from a model problem.
edits.after: The robot learning curriculum for ML engineers is a staged path through the robotics that policy experiments depend on: geometry, data, imitation, action representation, evaluation and deployment, each learned just before an experiment needs it. A 2025 open tutorial runs from behavior cloning and reinforcement learning to generalist policies <Cite id="robot-learning-tutorial-2025" />. Try the check below.

edits.before: ## Stage 1: make coordinates concrete
edits.after: ## Stage 1: coordinates

edits.before: Start with [kinematics](/classical/kinematics); the reason is that observations and actions live in frames, with no expectation that every learner implements an inverse-kinematics solver. You should be able to answer four questions without looking at the training code: which frame an object pose uses, which frame an end-effector delta uses, whether rotations compose on the left or right, and where joint limits enter. *Modern Robotics* supplies the compact mathematical vocabulary for this layer <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />.
edits.after: Start with [kinematics](/classical/kinematics/): know which frame an object pose and an end-effector delta use, whether rotations compose on the left or right, and where joint limits enter. *Modern Robotics* supplies the vocabulary <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />, and Tedrake warns that sloppy kinematic notation "will inevitably lead to confusion and bugs" <Cite id="tedrake-manipulation-2026" />.

edits.before: Then read [calibration](/classical/calibration) and [state estimation](/classical/state-estimation). A policy can appear stochastic when the real defect is a drifting camera transform or a timestamp mismatch. This is the first habit to import from robotics: before changing the network, prove that the target the network sees refers to the same physical state as the action in the label.
edits.after: Then study [calibration](/classical/calibration/) and [state estimation](/classical/state-estimation/): a drifting camera transform or timestamp mismatch can look like a stochastic policy. Kalibr estimates sensor time offsets to a fraction of the smallest measurement period <Cite id="kalibr-2013" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 2: treat data collection as a system
edits.after: ## Stage 2: data as a system

edits.before: Robot data is a coupled record; a folder of images carries none of the coupling. Each transition needs synchronized observations, the commanded action, the action actually realized when available, robot state, task identity, termination, and enough provenance to reproduce the split. DROID reports 76k episodes collected across 13 institutions <Cite id="droid-2024" />.
edits.after: Each transition couples synchronized observations, commanded and realized actions, robot state, task identity, termination and provenance; RLDS stores such episodes losslessly <Cite id="rlds-2021" />. Among public [datasets](/data-hardware/datasets/), Open X-Embodiment pools 22 robots from 21 institutions <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" />, and DROID holds 76k trajectories from 13 institutions <Cite id="droid-2024" />.

edits.before: Before collecting at scale, record ten episodes and replay them end to end. Plot timestamp gaps. Render actions back onto the robot state. Verify units and rotation conventions. Check that train and test environments do not share nearly identical episodes. These checks are cheaper than discovering after substantial teleoperation that camera and joint streams were misaligned.
edits.after: Before scaling, record ten episodes and replay them: plot timestamp gaps, render actions onto the robot state, and check units and rotation conventions. Past a threshold per environment or object, more demonstrations add little, and diversity matters far more <Cite id="lin-data-scaling-laws-2024" />.

edits.before: The [datasets guide](/data-hardware/datasets) explains the public corpora; the [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack) explains the machinery around your own.
edits.after: GELLO collects demonstrations more reliably than VR controllers or 3D spacemice <Cite id="gello-2023" />, and LeRobot spans the [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack/) from motor middleware to dataset streaming <Cite id="lerobot-paper-2026" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 3: establish the imitation baseline
edits.after: ## Stage 3: imitation baseline

edits.before: Behavior cloning is supervised learning with a closed-loop distribution shift. The learner sees expert states during training and its own imperfect states at deployment. DAgger formalized why errors compound and why collecting corrective actions on learner-induced states changes the problem <Cite id="dagger-2011" />.
edits.after: [Behavior cloning](/manipulation/bc-foundations/) trains on expert states and then visits its own, a closed-loop distribution shift. DAgger formalized why errors compound and why corrective labels on learner-induced states change the problem <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. HG-DAgger adapts it for human experts, whose labels can degrade without full control <Cite id="hg-dagger-2019" />.

edits.before: Run the smallest baseline that can close the loop. For image observations, that might be an encoder plus an MLP or a short transformer. Keep one camera, one task and one action convention. If it fails, inspect data alignment, normalization, reset diversity and label multimodality before adding scale.
edits.after: Run the smallest closed-loop baseline, such as an image encoder and MLP, on one camera, task and action convention. If it fails, inspect alignment, normalization, reset diversity and label multimodality before adding scale. robomimic found results sensitive to design choices, demonstration quality and stopping criteria <Cite id="robomimic-2021" />.

edits.before: Once the baseline is legible, add temporal structure. ACT predicts action chunks and temporally ensembles overlapping predictions at execution <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. Diffusion Policy represents a multimodal distribution over action sequences and executes it in a receding horizon <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. Both methods produce temporal action sequences; their objectives and inference procedures differ, so compare their controller and execution contracts directly.
edits.after: Add temporal structure. ACT predicts action chunks and temporally ensembles overlapping predictions <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. Diffusion Policy models a multimodal distribution over action sequences, executed in a receding horizon <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 4: choose the action contract
edits.after: ## Stage 4: action contract

edits.before: Read [action spaces](/manipulation/action-spaces) before comparing policy architectures. Joint positions are mechanism-specific. End-effector deltas can provide a shared task-space convention when each robot has a compatible controller and frame convention. Torque and tokens impose different low-level and decoding costs.
edits.after: Among [action spaces](/manipulation/action-spaces/), joint positions are mechanism-specific; end-effector deltas share a task-space convention across compatible controllers and frames. Torque and tokens add low-level and decoding costs, and per-dimension binning tokenizers handle high-frequency dexterous data poorly <Cite id="pi0-fast-2025" />.

edits.before: The action representation is part of the dataset. Changing it changes the labels, the controller under the policy, the error modes and often the set of robots that can share data. No model comparison is clean if those changed at the same time.
edits.after: The action representation is part of the dataset: it fixes the labels, the controller, the error modes and which robots can share data. Change it apart from the model. Variable-impedance end-effector actions improved sample efficiency and safety in three manipulation tasks <Cite id="martin-martin-2019" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 5: add pretraining only after the interfaces hold
edits.after: ## Stage 5: pretraining

edits.before: A VLA is useful when task language, semantic generalization or multi-task transfer matters. OpenVLA made the recipe reproducible: fuse spatial and semantic vision features into a language backbone, then fine-tune it to emit robot actions <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. The starting checkpoint is valuable, but the same data alignment and action-space constraints remain.
edits.after: A VLA helps when language, semantic generalization or multi-task transfer matters. OpenVLA made the recipe reproducible: fuse spatial and semantic vision features into a language backbone, then fine-tune it to emit actions <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. π0 pretrains on over 10,000 hours of robot data <Cite id="pi0-2024" />, and SmolVLA trains on one GPU yet performs comparably to VLAs ten times larger <Cite id="smolvla-2025" />.

edits.before: Ask what pretraining is supposed to provide. If the missing capability is recognizing an unseen object category, web-scale vision-language pretraining is a plausible intervention. If the failure is a gripper colliding because the hand-eye transform is wrong, it is not. The [foundation-model guide](/manipulation/foundation-models) separates transfer claims from architecture labels.
edits.after: [Pretraining](/manipulation/foundation-models/) can help recognize an unseen object category; a wrong hand-eye transform still needs calibration. In TRI's blind, randomized trials, multitask pretraining made policies more successful and robust and taught new tasks with a fraction of the data <Cite id="tri-lbm-2025" />.

edits.before: ## Stage 6: make evaluation harder than the demo
edits.after: ## Stage 6: evaluation

edits.before: Create the evaluation protocol before the main training run. Define task success, failure, intervention, reset and timeout. Separate familiar configurations from changed objects, backgrounds, lighting and geometry. Report trial counts and uncertainty alongside the average. LIBERO-Plus tests VLA robustness under controlled changes to object layout, camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language, lighting, background texture and sensor noise <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />.
edits.after: Define success, failure, intervention, reset and timeout before the main run, and separate familiar configurations from changed objects, backgrounds, lighting and geometry. Papers often give little or no information on run counts, initial conditions, success criteria or statistics <Cite id="kress-gazit-evaluation-2024" />. Report trial counts and uncertainty; STEP's sequential test needs up to 32% fewer trials than prior tests <Cite id="optimal-stopping-2025" />.

edits.before: Open-loop loss is a diagnostic; the result sits elsewhere. A useful evaluation pyramid has four levels:
edits.after: Open-loop loss is a diagnostic. Check datasets for leakage, action distributions, timestamps and annotations; open-loop error and calibration on held-out episodes; closed-loop success, interventions and failures under controlled shifts; and deployment cycle time, recovery, resets, faults and operator load. LIBERO-Plus shifts object layout, camera viewpoint, initial state, language, lighting, background and sensor noise <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />. SIMPLER's simulated scores correlate with real performance <Cite id="simpler-2024" />, and RoboArena's double-blind pairwise trials rank generalist policies better than centralized evaluation <Cite id="roboarena-2025" />. For deployment, [ROS 2](/classical/ros2-for-ml-engineers/) was rebuilt with the production-grade features ROS 1 lacked <Cite id="ros2-science-robotics-2022" />.

edits.before:
1. **Dataset checks:** leakage, action distributions, timestamps and annotation quality.
2. **Open-loop checks:** prediction error and calibration on held-out episodes.
3. **Closed-loop checks:** success, interventions and failure modes under controlled shifts.
4. **Deployment checks:** cycle time, recovery, resets, hardware faults and operator load.
edits.after: ## Simulation and RL

edits.before: ## When simulation and RL enter
edits.after: Simulation tests controller stability, robustness to parameter variation and safe reward optimization. Domain randomization aims to make the real world look like one more simulated variation <Cite id="tobin-2017" />. Isaac Lab targets large-scale, multi-modal robot learning <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />; measure its dynamics gap to the hardware.

edits.before:
Simulation belongs where it answers a concrete question: whether a controller is stable, whether a policy survives parameter variation, or whether a reward can be optimized safely. Isaac Lab is designed for large-scale, multi-modal robot-learning workflows and is an appropriate environment once the task's contact and sensor assumptions are credible <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />. It is not a substitute for measuring the gap between its dynamics and the hardware.

Offline RL belongs when a logged dataset contains meaningful variation in outcome quality and a reward can rank that variation. Online RL belongs when the system can explore safely, reset automatically and evaluate cheaply. When reward, safe exploration and resets are missing, <Term id="imitation-learning">imitation learning</Term> is a practical first use of collected demonstrations.
edits.after: Offline RL learns from logged data without new collection <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />, so it fits logs whose outcome quality varies and a reward can rank. Online RL needs safe exploration, automatic resets and cheap evaluation; SERL bundles an off-policy learner with reward computation, resets and a controller <Cite id="serl-2024" />. Without those, <Term id="imitation-learning">imitation learning</Term> is the practical first use of demonstrations. In simulation, RL can stand in for scarce demonstrations: SimpleVLA-RL lifted OpenVLA-OFT trained on one demonstration per task from 48.9% to 96.9% average LIBERO success <Cite id="simplevla-rl-2025" />.

edits.before:
For a first serious project, spend the opening phase on replayable data and a deterministic evaluation harness. Build behavior cloning next. Add action chunks or a multimodal head only when the baseline exposes the need. Add a VLA when semantic transfer is part of the task. Add RL only when the reward, coverage and reset loop are real.

The sequence is conservative because robot experiments are expensive and confounded. Its benefit is speed: every stage produces an artifact you keep, and every added method answers a failure you can already name.
edits.after: Build replayable data and a deterministic evaluation harness, then behavior cloning; add chunks when the baseline needs them, a VLA for semantic transfer, and RL once reward, coverage and resets are real. The tutorial provides ready-to-use LeRobot examples <Cite id="robot-learning-tutorial-2025" />.

edits.before:
A <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action (VLA)</Term> model is a robot policy built by adapting a vision-language model to output robot actions. The modules so far covered policies trained from scratch on robot data alone: [behavior cloning](/manipulation/bc-foundations), [ACT](/manipulation/action-chunking), and [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy). The VLA line changes the starting point. Instead of training a policy from nothing, take a model that already understands images and language from web-scale pretraining, and teach it to emit robot actions. The design question that defines this lineage is how to get actions out of a model whose output space is text.

The interactive below is an illustrative seven-coordinate action sequence; it is neither a recorded rollout nor a literal tokenizer vocabulary. It places values in 256 uniform bins on a fixed normalized interval and uses synthetic token labels. Drag “Moment in the movement” to see each motion’s nudge land in one of the 256 slots and become a word; the motion buttons and the full 256-slot strip are under “Adjust more”, and the reconstruction error is under “How this was made”. edits.before: RT-2 (2023) attacked the knowledge problem directly <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. It skips bolting a robot head onto a <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term>: each action dimension is discretized into 256 bins, and the bin indices are serialized into the VLM's existing token stream as strings. The two backbones handle the vocabulary differently, which is a detail worth keeping: PaLI-X already has a token for every integer up to 1000, so bins map onto existing number tokens, while PaLM-E overwrites the 256 least frequently used tokens with the action vocabulary. The backbone (PaLI-X or PaLM-E, up to 55B parameters) is then co-fine-tuned on a mixture of robot trajectories and the original web vision-language data. The authors report that mixing the original web data with robot data during co-fine-tuning produces more generalizable policies than fine-tuning on robot data alone <Cite id="rt2-2023" />.

## Where this leaves the field

These studies demonstrate particular transfers from web pretraining and pooled robot data; universal improvement from scale alone is a stronger claim than they support. Their action interfaces, data mixtures, input modalities and execution protocols differ. Read the reported token-generation rates and robot-control rates separately, and compare results only with their task and evaluation settings attached. <Cite id="rt2-2023" /> <Cite id="openvla-2024" />

With LIBERO near its ceiling, ranking needs harder tests ([evaluation crisis](/data-hardware/evaluation-crisis/)): RoboArena compares generalist policies in double-blind pairs on DROID robots at seven institutions <Cite id="roboarena-2025" />, and SIMPLER's simulated scores correlate with real performance <Cite id="simpler-2024" />.

edits.before: Treat “VLA” as two decisions behind one label. The first is the prior: which visual, language and robot experience the backbone brings to the task. A large semantic prior can improve instruction following while a poor action interface still makes the system unusable at contact. OpenVLA-OFT is the clean example because changing the decoding and action head materially changed both throughput and success without replacing the underlying VLA <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />.

seeAlso: - "manipulation/vla-models" - "manipulation/hierarchical" - "data-hardware/teleop-rigs" --- import { WbcDecomposition } from '@/components/interactive/wbc-decomposition'; import { Gr2ResultsTable } from '@/components/mdx/gr2-results-table'; Humanoid whole-body control is treating every actuated joint of a humanoid, from legs to hands, as one coupled control problem. The previous module covered how learned policies took over legged locomotion. This one covers the harder problem those same groups attacked next: making a full humanoid, legs through torso through arms through hands, do useful work without falling. The organizing idea across nearly all of it is motion tracking. Treat whole-body control as following a reference human motion, retargeted onto the robot's kinematics, and use reinforcement learning to learn tracking under the robot's dynamics and hardware constraints. Retargeted human motion can be infeasible for the robot . The human demonstration carries the intent; the policy solves balance, contact timing, and actuator limits. Where task-level intelligence plugs into that is unsettled, and the three answers shipping in 2026 are below. Switch between motion-tracking RL, the latent-action hierarchy, and end-to-end VLA, and watch the learning boundary move: each program drew it somewhere different.
All four figures are vendor-reported: the Helix 02 numbers from Figure's announcement and the Gemini Robotics 2 numbers from DeepMind's announcement . ## The tracking lineage PHC (Perpetual Humanoid Control) demonstrated motion tracking and fall recovery for simulated avatars; it did not test a physical robot. Its rotation-based controller achieved 98.9% imitation success on 11,313 filtered AMASS training clips. That is a training-set result and does not establish universal tracking success. Imitation counts as a failure if mean body-joint deviation from the reference exceeds 0.5 m at any point. PMCP freezes learned motion primitives, trains new primitives on progressively harder failed subsets, adds a separate recovery primitive, and learns a multiplicative composer. The result is one composite controller spanning the clips. The paper demonstrates reset-free avatar control with webcam pose estimates and tracking of language-generated motion, but highly dynamic clips, noisy real-time estimates, and recovery artifacts remain limitations . H2O adapts ideas from simulated humanoid animation to the Unitree H1. It does not transfer PHC unchanged. Its paper calls the privileged motion-filtering imitator "similar to PHC" and follows PULSE for that imitator's state space and training procedure. A separate policy learns whole-body tracking from the cleaned retargeted motion set with domain randomization, then follows human keypoints estimated in real time from an RGB camera. The deployed teleoperation system uses robot-side motion capture for linear velocity and a PD controller below the 19-dimensional joint-target policy . OmniH2O uses kinematic motion goals as a shared interface for its Unitree H1 system. A deployable student is distilled from a privileged RL teacher and tracks head-and-hand position goals using proprioceptive history. It has no explicit global-linear-velocity input, although robot root odometry is still needed to transform goals into the robot frame. The method defines target joint angles followed by PD control, while Appendix A describes torque outputs; the paper leaves that action-interface wording inconsistent . VR and RGB pose input use the same tracker; language instructions first pass through a text-to-motion model. In the demonstrated GPT-4o setup, robot-camera images select among motion primitives because the model responds too slowly for direct low-level motor control. For learning from teleoperated demonstrations, a visual policy predicts motion-goal sequences and hand commands, with the tracking policy underneath. The imitation-learning evaluation covers four of the six recorded tasks, with ten runs per task. These examples do not establish unrestricted task generalization. The authors also report no safety guarantees for extreme disturbances or out-of-distribution motion goals . HumanPlus uses a single RGB camera to estimate the human operator’s body and hand poses. The robot has other sensors. Its Humanoid Shadowing Transformer is trained with PPO on retargeted human motion in simulation and deployed zero-shot on a customized Unitree H1. The robot supplies IMU and joint-encoder observations; the policy outputs body-joint position setpoints for PD control. Hand targets pass directly to the controller, and seated operation bypasses the learned body controller. Operators collect demonstrations through shadowing while two head-mounted RGB cameras record the robot’s view. Supervised behavior cloning then trains a separate Humanoid Imitation Transformer from binocular images and proprioception to supply target poses to the low-level controller. The paper demonstrates task-specific autonomous skills; unrestricted skill generalization remains untested. Occlusion, fixed retargeting, and limited locomotion scope remain constraints . ExBody2 reports that drifting global keypoint targets can accumulate tracking errors. It uses local keypoint targets with separate velocity tracking. An initial policy ranks reference motions by lower-body tracking error for dataset filtering; a privileged PPO teacher is distilled into a student using observation history. The authors report walking, squatting, and dancing on Unitree G1. Their generalist and fine-tuned specialist policies trade broad coverage against motion-specific precision, and the paper leaves transitions between specialists unresolved . ASAP then attacked the residual dynamics gap with the delta-action stage covered in the [sim-to-real module](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer): train the tracking policy in sim, roll it out on the real Unitree G1, learn a correction model from the mismatch, and fine-tune against the corrected simulator. That produced jumps and sports-style motions on hardware . The 2025 to 2026 work consolidated. KungfuBot trains a separate policy for each processed reference motion. Its adaptive tracking rule tightens the exponential reward’s error tolerance from an exponential moving average of tracking error, with a non-increasing update. Separate curricula lower the early-termination threshold and increase regularization penalties. The authors demonstrate dynamic motions on Unitree G1; their quantitative hardware comparison covers ten Tai Chi trials with the robot root fixed to the origin for evaluation . GMT takes the other approach: it trains a unified motion-tracking controller without merging already-trained per-skill policies. Adaptive sampling re-clips long motions and adjusts sampling probabilities using completion and tracking errors. Its privileged teacher uses a learned soft mixture-of-experts: a gating network combines expert action outputs, and a deployable student learns from the teacher through DAgger. The authors demonstrate tracking on Unitree G1, but report the baseline comparisons and ablations in simulation. The controller does not support getting up after a fall or rolling, and is not designed for tracking on slopes and stairs . The 2026 robustness work targets what retargeting breaks: references that arrive noisy or locally infeasible in the robot's morphology get selectively aggregated by a multi-head cross-attention command encoder inside a dynamics-conditioned command aggregation framework, with a fall-recovery curriculum, so the controller survives reference defects instead of amplifying them . ## Three decompositions ship in 2026 The lineage above answers how to make a humanoid move like a reference. It does not answer where task-level intelligence plugs in, which is the split drawn in the figure at the top of this module. All three frontier humanoid programs shipped whole-body control in 2026, and each drew the learning boundary in a different place. ### A unified motion-tracking policy: Figure Helix 02 S0 Figure kept the tracking decomposition and industrialized it. Helix 02 is a three-layer stack: S2 does semantic reasoning over scenes and language and emits latent goals; S1, a visuomotor transformer at 200 Hz, takes every sensor in (head cameras, palm cameras, fingertip tactile, full proprioception) and emits complete joint targets for the whole robot; S0, a 10M-parameter whole-body controller at 1 kHz, converts joint state and base motion into actuator commands. S0 was trained on over 1,000 hours of joint-level retargeted human motion plus sim-to-real RL across more than 200,000 parallel simulation environments, and Figure states it replaced 109,504 lines of hand-engineered C++ . The architectural bet is the lineage's: learn one prior over how humans move while balancing, so the layers above never reason about footsteps. The headline demo, a 4-minute dishwasher unload of 61 loco-manipulation actions, is vendor-reported with no paper and no success rates. ### A VLA above a learned controller: GR00T + GEAR-SONIC NVIDIA kept the VLA and the whole-body controller as separate learned systems with a narrow interface between them. GR00T N1.7, a 3B-parameter VLA with a Cosmos-Reason2-2B backbone and a flow-matching action head, predicts compact latent action tokens; the GEAR-SONIC whole-body controller, exposed as the `UNITREE_G1_SONIC` embodiment, decodes those tokens into full-body joint commands for legs, arms, and hands . One language-conditioned policy thereby produces coordinated locomotion and manipulation without the VLA ever naming a joint. The academic versions of the same decomposition are explicit about the interface: LeVERB learns a latent vision-language verb vocabulary from rendered kinematic demonstrations and hands it to an RL whole-body controller , and WholeBodyVLA learns latent actions from action-free egocentric video for loco-manipulation . GR00T's bet is that a constrained interface is a feature: the VLA can be retrained or swapped without touching the controller, and the controller's dynamics stay out of the VLA's context. This is also the only one of the three stacks with public code (Apache-2.0) and released weights ; as of September 2026, Figure and DeepMind have published no code or weights for theirs. ### One VLA, feet to fingertips: Gemini Robotics 2 Google DeepMind removed the boundary. Gemini Robotics 2 is a single frontier VLA controlling an Apptronik Apollo 2 from feet to fingertips under one policy, dynamically managing center of mass so the robot steps, squats, and bends instead of reaching from a static base, and driving a 22-DoF five-fingered SharpaWave hand as well as parallel grippers on a Franka Duo. The same checkpoint runs across Apollo 2 with SharpaWave hands, Apollo 2 with Inspire hands, and Franka Duo with Robotiq grippers, and the On-Device variant adapts to a new bi-arm embodiment in a few hours, typically with under 200 examples . The trade-off is opacity: the action representation, control frequency, and parameter counts are all undisclosed in the announcement, so the decomposition can be verified only through its published behavior. The published numbers are where that verification starts. ## The Gemini Robotics 2 numbers, as published DeepMind published per-task success rates with the announcement, and they are the most honest snapshot of where whole-body capability actually is. Whole-body picking succeeds most of the time and falls with height: 76.3% from a shelf, 68.4% from a table, 45.7% from the floor, measured on Apollo 2 with Inspire hands. Gripper-based precise insertion reaches 89.6% on the Franka Duo. Multi-finger dexterity on the Apollo 2 Sharpa hand spans 92% (unscrewing a bulb) down to 32% (dustpan), a 60-point spread on the same hand under the same policy, and the vendor's own caption calls multi-finger manipulation the remaining challenge . Every figure in this table comes from the vendor's own announcement. No external lab has replicated these results, and no standardized humanoid benchmark exists to compare them against. DeepMind also flags movement speed as unsolved in the same post. The table reports the vendor's task-specific results; its numbers are not independently verified. ## What tracking does not solve Three limits carry forward into everything built on this lineage. First, motion tracking inherits the human demonstrator's envelope. A tracking policy reproduces motion; it does not decide what task the motion should accomplish, and goal-directed loco-manipulation still has to come from somewhere upstream. Second, retargeting is lossy. Human kinematics are not robot kinematics, and morphologically infeasible references remain a persistent failure source, which is the explicit motivation of the 2026 robustness work . Third, the frontier results are vendor communications. Helix 02's 61-action dishwasher run and Gemini Robotics 2's success table both lack papers, baselines, and external replication. There is also a structural question the three decompositions answer differently: whether balance and contact belong inside the foundation model or beneath it. Figure and NVIDIA both say beneath it, and disagree only on whether the interface is a tracked reference motion or a latent token. DeepMind says inside it, one policy for everything, and its own numbers show the cost: whole-body tasks succeed at 45.7 to 76.3% where specialized gripper insertion reaches 89.6%. Whether that gap closes with scale or is the price of the unified decomposition is the open empirical question.

<Term id="legged-locomotion">Legged locomotion</Term> is the domain where sim-to-real reinforcement learning became a shipping default, with an unusually well documented chain of results. The previous modules built the machinery: massively parallel simulation that trains a walking policy in minutes, and the transfer techniques that get it onto hardware. This module follows its deployment. Between 2019 and 2022, the ETH Zurich line around ANYmal took a quadruped from fragile lab behavior to blind alpine hiking, and every humanoid program since has tried to rerun the same recipe on two legs.

Underneath all of it sits an older idea that learning did not replace: the gait. Press Play on the scene below, then try Step forward from walk to trot to bound and watch the support readout, three feet always down, then two, then a flight phase with none. That progression is the stability story of legged locomotion in miniature.
edits.after: <Term id="legged-locomotion">Legged locomotion</Term> is the control of walking and running robots, and the area where sim-to-real reinforcement learning reached shipping products such as Spot <Cite id="bd-spot-rl-2024" />. ETH Zurich's ANYmal line went from simulation-trained policies on hardware in 2019 <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" /> to a 2.2 km alpine hike in 2022 <Cite id="miki-2022" />.

edits.before: Hwangbo and colleagues learned an actuator network for ANYmal's series-elastic actuators. It predicts joint torque from current and past joint-position errors and velocities, using supervised data collected by exciting the real robot's legs and manually disturbing it. The network models actuation inside the simulator; the control policies are trained there and then deployed on the robot. Policies trained with ideal or analytical actuator models could not take a single step without falling in the reported ablations. A separately trained recovery policy flipped ANYmal upright from nine tested configurations, including upside-down and folded-leg poses. The authors report relaxing joint-velocity constraints after the first successful hardware recovery attempt <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />.
edits.after: Hwangbo and colleagues learned an actuator network for ANYmal's series-elastic actuators. It predicts joint torque from current and past joint-position errors and velocities, trained on data from exciting the real legs and disturbing the robot by hand. It stands in for actuation in the simulator. Policies trained with ideal or analytical actuator models failed to take a single step without falling. A separate recovery policy flipped ANYmal upright from nine tested configurations, including a nearly upside-down pose and two resting on its own legs, after the authors relaxed joint-velocity constraints following the first hardware attempt <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />.

edits.before: Lee and colleagues used a privileged RL teacher to supervise both the actions and latent features of a temporal convolutional network student. Its deployed default uses two seconds of proprioceptive history from joint encoders and an IMU, alongside the command and current state. Trained on rigid, procedurally generated terrain, controllers for ANYmal-B and ANYmal-C traversed mud, snow, rubble, and vegetation outside the training conditions, without environment-specific tuning for robots of the same generation. The student has no external terrain map: it infers terrain properties from bodily feedback. This blindness still limits foresight: Lee and colleagues explicitly warn that a robot commanded off a cliff will walk off it . The [sim-to-real module](/rl-sim2real/sim2real-transfer) covers the distillation mechanics.

edits.before: Miki and colleagues combined height samples from an elevation map with proprioception in a GRU-based recurrent belief encoder. A learned attention gate controls how much exteroceptive information enters the belief state; the student is trained to imitate a privileged teacher and reconstruct terrain information from noisy observations. In covered-sensor stair and slippery-platform tests, the controller fell back on proprioception and revised its terrain estimate after contact; it could not anticipate every obstacle. On ANYmal C, deployment used either two Robosense Bpearl LiDAR sensors or four Intel RealSense D435 cameras, with elevation mapping at 20 Hz and the policy at 50 Hz. Their Etzel mountain hike covered 2.2 km with 120 m of elevation gain in 78 minutes, compared with a hiking planner's 76 minutes; it had no falls but included stops to reattach a shoe and swap batteries. The paper's “hour-long” description is not an exact one-hour traversal. Its limitations include possible falls at occluded cliffs or stepping stones, so the result does not establish all-terrain robustness <Cite id="miki-2022" />.

edits.before: Rudin and colleagues report flat-terrain walking policies trained in under four minutes on a single workstation GPU. Separately, their documented simulation-and-deployment policy used 4,096 parallel ANYmal robots, batches of 98,304 RL transitions (24 steps per robot), and 1,500 policy updates in under twenty minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. Their game-inspired terrain curriculum promotes robots that cross a tile boundary, demotes those that cover less than half the commanded distance, and returns robots that solve the hardest level to a random level . The paper links its released training code, `legged_gym`; the pinned October 2021 repository identifies itself as the Isaac Gym environment used to train ANYmal on rough terrain .
