edits.before: A quadruped's gait is a footfall-timing pattern, described by two numbers per leg: the phase offset (when in the stride cycle the foot strikes) and the duty factor $\beta$, the fraction of the cycle the foot spends on the ground. The diagram at the top of this module uses four authored timing examples.
edits.after: A gait is a footfall-timing pattern: each leg's phase offset in the stride and its duty factor $\beta$, the fraction of the cycle on the ground. Walk These Ways commands a gait as three timing offsets between foot pairs plus a stepping frequency: (0.5, 0, 0) trots, (0, 0.5, 0) bounds and (0, 0, 0) pronks <Cite id="walk-these-ways-2022" />. Alexander linked dynamically similar movement in mammals of different sizes to equal Froude numbers $u^2/gh$ <Cite id="alexander-1984" />.

edits.before:
The walk spreads footfalls evenly and keeps three feet down at all times, so a static support polygon always exists. The trot, the working gait of most quadruped robots including ANYmal, strikes diagonal pairs together and balances dynamically on two feet. The bound alternates the front pair against the hind pair with a suspension interval in between. In the MIT Cheetah 2 control design, Park, Wensing and Kim plan stance time from stride length and desired speed, $T_{st} = L/v_d$, keep swing duration fixed, and modulate the duty cycle via vertical impulse scaling (the paper’s Sec. 4.3 is literally titled “Duty cycle modulation via vertical impulse scaling”). Experimentally the stride length grows with speed only up to 3 m/s and is fixed above it, so the stance-time scaling is one classical controller’s schedule rather than a universal timing law, and the abstract’s 6.4 m/s bounding result with cost of transport 0.47 is qualified by side-wall contact and roll instability <Cite id="park-2017-bounding" />. The pronk throws all four feet down and up together and spends most of the cycle airborne.

Learned policies discover whichever gait the foot-air-time and footfall-style reward terms make cheapest. The diagram fixes authored illustrative duty factors: walk 0.75, trot 0.50, bound 0.45, and pronk 0.35. Its phase offsets and support readouts describe those chosen timing examples, not a universal gait law or a measured controller’s response to speed.
edits.after: In the MIT Cheetah 2 design, Park, Wensing and Kim plan stance time from stride length and speed, $T_{st} = L/v_d$, keep swing duration fixed, and modulate duty cycle by vertical impulse scaling. Stride length grows with speed only up to 3 m/s, so this is one controller's schedule. Roll instability ended the 6.4 m/s top-speed treadmill run, and at the highest speeds the robot partly leaned on the side wall. The minimum cost of transport, 0.47, came at 4 m/s <Cite id="park-2017-bounding" />. Margolis and colleagues report record agility for the MIT Mini Cheetah with a learned controller, sustaining speeds up to 3.9 m/s <Cite id="margolis-rapid-2022" />. Learned gaits can be specified as well as discovered: periodic reward composition yields standing, walking, hopping, running and skipping on Cassie <Cite id="siekmann-2020" />.

## Limits of the lineage

edits.before:
In August 2025, Boston Dynamics and Toyota Research Institute reported Large Behavior Models on Atlas for long-horizon manipulation involving locomotion: a 450M-parameter diffusion transformer trained with a <Term id="flow-matching">flow-matching</Term> objective and conditioned on proprioception, images, and a language prompt. Training draws on curated teleoperated demonstrations from hardware and simulation. The article describes actions controlling the full robot at 30 Hz. The network does not infer on every control tick: images arrive at 30 Hz, the network predicts 48 actions (1.6 seconds), and generally 24 actions (0.8 seconds at 1x speed) are executed per inference. Its teleoperation system is built on MPC, and the neural policies use the same robot control interface. These are reported research policies deployed on hardware. The account does not claim every Atlas behavior or the complete controls stack has been replaced <Cite id="bd-atlas-lbm-2025" />.



## What the lineage does not solve

Hold onto three limits. First, these controllers walk, and walking is not fetching: nothing in the legged success story transfers directly to contact-rich manipulation, where the [first module in this domain](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion) showed the MDP itself resists simulation. Second, motion tracking inherits the human demonstrator's envelope, and retargeted references can be morphologically infeasible for the robot, which is the explicit motivation of the 2026 robustness work the humanoid module covers. Third, the lineage's center of gravity turned out to be reward design: the gait a policy learns is whichever pattern the reward makes cheapest, and getting that objective right is still hand labor, now with LLM assistants.
edits.after: Walking is not manipulation. Acosta and colleagues call dynamic contact the computational bottleneck for most simulations <Cite id="acosta-2021" />, and the [first module in this domain](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion) shows why manipulation's MDP resists simulation. Motion tracking needs feasible references, and naive retargeting can break them <Cite id="h2o-2024" />. Eureka's LLM-written rewards beat human experts on 83% of 29 environments <Cite id="eureka-2024" />, and DrEureka writes both reward functions and domain-randomization distributions, getting a quadruped to walk atop a yoga ball <Cite id="dreureka-2024" />.

edits.before:
Offline reinforcement learning is training a robot policy from a fixed dataset of past experience. It asks a useful but dangerous question: can a robot improve beyond the behavior in a fixed log without collecting another transition? The attraction is obvious when every rollout consumes hardware time. The danger is equally basic. A learned value function can assign high value to actions the dataset never tested, and there is no live environment to correct it.

The right starting point is therefore not an algorithm. It is an evidence audit: what behavior is covered, which outcomes are labelled, and whether improvement requires choosing actions outside that support.

Try the check below. Choose the dataset in which offline RL has the clearest reason to outperform a strong behavior-cloning baseline.
edits.after: Offline reinforcement learning is training a robot policy from a fixed dataset of past experience, without new transitions. Levine and colleagues name its central difficulty: a learned value function can overrate actions the data never tested, and no live environment corrects it <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />.

edits.before: In online RL, a policy can try an uncertain action and observe the result. <Term id="offline-reinforcement-learning">Offline RL</Term> cannot. It learns from a static collection of transitions `(observation, action, reward, next observation, termination)` generated by one or more behavior policies. Its optimization may propose a new policy, but its evidence never changes.
edits.after: <Term id="offline-reinforcement-learning">Offline RL</Term> learns from a static set of transitions `(observation, action, reward, next observation, termination)` produced by one or more behavior policies <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />. Value learning bootstraps, so error from actions outside the data accumulates through the Bellman backup <Cite id="bear-2019" />. For robots, support also spans commanded frame, controller mode, action magnitude, contact regime, task stage and recovery. Real-ORL, built on over 6,500 trajectories from 800 robot hours, found that offline RL and imitation prefer different action spaces <Cite id="real-orl-2022" />.

edits.before:
That bargain removes the collection loop and introduces a distribution-shift problem. Standard value learning bootstraps: an estimated value becomes part of the target for another estimate. If the policy selects an unsupported action whose value was accidentally overestimated, the error can reinforce itself. The foundational offline-RL tutorial identifies this mismatch between the learned policy and the dataset distribution as the central difficulty <Cite id="offline-rl-tutorial-2020" />.

For robots, support is more specific than “similar images.” It includes the commanded frame, controller mode, action magnitude, contact regime, task stage and recovery behavior. A dataset rich in free-space motion may offer almost no support for the forces encountered after contact. An action that looks numerically close can still cross a controller or safety boundary.

## Audit the dataset before choosing a method

An offline-RL project should begin with four maps.
edits.after:
NEEDLE, from Shuran Song (Stanford) and colleagues (October 2026), adds short, verified action bridges between recorded observations, using only images, proprioception and episode outcomes, so training can skip detours and reuse failed episodes. On real-robot tasks it beat the strongest baseline on each task by 21 percentage points on average <Cite id="needlework-2026" />.

## Audit the dataset before choosing a method

edits.before: Identify who or what generated each episode: expert teleoperator, novice, scripted controller, older policy or exploration process. Plot action distributions by task stage as well as over the full corpus. Measure coverage near contacts, failures and resets. If all successful trajectories occupy one narrow mode, extrapolating away from it needs evidence.
edits.after: Each episode's source (expert, novice, scripted controller, older policy or exploration) and its actions by task stage need mapping. D4RL builds its datasets from hand-designed controllers, human demonstrators, multitask data and policy mixtures <Cite id="d4rl-2020" />.

edits.before: Count successes, partial progress, recoverable failures and terminal failures. Check whether the reward distinguishes them at the time scale used for learning. A single final binary label can be enough for some long-horizon objectives, but it makes credit assignment harder and can hide reward ambiguity.
edits.after: The reward must separate successes, partial progress and failures at the learning time scale, though a completion label can suffice. COG chained four robot skills under a +1/0 reward, from prior data that never solved the new task <Cite id="cog-2020" />.

edits.before: Verify timestamp alignment, episode boundaries, termination semantics and action units. A missing timeout flag can turn an administrative truncation into a learned terminal state. A logged command is not necessarily the action the robot executed; saturation, command gating and low-level control may change it.
edits.after: Timestamps, episode boundaries, terminations and action units need checks. Mishandled time limits cause state aliasing and invalidate experience replay; when limits only aid training, Pardo and colleagues bootstrap from each partial episode's final state <Cite id="time-limits-2017" />.

edits.before:
State what the deployed robot, task and controller share with the logs. Dataset support should be evaluated in the representation the policy actually consumes and in physical operating variables. A camera, gripper or control-rate change can matter more than the nominal task label.

The [datasets guide](/data-hardware/datasets) covers corpus selection, and the [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack) defines the provenance needed to make this audit repeatable.
edits.after: Support is judged in the policy's input representation and in physical operating variables, where a camera or control-rate change can outweigh the task label. PTR learned new tasks in a new domain on a real WidowX from as few as 10 demonstrations after offline RL pretraining <Cite id="ptr-2022" />. The [datasets guide](/data-hardware/datasets) and the [robot-learning stack](/data-hardware/robot-learning-stack) cover selection and provenance.

edits.before: Offline-RL algorithms differ mainly in how they stop policy improvement from exploiting unsupported value estimates.
edits.after: Offline-RL methods differ in how they keep improvement away from unsupported values, and Park and colleagues find the policy-extraction step often matters more than the value objective <Cite id="park-bottleneck-2024" />.

edits.before: Conservative Q-Learning penalizes high values on actions sampled outside the dataset while preserving values for observed actions. Its objective targets a conservative estimate of policy value and counters the optimistic estimates ordinary off-policy learning can produce <Cite id="cql-2020" />. The tradeoff is deliberate pessimism: excessive conservatism can prevent a policy from combining useful behavior already present in the data.
edits.after: Conservative Q-Learning penalizes high values on actions outside the dataset while preserving observed ones <Cite id="cql-2020" />. RankQ's authors argue that such pessimism anchors policies to suboptimal data, and their action ranking raised a VLA's real cube-stacking success from 43.1% to 88.9% <Cite id="rankq-2026" />.

edits.before: Implicit Q-Learning fits a state value through expectile regression over dataset actions, then extracts a policy by weighting observed actions according to their estimated advantage. It never needs to evaluate the critic on a new action during value fitting <Cite id="iql-2022" />. That makes the support constraint structurally clear, though performance still depends on reward quality and value estimation.
edits.after: Implicit Q-Learning fits a state value by expectile regression over dataset actions and extracts a policy by advantage weighting, so value fitting never queries a new action <Cite id="iql-2022" />.

edits.before: TD3+BC combines an off-policy actor-critic objective with a behavior-cloning term and simple state normalization. Its result is important precisely because the modification is small: a well-tuned regularized baseline can match more elaborate offline algorithms <Cite id="td3-bc-2021" />. The regularization strength is a practical dial between imitation and estimated improvement.
edits.after: TD3+BC adds a cloning term and state normalization to an off-policy actor-critic and matches more elaborate algorithms <Cite id="td3-bc-2021" />. Flow Q-Learning trains a one-step policy with RL instead of steering an iterative flow policy, and performs strongly on 73 benchmark tasks <Cite id="flow-q-learning-2025" />.

edits.before: Q-Transformer predicts Q-values autoregressively across discretized action dimensions. This lets a transformer train on large, diverse robot logs while choosing actions one dimension at a time <Cite id="q-transformer-2023" />. Discretization makes the action search tractable, but the semantic contract of each action dimension still has to be stable across the dataset.
edits.after: QT-Opt trained a Q-function on over 580,000 real grasp attempts and reached 96% success on unseen objects <Cite id="qt-opt-2018" />. Q-Transformer predicts Q-values autoregressively over discretized action dimensions, so it can train on large robot logs <Cite id="q-transformer-2023" />. With datasets up to 1000 times the usual size, many offline RL algorithms saturate well short of maximum performance, and long horizons form a fundamental barrier <Cite id="horizon-reduction-2025" />.

edits.before: These are not interchangeable labels on a benchmark table. They encode different assumptions about how much extrapolation is acceptable and where to impose the constraint.
edits.after: In SeeQ (September 2026), Aviral Kumar (Carnegie Mellon) and colleagues shorten the horizon by learning Q-values for the active subtask, which the model names in text before scoring it. Subtask labels in offline robot data let temporal-difference learning use broad, suboptimal datasets, and the reported gains are in best-of-N policy steering on four real tasks with two bimanual robots <Cite id="seeq-2026" />.

edits.before: Behavior cloning is the correct default for clean expert demonstrations. It optimizes the action labels the dataset actually contains, has no bootstrapped critic and is easy to validate with held-out prediction and real rollouts. The burden is on offline RL to demonstrate an advantage over that baseline.
edits.after: Behavior cloning is the default for clean expert demonstrations: it fits the action labels and has no bootstrapped critic. Robomimic found recurrent cloning a strong baseline on human demonstrations, where batch-RL methods struggled <Cite id="robomimic-2021" />. Kumar and colleagues favor offline RL for sparse rewards, suboptimal or noisy data, and long horizons with composable trajectories <Cite id="offline-rl-vs-bc-2022" />.

edits.before: The robomimic study found recurrent behavior cloning consistently strong on human demonstration datasets, while the tested batch-RL methods struggled there <Cite id="robomimic-2021" />. A separate analysis of offline RL versus cloning found the conditions more favorable to offline RL: sparse rewards, suboptimal or noisy data, and long horizons where useful parts of different trajectories can be composed <Cite id="offline-rl-vs-bc-2022" />.
edits.after: Neither method repairs missing support. Robo-ValueRL ties success to value reliability over 240 hours of demonstrations and over 3,000 rollouts; reliable values let offline RL scale better than quality-agnostic cloning <Cite id="robo-valuerl-2026" />. With online improvement added, the full system reaches 86% on millimeter-level chip insertion <Cite id="robo-valuerl-2026" />. From 30 to 60 demonstrations, CO-RFT's chunked offline RL raised a VLA's success rate 57% over supervised fine-tuning <Cite id="co-rft-2025" />. The [behavior-cloning guide](/manipulation/bc-foundations) covers the baseline.

## A six-step evaluation protocol

Checkpoints are not chosen by the Q-values they maximize. Paine and colleagues found offline RL algorithms not robust to hyperparameters, yet able to rank policies reliably once the algorithm and Q-estimation method are controlled <Cite id="paine-hparam-2020" />.

edits.before: Hold out the environments, objects, operators or time periods across which the policy is supposed to generalize. Random transition splits leak adjacent frames and make a dataset look much larger than its independent evidence.
edits.after: Held-out environments, objects, operators or periods match the intended generalization, since random transition splits leak adjacent frames. Kumar and colleagues' workflow adapts cross-validation to tune offline RL without online evaluation, tested on two real robots <Cite id="offline-rl-workflow-2021" />.

edits.before: Train behavior cloning, a sequence-aware or recurrent cloning model when history matters, and the simplest regularized offline-RL method appropriate to the action space. Keep encoders and capacity comparable.
edits.after: The baselines are cloning, a recurrent cloner when history matters, and the simplest regularized offline-RL method. RvS's goal- or reward-conditioned two-layer MLP competes with TD and transformer methods but is weak on random data <Cite id="rvs-2021" />.

edits.before: Alongside return or task success, report action distance from the dataset, critic disagreement, saturation rate and performance by behavior-source cohort. These diagnostics can expose dependence on unsupported commands. They do not by themselves establish safety.
edits.after: Reports add action distance from the data, critic disagreement, saturation rate and per-source performance. EDAC penalizes out-of-distribution actions through Q-ensemble uncertainty <Cite id="edac-2021" />.

edits.before: Simulation can reject obviously unstable policies and test perturbations at scale. It should not rank close checkpoints on contact-rich tasks unless that ranking has been shown to correlate with hardware. Preserve the simulator version and scenario seeds with the result.
edits.after: Simulation rejects unstable policies but ranks close checkpoints only where its link to hardware is measured, as SIMPLER did with paired real evaluations <Cite id="simpler-2024" />. SCORE limits simulated RL to the support of a real-data policy, raising eight real dexterous tasks from 37.8% to 89.9% average success, against 59.5% for the best baseline <Cite id="score-2026" />.

edits.before: Choose the final protocol before seeing policy identities. Randomize conditions, include failure recovery, report uncertainty and count interventions. Evaluate nominal success alongside collision, force, deadline miss and reset burden.
edits.after: The protocol is fixed before policy identities are known, with randomized conditions and counted interventions, collisions and resets. TRI compared policies through blind, randomized trials <Cite id="tri-lbm-2025" />.

edits.before:
Maintain a small, repeatable physical suite for every candidate and a broader suite for promotion. Store episode IDs so every aggregate can be inspected and recomputed.

An offline result is credible when the selection rule can be explained without referring to the candidate critic's own confidence.
edits.after: A repeatable physical suite runs for every candidate, with episode IDs kept. The TriFinger benchmark offers a reproducible real-hardware setup with simulation for debugging <Cite id="trifinger-offline-2023" />.

edits.before: Offline training need not be the final stage. It can initialize a policy and replay buffer before carefully bounded online interaction. RLPD mixes offline data into off-policy online learning without requiring a separate conservative pretraining objective, improving sample efficiency from the start <Cite id="rlpd-2023" />.
edits.after: RLPD mixes offline data into off-policy online learning without separate conservative pretraining <Cite id="rlpd-2023" />. Conservative critics fine-tune poorly, so Cal-QL calibrates CQL with a one-line change and leads on 9 of 11 benchmarks <Cite id="cal-ql-2023" />. Q-chunking runs TD learning over chunks of future actions, so the offline data's temporally consistent behavior guides online exploration, and it beat prior offline-to-online methods on long-horizon, sparse-reward manipulation tasks <Cite id="q-chunking-2025" />.

edits.before: The transition changes the risk model. Before online fine-tuning:
edits.after: Action bounds and command validation sit outside the learned policy, interventions and resets are defined, and each promotion is compared with the frozen offline checkpoint. Retaining offline data in replay is a safety default; WSRL shows it is unnecessary with a well-designed online method <Cite id="wsrl-2024" />. Dong and colleagues find naive Q-function pretraining often helps little over random initialization <Cite id="dong-q-pretrain-2026" />.

PA-RL fine-tuned the 7B OpenVLA with Cal-QL from 40% to 70% real-world success in 40 minutes <Cite id="pa-rl-2024" />. Physical Intelligence pretrains π\*0.6 with offline RL and reports more than doubled throughput on some of the hardest tasks <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />. LWD applies offline-to-online RL to a pretrained VLA across a fleet of 16 dual-arm robots and reports 95% average success over eight tasks <Cite id="lwd-2026" />. Q2RL keeps a behavior-cloning policy's good actions by gating between cloned and RL actions on their Q-values, and learned contact-rich pipe assembly and kitting on a robot in one to two hours <Cite id="q2rl-2026" />. BORA updates only a residual actor on a frozen VLA, raising success on standard objects from 60.8% to 82.5% with 20 online trajectories per task <Cite id="bora-2026" />. The [RL fine-tuning guide](/manipulation/rl-finetuning) covers this phase.

An offline-RL experiment proceeds when actions, rewards, terminations and timing are trustworthy, and the data holds behavior that cloning should not imitate uniformly. Deployment must lie inside the data's support, since generalization to out-of-support states is often a big barrier <Cite id="park-bottleneck-2024" />. A cloning baseline must reproduce, selection must not rest on learned Q-values alone, and any online phase needs external command limits and rollback.

Massively parallel simulation is training a robot policy across thousands of simulated copies of its environment at once, with the physics running on a GPU. The four-minute training run from the [previous module](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion) came from a change in infrastructure. <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term> was already four years old when Rudin and colleagues used it to train ANYmal to walk in minutes <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Between 2021 and 2026, physics moved onto the GPU, environment counts went from dozens to tens of thousands, and the wall-clock cost of a walking policy collapsed by orders of magnitude. This module examines those throughput numbers and the remaining bottleneck.

edits.after: Massively parallel simulation is training a robot policy across thousands of simulated copies of its environment at once, with the physics on a GPU. It produced the four-minute walking run in the [previous module](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion), trained by Rudin and colleagues <Cite id="rudin-2021" /> with the 2017 <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term> algorithm <Cite id="ppo-2017" />.

edits.before: Isaac Gym ran an end-to-end GPU accelerated training pipeline for complex robot tasks on a single GPU. PhysX simulated on the GPU and exposed the simulation state directly as PyTorch tensors, so the physics buffers and the policy network never round-tripped through the CPU. The authors report two to three orders of magnitude improvement over the conventional split of a CPU simulator feeding a GPU network <Cite id="isaac-gym-2021" />.
edits.after:
Isaac Gym kept physics and policy training on one GPU, passing PhysX buffers straight to PyTorch tensors without CPU round trips. Its authors report 2 to 3 orders of magnitude improvement over a CPU simulator feeding a GPU network <Cite id="isaac-gym-2021" />.

Rudin and colleagues scaled from 128 robots, typical of CPU implementations, to 16,384 on one workstation GPU. Flat terrain took under four minutes and uneven terrain twenty, "a speedup of multiple orders of magnitude compared to previous work". Their deployment policy used 4,096 robots, 98,304-transition batches (24 steps per robot) and 1,500 updates in under 20 minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

edits.before: Rudin and colleagues report flat-terrain walking policies trained in under four minutes on a single workstation GPU. Separately, their documented simulation-and-deployment policy used 4,096 parallel ANYmal robots, batches of 98,304 RL transitions (24 steps per robot), and 1,500 policy updates in under twenty minutes on an i9-11900k CPU and NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. Their game-inspired terrain curriculum promotes robots that cross a tile boundary, demotes those that cover less than half the commanded distance, and returns robots that solve the hardest level to a random level . The paper links its released training code, `legged_gym`; the pinned October 2021 repository identifies itself as the Isaac Gym environment used to train ANYmal on rough terrain .
edits.after: Their game-inspired curriculum promotes robots that cross their tile, demotes those covering under half the commanded distance, and loops hardest-level solvers back to a random level . edits.before: The <Term id="parallel-simulation">massively parallel</Term> regime inverts the usual PPO instincts. Rollouts are short (a few dozen steps per environment per iteration, with bootstrapping covering the rest), batches are enormous (on the order of 100k transitions), and the learning rate adapts to a KL-divergence target instead of following a fixed schedule. This regime depends on the 4,096-environment scale; 16 environments do not yield the same batch economics.
edits.after: In the <Term id="parallel-simulation">massively parallel</Term> regime, Rudin's PPO also bootstraps the critic at time-outs and adapts the learning rate to a KL target of 0.01 <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

edits.after:

edits.before:
Reward design is writing the objective that a reinforcement learning policy learns to maximize. Every module so far in this domain assumed someone had already written the objective. The parallel-training module showed thousands of robots collecting reward in lockstep; the sim-to-real module showed how to make the resulting policy survive contact with hardware. This module is about where the reward comes from, and it closes with the argument the whole domain has been circling: whether you need a learned policy at all, when classical trajectory optimization keeps taking back ground.

Twelve weighted terms sit on the illustrative behavior preview below. Its weights, per-term magnitudes and freeze/prance/chatter categories are teaching choices. The paper's nine-term objective and a runnable `legged_gym` configuration are separate. Drag the controls to explore this toy weighted sum.
edits.after: Reward design is writing the objective that a reinforcement learning policy learns to maximize. Legged-locomotion rewards are weighted sums of terms whose weights are tuned by hand <Cite id="rudin-2021" />, and language models now write reward code <Cite id="eureka-2024" />. Model-predictive control instead plans actions online with an explicit dynamics model <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />.

edits.before: Rudin and colleagues define a weighted sum of nine reward terms in the paper, including feet air time; gait-independent means the reward prescribes no gait schedule, while air time remains present . The separate `legged_gym` initial commit (October 2021, pinned by commit hash in the cited record's audit trail) declares fifteen entries in `LeggedRobotCfg.rewards.scales`, of which nine are nonzero: linear- and angular-velocity tracking, vertical linear velocity, roll/pitch angular velocity, joint torque, joint acceleration, feet air time, collisions, and action rate. `_prepare_reward_function` removes zero scales and multiplies the remaining scales by the environment time step. The base class implements nineteen reward functions, including joint-limit and contact-force functions, but those definitions remain inactive in this config. Its zero-valued `feet_stumble` entry does not even match the `_reward_stumble` function name. That function penalizes feet hitting vertical surfaces; foot slip is a different failure. The air-time function rewards long steps on first contact and requires a planar-command norm above 0.1. These details describe the pinned base code. A production reward recipe needs its own specification .
edits.after: Rudin and colleagues define a weighted sum of nine reward terms, including feet air time; the reward is gait-independent, prescribing no gait schedule <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. The initial `legged_gym` commit (October 2021) declares fifteen entries in `LeggedRobotCfg.rewards.scales`. Nine are nonzero: linear- and angular-velocity tracking, vertical linear velocity, roll/pitch angular velocity, joint torque, joint acceleration, feet air time, collisions and action rate. `_prepare_reward_function` drops zero scales and multiplies the rest by the time step. The joint-limit and contact-force functions among its nineteen reward functions are inactive in this config, and the zero-valued `feet_stumble` entry does not match the `_reward_stumble` function, which penalizes feet hitting vertical surfaces. The air-time term rewards long steps on first contact when the planar command norm exceeds 0.1 <Cite id="legged-gym-repo-2021" />.

edits.before:
The preview maps weight settings to three illustrative categories: freeze, prance, and chatter. Those classifications and the displayed motion come from the local teaching model. The cited simulator trained no policy with these categories. Rudin and colleagues report different observed artifacts, including a dragging leg and unusually high or low base height, and describe tuning reward weights before transferring their policy to hardware <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

Rudin and colleagues use an adaptive learning rate in their <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term> implementation, based on the KL divergence between the updated and previous policies. The paper gives a desired KL of 0.01; its update algorithm lowers the learning rate when KL exceeds twice the target and raises it when KL is below half the target, within stated learning-rate limits <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. This mechanism does not establish that reward retuning is stable.
edits.after: Rudin and colleagues report artifacts such as a dragging leg and unreasonably high or low base heights, and tuned the reward weights before hardware transfer <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Margolis and Agrawal note that a policy failing in a new environment needs "a slow and iterative cycle of reward and environment redesign" <Cite id="walk-these-ways-2022" />. Rudin's <Term id="ppo">PPO</Term> adapts its learning rate from the KL divergence between new and old policies: with a target of 0.01, it lowers the rate when KL exceeds twice the target and raises it under half, within stated limits <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

edits.before: The field has responded to the tuning burden along three distinct lines, and they should not be conflated.
edits.after: The first answer adds constraints. Yunho Kim and colleagues use three rewards (command tracking, joint torque, action smoothness) and 11 constraints, six probabilistic and five average. They trained separate controllers in simulation for Raibo, Mini-cheetah, Hound, ANYmal B, ANYmal C, Unitree Go1 and Atlas, deploying on Raibo and Mini-cheetah. Across robots they adjusted only the torque coefficient among the rewards, found for the reference robot by trial and error, though constraint limits and PD gains still changed. Their IPO-based optimizer uses TRPO with adaptive constraint thresholds, and its probabilistic and average limits are not per-step hard bounds <Cite id="rewards-constraints-2024" />.

edits.before: The first approach reduces reward tuning by adding explicit constraints. They trained separate controllers in simulation for Raibo, Mini-cheetah, Hound, ANYmal B, ANYmal C, Unitree Go1, and Atlas; hardware deployment was on Raibo and Mini-cheetah. For transfer between robots, they adjusted only the torque-reward coefficient among the three reward coefficients, after choosing a reference-robot coefficient by trial and error. Their IPO-based optimizer uses TRPO and adaptive constraint thresholds; these probabilistic and average limits are not hard bounds enforced at every training step <Cite id="rewards-constraints-2024" />.

edits.before:
The second approach adapts reward weights during training. Srisuchinnawong and Manoonpong’s ROGER uses estimates of nonnegative penalty magnitudes relative to selected constraint thresholds to reduce the primary-reward gain and increase penalty gains near the thresholds, reversing that balance farther away. The penalties are subtracted from the primary reward; they are no bonuses. The revised paper reports an exploration-induced violation in its simulated quadruped experiment and explicitly limits its safety claims to assumptions about zero-penalty optimality and gentle system and learning dynamics. It offers no universal constraint-satisfaction guarantee <Cite id="gain-adaptation-2025" />.

Eureka searches over reward code; PPO learns the policies. In the default experiment, GPT-4 receives a task description and environment observation code with the existing reward excluded, then proposes Python reward functions. Candidate rewards train PPO policies in Isaac Gym. Selection uses a separate task-fitness function, while scalar snapshots of that fitness and each reward component provide feedback for the next reward-code mutation. The implementation trims the context to the relevant observation code and the last reward/reflection pair.

edits.before: The evaluation covers 29 simulated tasks: nine original Isaac Gym environments and 20 Dexterity tasks, spanning 10 robot morphologies. The paper's headline reports 83% of tasks and 52% average normalized improvement over human-expert rewards; its detailed results describe matching or exceeding the human reward on all nine Isaac tasks and 15 of the 20 Dexterity tasks. The human baseline is each benchmark's original shaped reward . Search uses five independent runs, five iterations per run and 16 candidate rewards per iteration. The reported comparison uses the best reward across search restarts; the separate reward-reflection ablation instead averages restarts. Intermediate rewards receive one PPO run; final rewards receive five, scored by the average of the maximum task fitness over ten fixed-interval checkpoints . The human-normalized score is `(Method - Sparse) / abs(Human - Sparse)`; for the headline average across all 29 tasks, the authors adjust each score to lie in `[0, 3]`. The 52% headline measures normalized reward improvement. It does not express a 52-percentage-point increase in success rate .
edits.after: The evaluation covers 29 simulated tasks, nine Isaac Gym environments and 20 Dexterity tasks across 10 morphologies. The headline is 83% of tasks and 52% average normalized improvement over each benchmark's original shaped reward; Eureka matches or beats the human reward on all nine Isaac tasks and 15 of 20 Dexterity tasks. Search uses five runs of five iterations with 16 candidates each and reports the best reward across restarts. Final rewards get five PPO runs, scored by the mean of maximum task fitness over ten checkpoints. Human-normalized scores are bounded to `[0, 3]` for the headline, so 52% measures normalized reward improvement .

edits.before: The limitations are structural, and the 2026 literature treats them as open. Eureka needs a fitness function, which is itself a reward-specification problem one level up. It needs cheap parallel training per candidate, so it inherits the locomotion-manipulation asymmetry from the first module in this domain. And LLM-written rewards are prone to specification gaming that only shows up on hardware; nobody has published a systematic study of whether they induce more or less contact-solver exploitation than human-written ones.
edits.after:
Eureka needs a task-fitness function, which its authors say can diverge from human intent; they show an extension with human-written reward reflection <Cite id="eureka-2024" />. Specification gaming satisfies the literal objective without achieving the intended outcome, and DeepMind researchers have collected around 60 examples <Cite id="specification-gaming-2020" />. Task-only rewards for athletic hardware skills invite reward hacking, which an actuator model fitted to real data reduced <Cite id="fey-athletic-2025" />. MAPL learns quadruped rewards from objective-wise LLM preferences and matches or beats expert rewards in four environments <Cite id="mapl-2026" />. No published study compares how often LLM-written and human-written rewards exploit the contact solver.

DrEureka writes both reward functions and domain-randomization distributions, getting a quadruped to walk atop a yoga ball <Cite id="dreureka-2024" />.

edits.before: Lee and colleagues' Reward Design Agent (RDA) compares against a matched Eureka implementation with the same GPT-5 backbone, task instructions, and training budget. That baseline reflects on numerical reward-component statistics; RDA additionally analyzes rendered trajectories together with reward logs, scores subtasks, summarizes failures, and revises both the subtask descriptions and reward code. Its experiments cover 12 ManiSkill tabletop tasks and four HumanoidBench whole-body tasks, using SAC with SimbaV2. On HumanoidBench, the paper reports higher VLM-rated alignment for RDA (0.70 versus Eureka's 0.47), with RDA success at 0.42 and slightly below Eureka's: reaching the goal and following the intended behavior are different measurements. The package example illustrates the distinction, contrasting throwing or torso-pushing with the requested hand-contact pushing. Reported alignment comes from GPT-4.1 ratings of five rollout videos, each queried four times. The authors identify costly RL training, imperfect fine-grained visual reasoning, and conflicting catch-versus-throw rewards in basketball as limitations; the ratings give no guarantee of instruction correctness . Eureka itself already noted that task fitness need not match human intent and demonstrated an extension using human-written reward reflection. RDA's automated visual diagnostics are the comparison's contribution; Eureka acknowledged the underlying limitation earlier .

edits.before: <Term id="reward-shaping">Reward shaping</Term> decides what to optimize; <Term id="curriculum-learning">curriculum</Term> decides in what order the policy is allowed to see difficulty. Three mechanisms dominate, and they are different enough to keep separate.
edits.after: <Term id="reward-shaping">Reward shaping</Term> decides what to optimize; <Term id="curriculum-learning">curriculum</Term> decides in what order difficulty appears. Ng and colleagues showed that a shaping reward expressible as a difference of potentials leaves the optimal policy unchanged, that this form is necessary for invariance, and that well-known shaping bugs come from non-potential-based rewards <Cite id="ng-reward-shaping-1999" />.

edits.before: Terrain curriculum is the game-inspired scheme from the massively parallel walking work: robots that succeed on a terrain tile get promoted to a harder one, robots that fail get demoted, and thousands of parallel robots make the difficulty frontier measurable <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Automatic Domain Randomization widens the randomization distribution itself as success crosses a threshold, an idea from OpenAI's dexterous hand work that now ships in Isaac Lab as a configurable curriculum <Cite id="openai-rubiks-cube-2019" /> <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />.

Curriculum is a dividend of the throughput covered in the parallel-sim module, and it is one more reason the same machinery does not transfer to manipulation, where the [MDP is not cheaply simulatable](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion).

Isaac Lab's DexPBT workers run independent RL processes with their own hyperparameters, and strong workers replace weak workers' weights and hyperparameters. Its RL-Games implementation reproduces a 6D reposing task with eight workers on one to two GPUs each, converging in about 16 hours on NVIDIA OVX L40 hardware <Cite id="isaac-lab-2025" />. Eurekaverse has a language model write progressively harder parkour environments as code, and its curriculum transfers to a real quadruped, outperforming courses designed by humans <Cite id="eurekaverse-2024" />.

BVER, from Marco Hutter (ETH Zurich) and colleagues (October 2026), borrows from [bidirectional RRT](/classical/motion-planning/): it grows start states outward from the goal and goals outward from the start, steering them toward each other. On quadruped box climbing it reached 95% success on a 0.4 m box in about 65% fewer iterations than the best reference-free curriculum it was compared with. It was also the only one of them to learn a 0.7 m box <Cite id="bver-2026" />. Model-based control can also drive the curriculum: ZEST adds a model-based assistive wrench as an automatic curriculum during RL training <Cite id="zest-2026" />.

edits.before: Everything above is about making learning work. The learning-vs-model-based debate asks whether it had to. The classical stack for legged control is a hierarchy: a footstep and contact planner, an <Term id="mpc">MPC</Term> layer optimizing a reduced-order model, and a whole-body QP tracking the MPC output against full rigid-body dynamics, friction cones, and actuator limits. The reduced-order model in the middle layer existed because full-order MPC was assumed too slow to run online. Whole-body MPC work describes the tradition it replaces as the "model hierarchies commonly seen in traditional model-based MPC", built on "reduced-order models and hierarchical control approaches" <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />.
edits.after: Classical legged control simplifies the model in its <Term id="mpc">MPC</Term> layer. MIT Cheetah 3 cast its dynamics as a convex problem that still captures the full 3D system, planning ground reaction forces over horizons up to 0.5 s and solving in under 1 ms at 20 to 30 Hz <Cite id="di-carlo-2018" />. Zhang and colleagues call this tradition the "model hierarchies commonly seen in traditional model-based MPC", built on "reduced-order models and hierarchical control approaches" <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />.

edits.before: Zhang and colleagues' March 2026 revision, listed on arXiv as "to appear at ICRA 2026", demonstrates a MuJoCo-based iLQR controller on Unitree Go1 and Go2 quadrupeds, a Go1 walking on its hind legs and transitioning to a handstand, and an H1 humanoid tracking a trotting gait. It uses forward finite differences for dynamics and residual Jacobians, analytical norm derivatives, approximate cost Hessians, and one warm-started iLQR update per solve without waiting for convergence. Joint-angle targets feed low-level PD control, which is also included in the planning model. On a desktop with a 20-core, 13th-generation Intel i9, the reported iLQR and intervening TV-LQR feedback rates are approximately 50 Hz and 300 Hz; the default horizon is 0.35 s with 100-Hz model discretization. H1 uses a 0.5-s horizon, ten active joint actuators, and four foot contact points after disabling upper-body DoFs with unreliable relative encoders and collision checking elsewhere on the body. These laboratory experiments use 100-Hz OptiTrack measurements fused with 500-Hz joint measurements. Onboard-only deployment remains untested here. The authors' phrase "few sim-to-real considerations" includes consequential setup choices: increasing MuJoCo's impratio from 1 to 100 to reduce slipping roughly doubled a quadruped iteration from 10 to 20 ms on a separate 12th-generation i7 test. An eight-second H1 feedback comparison also records a gantry-assisted recovery in the trial without TV-LQR feedback. The paper presents an accessible model-based baseline, while identifying motion-capture dependence, actuation/contact system identification, contact-mode exploration, and long-horizon numerical behavior as limitations. It does not establish calibration-free operation, zero total engineering cost, or blanket superiority over learned control <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />.
edits.after: Whole-body MPC itself ran on legged hardware earlier. Sleiman and colleagues' 2021 framework plans locomotion and manipulation as one multi-contact optimal control problem, solved in real time on the robot's onboard computer, and pushed and pulled a heavy resistive door <Cite id="sleiman-wbmpc-2021" />. Whole-body sampling-based MPC reached legged hardware in 2024. Alvarez-Padilla and colleagues report what they call the first whole-body sampling-based MPC deployment on real legged robots, including climbing a box about the robot's height <Cite id="mppi-whole-body-2024" />. DIAL-MPC optimizes full-order quadruped dynamics in real time without training and outperforms RL policies by 50% on climbing tasks <Cite id="dial-mpc-2024" />. An IROS 2026 paper from the RAI Institute uses continuous-time whole-body MPC on a Spot with an arm to return table-tennis balls of varying spin and rally with human players <Cite id="rai-iros-2026" />.

edits.before: The structural point is deeper than one paper. MPC has no sim-to-real gap in the RL sense: it re-solves against the measured state at every control step, so model error is rejected by feedback instead of being baked into weights. From this angle, <Term id="domain-randomization">domain randomization</Term> is an expensive workaround for leaving the model open-loop. Boston Dynamics describes a source-specific hybrid arrangement: its 2024 Spot account retains the model-based locomotion controller while a learned policy removes the need to evaluate multiple MPC instances in parallel <Cite id="bd-spot-rl-2024" />. Its August 2025 Atlas/TRI report concerns language-conditioned policies for whole-body manipulation, including locomotion; the teleoperation system is built on MPC, and the learned policies use that same robot control interface <Cite id="bd-atlas-lbm-2025" />. These two reports describe different robots and policy generations. Neither replaces an entire controls stack.
edits.after: Zhang and colleagues' MuJoCo-based iLQR controller was first posted in 2025 and revised in 2026 to appear at ICRA 2026. It runs on Unitree Go1 and Go2, a Go1 walking on its hind legs into a handstand, and an H1 humanoid tracking a trotting gait. It uses finite-difference derivatives and one warm-started iLQR update per solve, sending joint-angle targets to PD control that the planning model includes. On a 20-core 13th-generation Intel i9, iLQR and TV-LQR feedback run at about 50 Hz and 300 Hz, with a default 0.35 s horizon discretized at 100 Hz. The experiments fuse 100 Hz OptiTrack measurements with 500 Hz joint data, and onboard-only deployment is untested. Raising MuJoCo's impratio from 1 to 100 to reduce slipping doubled a quadruped iteration from 10 to 20 ms <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />.

## The case for each side

edits.before: The case for learning, at its strongest: locomotion is settled, and sim-trained controllers handle terrain, unknown payloads, and hardware variation, taking two generations of ANYmal through ground beyond the reach of prior published work in legged locomotion (in the papers' own words), at the cost of one forward pass at deploy time <Cite id="lee-2020" /> <Cite id="miki-2022" />. Perception integrates naturally; there is no clean way to put an RGB image into a QP. Contact schedules emerge from exploration without enumeration. Semantics exists only on the learned side: Gemini Robotics 2 controls three embodiments from one checkpoint, and no model-based stack does anything comparable <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />.
edits.after: The case for learning: sim-trained controllers took two generations of ANYmal through natural environments "beyond the reach of prior published work in legged locomotion", in Lee and colleagues' words, at the cost of one forward pass at deploy time <Cite id="lee-2020" />. Miki and colleagues later report traversal of harsh natural terrain at "unprecedented speeds" <Cite id="miki-2022" />. Miller and colleagues report an end-to-end RL policy on Spot at over 5.2 m/s, more than triple the default controller's maximum speed <Cite id="miller-spot-2025" />. In drone racing, RL beat optimal control because it "optimizes a better objective" and copes with model uncertainty through <Term id="domain-randomization">domain randomization</Term> <Cite id="racing-rl-vs-oc-2023" />. Semantic, language-conditioned control comes from the learned side, as Gemini Robotics 2 shows on [humanoid whole-body control](/rl-sim2real/humanoid-wbc/) <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />.

edits.before: The case for model-based control, at its strongest: the strongest single 2026 result in legged control comes from iLQR <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />. Constraints are enforced directly; a friction cone in a QP holds, a reward penalty merely advises. Data efficiency is infinite in the relevant sense, since MPC needs zero task data. The behavior is verifiable in ways a network is not. Contact fidelity is a modeling problem, which is why the learning stack is importing model-based contact research into its simulators: Newton's hydroelastic contact modeling is inspired by Drake's contact model, Drake-developer TRI now partners with Newton on solver and contact modeling, and Newton acts as the physics layer under Isaac Lab <Cite id="state-of-simulation-2026" /> <Cite id="newton-manipulation-blog-2026" />. The learning stack's current progress on manipulation is gated by better models, not better algorithms.
edits.after: The case for model-based control: a deliberately simple whole-body iLQR baseline on an off-the-shelf simulator runs in real time on quadruped and humanoid hardware, with no task data and hand-tuned cost weights <Cite id="mujoco-ilqr-2026" />. Grandia and colleagues optimize all of ANYmal's degrees of freedom in real time against foothold constraints from elevation maps <Cite id="grandia-2022" />. Sampling MPC now discovers gaits and contact sequences without handcrafted patterns, in real time on a CPU <Cite id="schramm-2025" />. Convex MPC can enforce friction-cone limits as hard constraints, as MIT Cheetah 3's ground-reaction-force planner does with a pyramid approximation, where a reward penalty only discourages violations <Cite id="di-carlo-2018" />. Newton's hydroelastic contact modeling is inspired by Drake's, Drake developer TRI partners with Newton on solvers and contact, and Newton is now a physics backend for Isaac Lab <Cite id="state-of-simulation-2026" /> <Cite id="newton-manipulation-blog-2026" />. NVIDIA presents higher-fidelity contact modeling as a route to better sim-to-real transfer for contact-rich manipulation <Cite id="newton-manipulation-blog-2026" />, and massively parallel sampling MPC on a real Franka reports contact sensitivity as a key challenge <Cite id="dierking-2026" />.

edits.before:
The field has mostly stopped arguing and hybridized along a clean division. Model-based control owns anything with a good analytic model, hard constraints, and a need for guarantees: whole-body torque control, force control, safety layers, and increasingly the low-level interface below a learned policy. Learning owns anything requiring perception, semantics, contact discovery, or generalization across embodiments. The newest position dissolves the boundary entirely: model-based methods as the training signal for learned ones, through differentiable simulation, MPC-as-teacher distillation, and learned models used as forward dynamics for planning.

The genuinely contested question in 2026 is not learning or models. It is where the learned model lives: in the weights of a policy, in a latent dynamics model, in a video generator, or nowhere at all because you re-solve online.
edits.after: Hybrids now combine the two. MPC-guided policy search used MPC with full state to generate training data for a simulated quadrotor's network, which runs at a fraction of MPC's cost <Cite id="mpc-gps-2015" />. DTC trains an RL policy to track footholds from a model-based planner and reports more robustness than model-based counterparts on slippery or deformable ground <Cite id="dtc-2023" />. A policy trained entirely in a differentiable simulator transferred zero-shot to a real quadruped <Cite id="schwarke-2024" />.

edits.before:
Reinforcement learning is one idea with two entirely different economies. The idea is a policy improved from its own experience of acting in an environment, formalized as a Markov decision process: states, actions, a transition rule, a reward <Cite id="sutton-barto-2018" />. The economies are what a step of that experience costs. In a GPU simulator, a step costs under ten microseconds of wall clock, amortized across the four thousand robots taking one at once <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. On a real robot, a step is a real moment of a real machine's life, and the machine has to be reset afterwards.

Most of what reads as an algorithmic preference in robot learning is that cost difference showing up somewhere else.

## What a budget buys, and what it forbids

Set the environment-step budget below, then switch from simulation to a single robot without changing the budget. The instrument holds collection rates constant to illustrate a cost difference. Its family bands are editorial toy categories. They impose no rule about which algorithms a robot can use.
edits.after:
Reinforcement learning (RL) for robotics is the training of robot policies from their own experience of acting, formalized as a Markov decision process of states, actions, transitions and rewards <Cite id="sutton-barto-2018" />. A simulated step is nearly free when thousands of GPU robots act at once <Cite id="rudin-2021" />, while a real step costs machine time and a reset.

## What a budget buys, and what it forbids

edits.before: The toy isolates collection cost. It does not measure task performance, predict a new robot’s collection rate or establish which learning algorithm will work.
edits.after: A review of robotic deep RL case studies lists real-world challenges that mainstream RL research, focused on games and simulated control, seldom addresses <Cite id="ibarz-2021" />. A 2025 survey of real-world successes names stable, sample-efficient real-world RL as a priority for future work <Cite id="tang-drl-survey-2025" />.

edits.before: The MDP formulation admits two families of method. Their practical difference is whether a transition can be used more than once.
edits.after: An <Term id="on-policy">on-policy</Term> method's update is valid only for data the current policy generated, so each batch is collected, consumed and discarded. PPO alternates sampling with optimizing a surrogate objective that allows several minibatch epochs per batch, where plain policy gradient takes one step <Cite id="ppo-2017" />. An <Term id="off-policy">off-policy</Term> method improves one policy from data another produced, so experience accumulates in a <Term id="replay-buffer">replay buffer</Term>. Underneath is <Term id="q-learning">Q-learning</Term>: fit the value of a state-action pair and bootstrap from the best next action, even one never taken <Cite id="sutton-barto-2018" />.

edits.before:
An <Term id="on-policy">on-policy</Term> method's update is only valid for data the current policy generated, so a batch is collected, consumed, and thrown away. PPO is the canonical instance, alternating between sampling interaction data and optimizing a surrogate objective, where the surrogate buys several minibatch epochs from one batch; plain policy gradient allows a single gradient step <Cite id="ppo-2017" />. An <Term id="off-policy">off-policy</Term> method can improve one policy from data another produced, which means experience survives the policy that made it and accumulates in a <Term id="replay-buffer">replay buffer</Term>. The mechanism underneath is <Term id="q-learning">Q-learning</Term>: fit the value of a state-action pair, and bootstrap from the best available next action even if that action was never taken <Cite id="sutton-barto-2018" />.

The continuous-control lineage of that idea is short and worth knowing by name. DDPG adapted deterministic policy gradients to deep function approximators and learned pixel-to-torque policies off-policy <Cite id="ddpg-2016" />. TD3 identified overestimation bias in DDPG and reduced its effects with clipped double critics, delayed policy updates and target policy smoothing <Cite id="td3-2018" />. Soft actor-critic added a maximum-entropy objective, and its authors were explicit that the target was sample complexity, one of the two challenges they named as keeping model-free deep RL out of complex real-world domains <Cite id="sac-2018" />.
edits.after: DDPG adapted deterministic policy gradients to deep networks and learned pixel-to-torque policies off-policy <Cite id="ddpg-2016" />. TD3 reduced DDPG's overestimation bias with clipped double critics, delayed policy updates and target policy smoothing <Cite id="td3-2018" />. Soft actor-critic added a maximum-entropy objective; its authors named sample complexity and brittle convergence as the two challenges keeping model-free deep RL out of complex real-world domains and designed SAC to address both <Cite id="sac-2018" />.

edits.before: On-policy learning wastes data by construction, so its dominance in simulation-trained robotics looks like a mistake until you price it. When the sampler is a GPU running thousands of environments, environment steps are close to free and the scarce resource is the researcher's patience with a training run that diverges. The SAC paper says that on-policy training "tends to improve stability but results in poor sample complexity"; it also calls the combination of off-policy learning and neural-network function approximation "a major challenge for stability and convergence" <Cite id="sac-2018" />. Rudin and colleagues trained ANYmal with 4,096 parallel robots at 98,304 steps per policy update, 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on one workstation GPU <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Discarding every one of those 147 million transitions after a single update is not extravagance, it is a rounding error.
edits.after: With thousands of GPU environments, steps are nearly free and training stability is the scarce resource. SAC's authors credit on-policy training with stability at the price of "poor sample complexity" and call off-policy learning with neural function approximation "a major challenge for stability and convergence" <Cite id="sac-2018" />. Rudin and colleagues trained ANYmal with 4,096 parallel robots, 98,304 steps per update and 1,500 updates in under twenty minutes on one workstation GPU, averaging more than 122,880 environment steps per second. The hardware was an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Minitaur's 160,000 control steps over about two hours average about 22 per second, under its 50 Hz rollout rate because resets and overhead count <Cite id="haarnoja-walk-2019" />. The [parallel-simulation module](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl) covers the first regime.

edits.before: The reported collection budgets differ sharply. Rudin’s 98,304 samples per update over 1,500 updates in under 1,200 seconds imply an end-to-end average greater than 122,880 environment steps per second on an i9-11900k CPU and RTX A6000 GPU <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Minitaur’s 160,000 control steps over about two hours imply approximately 22 control steps per second averaged over the whole training process; its 50 Hz rollout rate excludes resets and other training overhead <Cite id="haarnoja-walk-2019" />. The [parallel-simulation module](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl) explains the machinery behind the first regime. This article follows the cost of collecting steps on hardware.
edits.after: The default is now contested. Most GPU-simulation work used PPO for its simplicity and ease of scaling, while off-policy methods were more data-efficient but slower in wall-clock time; Parallel Q-Learning scales to tens of thousands of environments and beats PPO in wall-clock time <Cite id="pql-2023" />. FastTD3 solves a range of HumanoidBench tasks in under 3 hours on one A100 GPU <Cite id="fasttd3-2025" />, and FastSAC and FastTD3 train sim-to-real humanoid locomotion in 15 minutes on one RTX 4090 <Cite id="seo-2025" />.

## What sample efficiency looks like in step counts

The papers that trained on hardware published their budgets, and the numbers are small enough to be surprising.
edits.after: ## What sample efficiency looks like in step counts

edits.before: <Term id="sample-efficiency">Sample efficiency</Term> is the axis these results turn on. Haarnoja and colleagues learned Minitaur locomotion from 160,000 control steps, roughly 400 rollouts, in about two hours of real-world time, and that figure is end to end: it contains the resets and the operator, which is why it sits far below the control rate the rollouts ran at <Cite id="haarnoja-walk-2019" />. DayDreamer reports one Unitree A1 training run in which the robot learned to roll over, stand and walk in one hour without a simulator. After that hour, ten minutes of additional online learning under pushes produced resistance to light pushes or recovery after harder pushes. The authors manually intervened at the edge of the training area without changing the robot’s joint configuration or orientation. Their “without resets” description still allows those interventions <Cite id="daydreamer-2022" />.
edits.after: <Term id="sample-efficiency">Sample efficiency</Term> is the axis these results turn on. Haarnoja and colleagues learned Minitaur locomotion from 160,000 control steps, about 400 rollouts, in about two hours of real-world time that includes resets and the operator <Cite id="haarnoja-walk-2019" />. Smith and colleagues learned quadruped walking with model-free RL in 20 minutes in the real world <Cite id="walk-in-the-park-2022" />. DayDreamer trained a Unitree A1 to roll over, stand and walk in one hour without a simulator, and ten more minutes of online learning under pushes produced resistance to light pushes or recovery from harder ones. The authors intervened manually at the edge of the training area without changing the robot's joint configuration or orientation <Cite id="daydreamer-2022" />. In 2026, an online model-based RL controller learned directly on an 11.5-ton hydraulic excavator, without demonstrations or simulation pretraining. After 20 minutes of interaction its tracking accuracy was comparable to that of earlier learned controllers trained on 100 to 150 minutes of data <Cite id="excavator-mbrl-2026" />.

edits.before: Scale changes the shape of the cost rather than removing it. QT-Opt collected over 580,000 grasp attempts across seven robots in about 800 robot hours <Cite id="qt-opt-2018" />; the 2016 hand-eye coordination preprint reports about 800,000 grasp attempts over two months using between 6 and 14 robots at a time. Its abstract says “over 800,000,” while its introduction describes “several months”; the source gives differing descriptions, leaving exact campaign count and duration unresolved <Cite id="levine-hand-eye-2016" />. **Conservative value estimation** pushes the estimate down where the data is thin. CQL learns a lower bound on the policy's value by penalizing Q-values on out-of-distribution actions and maximizing them under the data distribution, which is the term that tightens the bound <Cite id="cql-2020" />.

**Implicit and expectile approaches** avoid the query entirely. IQL never evaluates an unseen action: it fits an expectile of the value distribution over the actions the dataset does contain, treating the state value function as an implicit maximum, and extracts the policy by advantage-weighted regression <Cite id="iql-2022" />.

**Behavior-regularized approaches** constrain the policy. TD3+BC adds a behavior-cloning term to a standard off-policy actor-critic and normalizes the states, and its authors' point is deliberately deflationary: that minimal change matches the performance of far more elaborate offline methods <Cite id="td3-bc-2021" />.

Q-Transformer combines scale with regularization. It discretizes each action dimension and uses a Transformer to represent Q-values conditioned on the observation history and earlier dimensions of the current action, backing them up autoregressively. Its offline objective also uses conservative regularization and augments temporal-difference learning with Monte Carlo and n-step returns. The real-robot experiments combine successful human demonstrations with failed autonomous trials for language-conditioned manipulation. Results on arbitrary mixed-quality datasets remain unestablished <Cite id="q-transformer-2023" />. The paper studies sparse success/failure rewards and leaves online fine-tuning for future work.

edits.before: The difference between simulation RL and real-world RL that no algorithm addresses is janitorial. A simulated episode ends and the next one begins from a fresh initial state, for free. That something is usually a person, and a person who has to intervene between episodes is the real limit on how long an experiment can run.

A D'Claw hand learned valve rotation and bead manipulation from RGB images after people supplied goal examples; training ran unattended, but evaluation included manual resets for bead manipulation. The authors leave sample complexity, exploration on harder tasks and safe operation to future work <Cite id="real-world-rl-ingredients-2020" />.

Sharma and colleagues distinguish **deployed-policy evaluation** from **continuing-policy evaluation** for non-episodic learning. The former sums gaps to optimal expected discounted deployment return over training, using evaluation rollouts from the initial-state distribution that never enter training. The latter is the limiting average reward from the agent’s actual actions, with no separate deployment phase. In their extension for irreversible, non-ergodic settings, an intervention budget `h` falls by `c(s,a)` for each requested or enforced intervention; `h - c(s,a) <= 0` sends the environment to an absorbing state and ends training. Interventions enter as constrained costs; the evaluation metric stays separate <Cite id="autonomous-rl-2022" />.

EARL’s experiments instead use scheduled resets during training and stop after a fixed step budget. They estimate deployed-policy performance with finite-horizon, undiscounted returns and continuing performance with average reward accumulated so far. They show learning curves and also report final deployed-policy returns. The paper notes that the two objectives can favor different behavior and that trading some human supervision for faster learning remains a practical question <Cite id="autonomous-rl-2022" />.

<Term id="reset-free-learning">Reset-free learning</Term> can replace manual episode resets with learned recovery behaviors. Gupta and colleagues' MTRF learns task-specific policies and uses a designer-provided task graph to sequence them: re-centering, pickup and flip-up can restore the conditions for in-hand reorientation after a dropped object. They evaluated a D’Hand mounted on a Sawyer arm on valve reorientation and pipe insertion, and report learning these tasks without manual episode resets during the training runs <Cite id="reset-free-rl-2021" />. The setup still used supplied rewards and task graphs; the in-hand experiment tracked the object with motion capture, and pickup used scripted arm motion while learning the hand controls. Pipe insertion used frozen fingers and separate approach and insertion tasks to reduce collisions <Cite id="reset-free-rl-2021" />. For the in-hand run, the user positioned the objects and started the robot. The method assumes that successful upstream tasks produce valid starting states for downstream ones; coverage of every downstream starting state remains unproven. This needs a suitable task family and a supplied task graph <Cite id="reset-free-rl-2021" />. Without one, a person handles the reset. The human-in-the-loop line chose to pay that cost deliberately <Cite id="hil-serl-2024" />.

The real robot differs from all of them in ways nobody can fully enumerate. Closing that difference is sim-to-real transfer, and it is where most of the engineering lives. The RL algorithm is usually the least interesting part of a successful sim-to-real system. Four method families do the work. ## Domain randomization: train on a distribution of simulators These two papers address different parts of transfer. Tobin and colleagues randomized textures, lighting and camera pose for tabletop object localization. They summarize real-world localization accuracy as around 1.5 cm, evaluated on 480 webcam images of eight geometric objects in object-only, distractor and partial-occlusion conditions. The paper reports the best network after a small hyperparameter search; the approximate 1.5 cm summary is not a bound for every object or condition. Most experiments used ImageNet initialization, but an ablation found that random initialization could achieve nearly the same transfer performance with enough simulated training data. The detector was also used with a motion planner on a Fetch robot . Peng and colleagues randomized link mass, joint damping, puck mass/friction/damping, table height, controller gains, action timing and observation noise. A recurrent policy trained only in simulation transferred to a seven-DoF Fetch arm pushing a puck to a target. Real evaluation used motion capture for puck position, 200 control steps per episode, and success within 7 cm of the target at the end of the episode; target and initial puck positions were randomized within a 30 cm by 30 cm area. The authors report substantial simulated-versus-real joint-trajectory mismatch after limited calibration. Calibration was limited but present . With enough variability in the simulator, the real world may appear to the model as just another variation, as Tobin's abstract puts it. OpenAI's Rubik's-cube system added the curriculum version: automatic domain randomization widens the randomization range as the agent succeeds, so the distribution grows with the policy's competence . The teacher-student pattern separates those problems. Phase one trains a teacher with privileged, simulator-only observations: terrain geometry under the feet, friction coefficients, applied disturbances. Phase two trains a student that sees only deployable sensing, usually a short history of proprioception, to imitate the teacher's actions. Lee and colleagues trained a privileged RL teacher with simulator-only terrain and contact information, then distilled its actions and latent features into a temporal convolutional network student. The deployed student uses two seconds of proprioceptive history from joint encoders and an IMU, together with the command and current state. It has no external terrain map. At deployment the base policy combines the current state, previous action and estimated extrinsics to predict desired joint positions. The adaptation module uses 50 state-action steps (0.5 seconds of history); on the tested Unitree A1 setup it updates extrinsics asynchronously at about 10 Hz, while the base policy runs at 100 Hz using the latest estimate. Hwangbo and colleagues learned an actuator network for ANYmal's series-elastic actuators: it predicts joint torque from joint-position errors and velocities at the current time and 0.01 and 0.02 seconds earlier.
