A second PPO policy takes the simulated state and a recorded action and outputs a delta action. Adding that delta before the simulator step lets its reward penalize disagreement with the recorded real trajectory; RL learns the delta without measured residual-action labels. The delta action model is then frozen while the tracking policy is fine-tuned in the modified simulator. Only the fine-tuned tracking policy is deployed: the delta model stays in simulation. The hardware study learns corrections for four ankle DoFs; the full 23-DoF simulation model has no corresponding hardware correction . The evaluation separates IsaacGym-to-IsaacSim and IsaacGym-to-Genesis transfer from the G1 hardware study. The simulation results test open-loop replay and closed-loop motion tracking separately. The simulation suite has 43 motion sequences grouped by difficulty, and reports mean tracking errors across motion sequences. SysID and delta-dynamics are explicit simulation baselines. ASAP does not win every metric: in the easy IsaacSim closed-loop group, its mean global joint-position error is 106 mm versus SysID's 105 mm. On hardware, ASAP is compared only with Vanilla on kicking and LeBron James's "Silencer": mean global joint-position error falls from 61.2 to 50.2 mm and from 159 to 112 mm, respectively. Basic domain randomization is used in pretraining; the separate random-action-noise fine-tuning ablation is an IsaacGym-to-Genesis test. It supplies no hardware comparison against every baseline . ASAP reports improved tracking on the held-out "Silencer" motion and better out-of-distribution replay with more training data. The tests do not establish arbitrary unseen-skill coverage. Its stated hardware limits are motor overheating and damage, motion-capture dependence during data collection, and the data required to learn a full 23-DoF delta model. These empirical limitations do not impose a mathematical rule that the correction works only near the pretrained policy's trajectories . ## Real-to-sim: rebuild the scene, keep the physics The newest family attacks the visual gap by reconstructing the actual deployment scene. SplatSim replaces mesh primitives in the rendering pipeline with Gaussian splats reconstructed from the deployment scene; PyBullet supplies the physics. Across four UR5 manipulation tasks, with 40 trials per task, the authors report 86.25% average zero-shot real-world success for diffusion policies trained on simulated demonstrations, versus 97.5% for policies trained on real-world demonstrations. That result includes training augmentations alongside the renderer . The setup uses a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper and two RealSense D455 cameras. Preparing the splats requires manual robot segmentation, CAD-derived link bounds and ICP alignment; robot kinematics and simulated object poses drive rendering. The paper lists RGB observations plus end-effector position and orientation in its setup figure, while its evaluation section says the policy relies solely on RGB at test time. Those descriptions disagree; an unqualified image-only input specification is unsupported . In its August 2025 revision, RoboGSim combines a Gaussian Reconstructor, Digital Twins Builder, Scene Composer and Interactive Engine in a real2sim2real system. Multi-view images and supplied robot MDH parameters feed reconstruction; mesh assets and measured layout alignment connect the scene to Isaac Sim. The synthesizer composes novel views, objects, scenes and trajectories. In closed-loop evaluation, a policy acts on splat-rendered images; Isaac Sim handles inverse kinematics, collisions and other physical interactions, and the resulting state drives the next rendering . This simulated evaluation cannot stand in for real-robot testing. On the UR5 ring-toss task, each model had ten trials with up to three grasp attempts per trial. The paper reports 90% placement for the real-data-trained model on the real robot but 30% in RoboGSim. Simulated evaluation avoids executing those actions on hardware; it gives no demonstrated safety guarantee for a deployed robot. The paper examines novel-pose rendering and trajectory replay separately from closed-loop policy evaluation . The Newton 1.0 release post describes a Warp-based tiled camera sensor whose ray-tracing backend supports both triangle meshes and Gaussian splats . Keep the division of labor straight: the splat supplies appearance, and a conventional physics engine still supplies dynamics. A 3DGS twin is a learned renderer bolted onto a simulator, and it reconstructs a static scene: articulated objects, deformables, and lighting changes each require extra machinery on top. Treating such a twin as a learned simulator is the most common misreading of the real-to-sim literature. ## The levers nobody demos The survey adds two cross-cutting options that rarely get headline systems. Sim-real co-training mixes real data into an otherwise simulated training set, so the real samples anchor the representation while simulation supplies coverage. State and action abstraction chooses the interface between policy and robot, such as end-effector velocities or foot positions in place of raw torques, so that a conventional low-level controller absorbs much of the gap . The survey emphasizes action-space choice in reducing the sim-to-real gap across navigation, locomotion, and manipulation. Successful deployments often combine randomization, identification and abstraction. ## Where each family breaks Each family's limits differ. The friction chart's conservatism cost is an authored assumption with no corresponding empirical result in the cited papers. The teacher-student panel likewise constructs its error; it measures no distillation limit. ASAP shows some held-out motion transfer, while broader coverage and affordable real-robot data collection remain open . Real-to-sim twins freeze the scene they captured.

Most runs used ImageNet initialization, though random initialization nearly matched it given enough simulated data, and a Fetch robot used the detector with a motion planner. Their abstract frames the real world as "just another variation" once the simulator varies enough . Peng and colleagues randomized link mass, joint damping, puck mass, friction and damping, table height, controller gains, action timing and observation noise, maximizing expected return over [that dynamics distribution](/how-robots-work/#worlds). A recurrent policy trained only in simulation pushed a puck with a seven-DoF Fetch arm. Real trials used motion capture, 200 control steps per episode, start and target positions randomized within a 30 cm square, and success within 7 cm at the end. The authors report substantial joint-trajectory mismatch after limited calibration and ablate their randomization choices . OpenAI's 2018 hand policy randomized friction coefficients and object appearance and transferred to the physical robot . Its Rubik's-cube successor added the curriculum version: automatic domain randomization widens ranges as the policy succeeds . Isaac Lab, the framework from the [previous module](/rl-sim2real/parallel-sim-rl), ships ADR as a configurable curriculum with reference configs in its dexterous-manipulation examples. In Isaac Lab, simulation state is GPU-resident, but mass, friction, contact offsets and joint armature change through PhysX CPU APIs. Most parameters randomize at runtime, mesh scale and collider type only before simulation starts, and CPU parameter writes can occur beyond episode resets . SPI-Active notes that poorly tuned randomization "can lead to overly conservative policies" , and Chen and colleagues bound the gap between a randomized policy and the real-world optimum, stressing history-dependent policies . Boston Dynamics reports that Atlas's fridge policy, trained for 50 to 70 pound loads, moved a fridge of over 100 pounds . ## Teacher-student distillation: privilege in, proprioception out Teacher-student training splits sensing from control: a teacher learns from privileged simulator state, then a student with deployable sensing imitates it. Learning by Cheating used this two-stage form for driving , after asymmetric actor-critic had given only the critic full state . Lee and colleagues distilled a privileged RL teacher, which saw simulator-only terrain and contact information, into a temporal convolutional student via its actions and latent features. The student uses two seconds of proprioceptive history from joint encoders and an IMU, plus the command and current state, with no terrain map. Trained on rigid procedural terrain, one controller per robot generation took ANYmal-B and ANYmal-C robots through mud, snow, rubble and vegetation without environment-specific tuning . Agarwal and colleagues distilled a teacher trained on a cheap depth variant into a depth-camera student , and Isaac Lab's DextrAH-RGB example distills a privileged KUKA and Allegro teacher into a stereo-RGB network . RMA trains a base policy and an environment-factor encoder jointly with RL, then regresses an adaptation module on simulated state-action histories to predict the latent extrinsics. At deployment the base policy maps current state, previous action and estimated extrinsics to desired joint positions. The module reads 50 state-action steps (0.5 seconds) and updates asynchronously at about 10 Hz on the A1, while the base policy runs at 100 Hz on the latest estimate, with no online gradient updates. Its latent encodes behavior-relevant conditions without guaranteeing each physical parameter . UP-OSI had earlier fed dynamics parameters predicted from recent history into a universal policy . Isaac Lab calls the failure mode an information gap due to input mismatch: the student must reconstruct unobserved states from partial observations such as images, hardest under heavy camera occlusion . Hwangbo and colleagues fitted an actuator network for ANYmal's series-elastic actuators to real excitation data and used it in simulation to train policies. It predicts torque from joint-position errors and velocities now and 0.01 and 0.02 seconds earlier. Policies trained with ideal or analytical actuator models failed to take a single step without falling . SPI-Active samples them in parallel with Fisher-information-driven excitation and beats baselines by 42 to 63% in locomotion tasks . Miller and colleagues score Spot simulation against hardware with Wasserstein distance and maximum mean discrepancy and tune it with CMA-ES . HALO calibrates a humanoid and then its payload in differentiable MuJoCo XLA . ZEST selects joint gains from approximate analytical armature values for closed-chain actuators and adds a refined actuator model; its policies, trained entirely in simulation, deploy zero-shot on Atlas, the Unitree G1 and Spot . Marco Hutter (ETH Zurich) and colleagues apply identification to the objects a robot handles in ForceTwin (September 2026). A person probes a door or another articulated object with a handheld force-sensing gripper, and the system fits inertia, friction, damping and a neural residual for configuration-dependent forces such as door closers. Zhang and colleagues build soft-body splat twins from video whose rollouts correlate strongly with real execution . It says the action space "plays a crucial role in reducing the sim-to-real gap" across navigation, locomotion and manipulation, citing joint-velocity control for manipulation, and that high-frequency impedance controllers can improve manipulation transfer . Locomotion and manipulation are the two robot problems where reinforcement learning in simulation has had opposite results. In 2021, Rudin and colleagues trained an ANYmal quadruped to walk on flat ground in under four minutes, and on uneven terrain in twenty minutes, on a single workstation GPU <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. Policies trained this way are now the default production approach for quadruped locomotion and, increasingly, for bipedal humanoids. General manipulation went the other direction: the field's strongest systems are trained by imitation on real, teleoperated demonstrations. In 2026 there is still no manipulation equivalent of the four-minute walking run.

The reason sits in the contact, and it is measurable. Drag the contact-model error slider below from its default 2 mm: the peg insertion is already jammed at that value while the quadruped notices nothing, and locomotion only fails past 20 mm, forty times the error that kills the insertion.
edits.after: The locomotion and manipulation asymmetry is the pattern in which simulation-trained reinforcement learning (RL) made legged locomotion robust well before general manipulation. In 2021 an ANYmal quadruped learned to walk on flat ground in under four minutes, and on uneven terrain in twenty, on one workstation GPU <Cite id="rudin-2021" />.

edits.before: The 2026 reality-gap survey describes the manipulation MDP as difficult to simulate cheaply <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. The [RL for Robotics module](/rl-sim2real/rl-for-robotics) covers the machinery side: what a sample budget buys, why robotics defaulted to PPO anyway, and where off-policy methods pay off. Locomotion asks the simulator for <Term id="proprioception">proprioception</Term>, a terrain heightfield, and a decent actuator model, all of which physics engines handle well. Manipulation asks for per-object geometry, friction, compliance, and deformation, resolved to millimeter-accurate multi-point contact, plus a visual pipeline good enough to stand in for object state. Each of those is a known hard problem; a single task needs all of them at once. The difference lies in how faithfully each task's MDP can be simulated.
edits.after:
Legged RL was mainly limited to simulation until Hwangbo and colleagues transferred simulation-trained policies to ANYmal in 2019 <Cite id="hwangbo-2019" />. Lee and colleagues' proprioceptive controller, trained on much simpler simulated terrain, proved robust in natural environments <Cite id="lee-2020" />. RMA needs no reference trajectories, trains on a terrain generator and deploys on an A1 without fine-tuning <Cite id="rma-2021" />. Radosavovic and colleagues' causal transformer over proprioceptive history carried the recipe to humanoids zero-shot <Cite id="radosavovic-2023" />, and an off-policy recipe now trains humanoid locomotion in 15 minutes on one RTX 4090 <Cite id="seo-2025" />.

Boston Dynamics says RL helps where conditions are easy to simulate but good strategies are hard to describe <Cite id="bd-spot-rl-2024" />.

The 2026 reality-gap survey notes that most simulators assume perfectly rigid bodies while real objects deform, and that perfect fidelity is computationally infeasible <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. Rudin and colleagues' locomotion policy observes <Term id="proprioception">proprioception</Term> and 108 terrain-height samples around the base, and because ANYmal's series-elastic actuators are hard to model in simulation, they learn an actuator network <Cite id="rudin-2021" />. For manipulation, the survey says mismatches from simplified contact models are particularly problematic in contact-rich tasks, where precise interaction modeling is crucial <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. It also lists photorealistic rendering among the open sim-to-real challenges <Cite id="reality-gap-survey-2026" />. Tang and colleagues trace RL's difficulty in [robotics](/rl-sim2real/rl-for-robotics) to the cost of interacting with the physical world <Cite id="tang-drl-survey-2025" />.

edits.before: This one fact explains why the two literatures read so differently. The locomotion literature is "<Term id="ppo">PPO</Term>, <Term id="domain-randomization">domain randomization</Term>, <Term id="curriculum-learning">curriculum</Term>." The manipulation literature is "collect a hundred thousand demonstrations and train a diffusion transformer," because real demonstration data sidesteps the simulability problem entirely: a real trajectory needs no contact model at all (the [behavior cloning module](/manipulation/bc-foundations) covers what that choice costs elsewhere).
edits.after: Locomotion papers read "<Term id="ppo">PPO</Term>, <Term id="domain-randomization">domain randomization</Term>, <Term id="curriculum-learning">curriculum</Term>." Manipulation papers often use real demonstrations, which need no contact model. Diffusion Policy beat prior methods by 46.9% on average across 12 tasks <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />, and ACT learned to slot a battery at 80 to 90% success from 10 minutes of [demonstrations](/manipulation/bc-foundations) <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />.

edits.after: A gait recovers from a wrong contact force on the next step; a jammed peg cannot. Acosta and colleagues call dynamic contact the computational bottleneck for most simulations; three tested simulators missed elastic impacts <Cite id="acosta-2021" />. Rigid-body contact models have a task-specific accuracy ceiling and hard-to-interpret parameters <Cite id="fazeli-2017" />. edits.before: The figure compares four near-point foot contacts with fourteen simultaneous distributed contacts. Every contact gives a solver approximation another place to produce a wrong force. A foot presses a near-point patch into a rigid substrate, while a peg slides through continuous wall contact that simple point-contact models do not represent. The quadruped's gait is an attractor that high-bandwidth feedback pulls it back into, so a wrong contact force can be corrected on the next step. A jammed peg has no next step.

## The honest snapshot comes from the imitation side

Gemini Robotics 2 offers a separate 2026 view of the manipulation bottleneck through published task-level numbers. It reports multi-finger household tasks spanning 32% (dustpan) to 92% (unscrewing a bulb), 89.6% on gripper-based precise insertion, and whole-body pick success of 68.4% from a table, 45.7% from the floor, and 76.3% from a shelf <Cite id="gemini-robotics-2-2026" />. The 32% dustpan result remains a substantial task-level shortfall.

The sourced numbers are the Rudin wall-clock figures (under four minutes and twenty minutes), the Gemini Robotics 2 success rates, and the Play2Perfect clearance result. The tolerance values (20 mm absorbable gait error versus 0.5 mm insertion clearance) are representative physical scales, consistent with the cited systems. This figure is a schematic comparison.

In its fourth revision, 4,186 generated 30-second closed-loop rollouts yield eight policy-level aggregate scores compared with the 26 February 2026 RoboArena leaderboard: Pearson r = 0.989 and Spearman rho = 0.970, with p < 0.001 reported for both. GPT-4o scores task progress from 0 to 5, using fixed external views for success and the wrist view only to identify world-model errors. The eight aggregates are the correlation points; 4,186 rollouts are neither independent points nor a per-task correlation. RoboWorld combines an autoregressive video world model with a task-progress-aware VLM scorer. Step Forcing trains on self-forwarded denoising priors while retaining data-grounded anchor contexts; four-step denoising and contextual KV caching support fast inference. In its fourth revision, 4,186 generated 30-second closed-loop rollouts yield eight policy-level aggregate scores compared with the 26 February 2026 RoboArena leaderboard: Pearson r = 0.989 and Spearman rho = 0.970, with p < 0.001 reported for both. GPT-4o scores task progress from 0 to 5, using fixed external views for success and the wrist view only to identify world-model errors. The eight aggregates are the correlation points; 4,186 rollouts are neither independent points nor a per-task correlation. The result is also not calibrated success probability or absolute agreement: the paper reports contact-induced object artifacts and VLM scores about one point above human scores in approximately 100 sampled rollouts. Its separate 256-trajectory held-out open-loop video test does not establish an independent tuning/test split for the headline closed-loop correlation <Cite id="roboworld-2026" />.

In February 2026 Runway reported a similar ranking test for its GWM-Robotics world model: across eight vision-language-action policies from RoboArena, with 1,450 simulated rollouts scored by human graders, the policies' simulated and real progress scores had a Pearson correlation of 0.95 <Cite id="runway-gwm-robotics-eval-2026" />. Runway says the study tests policy ranking only and does not predict absolute success rates <Cite id="runway-gwm-robotics-eval-2026" />. In September 2026 it announced Praxis-1, a world action model built on the video pretraining behind its general world models, which it is testing with partners before an open-weight release <Cite id="runway-praxis-1-2026" />.
